Consider the matrix [latex] A [/latex] below: [latex] A = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\
0 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\
0 & 0 & \alpha & \beta \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \gamma
\end{bmatrix} [/latex] For which of the following combinations of [latex] \alpha, \beta, \gamma [/latex], is the rank of [latex] A [/latex] at least three? (i) [latex] \alpha = 0 [/latex] and [latex] \beta = \gamma \ne 0 [/latex] (ii) [latex] \alpha = \beta = \gamma = 0 [/latex] (iii) [latex] \beta = \gamma = 0 [/latex] and [latex] \alpha \ne 0 [/latex] (iv) [latex] \alpha = \beta = \gamma \ne 0 [/latex]
2025.html:
Consider the matrix [latex] A [/latex] below:

[latex] A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 0 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & \alpha & \beta \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \gamma \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

For which of the following combinations of [latex] \alpha, \beta, \gamma [/latex], is the rank of [latex] A [/latex] at least three?

(i) [latex] \alpha = 0 [/latex] and [latex] \beta = \gamma \ne 0 [/latex]
(ii) [latex] \alpha = \beta = \gamma = 0 [/latex]
(iii) [latex] \beta = \gamma = 0 [/latex] and [latex] \alpha \ne 0 [/latex]
(iv) [latex] \alpha = \beta = \gamma \ne 0 [/latex]
2025.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
2025.explanation_text:
We are given an upper triangular matrix: [latex] A = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\
0 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\
0 & 0 & \alpha & \beta \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \gamma
\end{bmatrix} [/latex] The rank of a matrix is the number of non-zero rows in its row echelon form. For an upper triangular matrix, each non-zero pivot (i.e., leading diagonal entry) contributes to the rank. Let's analyze each case: (i) [latex] \alpha = 0 [/latex], [latex] \beta = \gamma \ne 0 [/latex] Row 3 becomes [latex] [0\ 0\ 0\ \beta] [/latex] and row 4 is [latex] [0\ 0\ 0\ \gamma] [/latex], but [latex] \beta = \gamma \ne 0 [/latex]. Since row 3 still has a non-zero entry (in column 4), and so does row 4, we still have all 4 non-zero rows. Hence, rank = 4 [latex] \geq 3 [/latex]. Valid (ii) [latex] \alpha = \beta = \gamma = 0 [/latex] Then rows 3 and 4 become all zero. Only rows 1 and 2 remain non-zero. So, rank = 2 [latex] < 3 [/latex]. Not valid (iii) [latex] \beta = \gamma = 0 [/latex], [latex] \alpha \ne 0 [/latex] Row 3 is [latex] [0\ 0\ \alpha\ 0] [/latex], which is non-zero, and row 4 is zero. So we have 3 non-zero rows. Rank = 3  Valid (iv) [latex] \alpha = \beta = \gamma \ne 0 [/latex] Then all rows are non-zero. Rank = 4 [latex] \geq 3 [/latex] Valid
2025.explanation_html:
We are given an upper triangular matrix:

[latex] A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 0 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & \alpha & \beta \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \gamma \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

The rank of a matrix is the number of non-zero rows in its row echelon form. For an upper triangular matrix, each non-zero pivot (i.e., leading diagonal entry) contributes to the rank.

Let's analyze each case:

(i) [latex] \alpha = 0 [/latex], [latex] \beta = \gamma \ne 0 [/latex]
Row 3 becomes [latex] [0\ 0\ 0\ \beta] [/latex] and row 4 is [latex] [0\ 0\ 0\ \gamma] [/latex], but [latex] \beta = \gamma \ne 0 [/latex]. Since row 3 still has a non-zero entry (in column 4), and so does row 4, we still have all 4 non-zero rows. Hence, rank = 4 [latex] \geq 3 [/latex]. Valid

(ii) [latex] \alpha = \beta = \gamma = 0 [/latex]
Then rows 3 and 4 become all zero. Only rows 1 and 2 remain non-zero. So, rank = 2 [latex] < 3 [/latex]. Not valid

(iii) [latex] \beta = \gamma = 0 [/latex], [latex] \alpha \ne 0 [/latex]
Row 3 is [latex] [0\ 0\ \alpha\ 0] [/latex], which is non-zero, and row 4 is zero. So we have 3 non-zero rows. Rank = 3 Valid

(iv) [latex] \alpha = \beta = \gamma \ne 0 [/latex]
Then all rows are non-zero. Rank = 4 [latex] \geq 3 [/latex] Valid

2025.text: Consider the following series: (i) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} [/latex] (ii) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n(n+1)} [/latex] (iii) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n!} [/latex] Choose the correct option.
2025.html:
Consider the following series:

(i) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} [/latex]

(ii) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n(n+1)} [/latex]

(iii) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n!} [/latex]

Choose the correct option.
2025.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Variables
2025.explanation_text:
(i) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} [/latex] This is a p-series with [latex] p = \frac{1}{2} < 1 [/latex].
A p-series [latex] \sum \frac{1}{n^p} [/latex] converges only if [latex] p > 1 [/latex].
So this series diverges. (ii) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n(n+1)} [/latex] We use partial fractions: [latex] \frac{1}{n(n+1)} = \frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1} [/latex] So it becomes a telescoping series:
[latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1} \right) = 1 + \left( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \right) + \left( \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \right) + \cdots [/latex] All terms cancel except the first one, so the sum is finite.
This series converges. (iii) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n!} [/latex] This is a standard exponential series (part of [latex] e^x [/latex] expansion).
Since [latex] n! [/latex] grows faster than any exponential or polynomial, this series converges absolutely.
2025.explanation_html:
(i) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} [/latex]
This is a p-series with [latex] p = \frac{1}{2} < 1 [/latex]. A p-series [latex] \sum \frac{1}{n^p} [/latex] converges only if [latex] p > 1 [/latex]. So this series diverges.

(ii) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n(n+1)} [/latex]
We use partial fractions:
[latex] \frac{1}{n(n+1)} = \frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1} [/latex]
So it becomes a telescoping series: [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1} \right) = 1 + \left( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \right) + \left( \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \right) + \cdots [/latex]
All terms cancel except the first one, so the sum is finite. This series converges.

(iii) [latex] \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n!} [/latex]
This is a standard exponential series (part of [latex] e^x [/latex] expansion). Since [latex] n! [/latex] grows faster than any exponential or polynomial, this series converges absolutely.

2025.text: A pot contains two red balls and two blue balls. Two balls are drawn from this pot randomly without replacement. What is the probability that the two balls drawn have different colours?
2025.html:
A pot contains two red balls and two blue balls. Two balls are drawn from this pot randomly without replacement.
What is the probability that the two balls drawn have different colours?
2025.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
2025.explanation_text:
Total balls = 2 red + 2 blue = 4 balls We draw 2 balls without replacement. Total number of ways to choose 2 balls from 4:
[latex] \binom{4}{2} = 6 [/latex] Now, we count the favorable outcomes where the two balls have different colours: Choose 1 red and 1 blue:
[latex] \binom{2}{1} \times \binom{2}{1} = 2 \times 2 = 4 [/latex] ways So the probability is:
[latex] \frac{\text{Favorable outcomes}}{\text{Total outcomes}} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3} [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Total balls = 2 red + 2 blue = 4 balls
We draw 2 balls without replacement. Total number of ways to choose 2 balls from 4: [latex] \binom{4}{2} = 6 [/latex]

Now, we count the favorable outcomes where the two balls have different colours:
Choose 1 red and 1 blue: [latex] \binom{2}{1} \times \binom{2}{1} = 2 \times 2 = 4 [/latex] ways

So the probability is: [latex] \frac{\text{Favorable outcomes}}{\text{Total outcomes}} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3} [/latex]

2025.text: Consider a frequency-modulated (FM) signal [latex] f(t) = A_c \cos\left(2\pi f_c t + 3\sin(2\pi f_1 t) + 4\sin(6\pi f_1 t)\right) [/latex], where [latex] A_c [/latex] and [latex] f_c [/latex] are, respectively, the amplitude and frequency (in Hz) of the carrier waveform. The frequency [latex] f_1 [/latex] is in Hz, and assume that [latex] f_c > 100f_1 [/latex]. The peak frequency deviation of the FM signal in Hz is _______.
2025.html:
Consider a frequency-modulated (FM) signal

[latex] f(t) = A_c \cos\left(2\pi f_c t + 3\sin(2\pi f_1 t) + 4\sin(6\pi f_1 t)\right) [/latex],

where [latex] A_c [/latex] and [latex] f_c [/latex] are, respectively, the amplitude and frequency (in Hz) of the carrier waveform. The frequency [latex] f_1 [/latex] is in Hz, and assume that [latex] f_c > 100f_1 [/latex].

The peak frequency deviation of the FM signal in Hz is _______.
2025.subject: Communication Systems - Analog Communication Systems
2025.explanation_text:
The general form of an FM signal is:
[latex] f(t) = A_c \cos\left(2\pi f_c t + \phi(t)\right) [/latex], where [latex] \phi(t) [/latex] is the instantaneous phase deviation. Here,
[latex] \phi(t) = 3\sin(2\pi f_1 t) + 4\sin(6\pi f_1 t) [/latex] To find instantaneous frequency deviation, we take the derivative of [latex] \phi(t) [/latex]: [latex] \frac{d\phi(t)}{dt} = 3 \cdot 2\pi f_1 \cos(2\pi f_1 t) + 4 \cdot 6\pi f_1 \cos(6\pi f_1 t) [/latex] [latex] = 6\pi f_1 \cos(2\pi f_1 t) + 24\pi f_1 \cos(6\pi f_1 t) [/latex] So, instantaneous frequency deviation: [latex] \Delta f(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \frac{d\phi(t)}{dt} = 3f_1 \cos(2\pi f_1 t) + 12f_1 \cos(6\pi f_1 t) [/latex] Peak frequency deviation is the maximum absolute value of [latex] \Delta f(t) [/latex]: [latex] \Delta f_{\text{peak}} = \max|\Delta f(t)| = 3f_1 + 12f_1 = 15f_1 [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
The general form of an FM signal is: [latex] f(t) = A_c \cos\left(2\pi f_c t + \phi(t)\right) [/latex],
where [latex] \phi(t) [/latex] is the instantaneous phase deviation.

Here, [latex] \phi(t) = 3\sin(2\pi f_1 t) + 4\sin(6\pi f_1 t) [/latex]

To find instantaneous frequency deviation, we take the derivative of [latex] \phi(t) [/latex]:

[latex] \frac{d\phi(t)}{dt} = 3 \cdot 2\pi f_1 \cos(2\pi f_1 t) + 4 \cdot 6\pi f_1 \cos(6\pi f_1 t) [/latex]
[latex] = 6\pi f_1 \cos(2\pi f_1 t) + 24\pi f_1 \cos(6\pi f_1 t) [/latex]

So, instantaneous frequency deviation:
[latex] \Delta f(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \frac{d\phi(t)}{dt} = 3f_1 \cos(2\pi f_1 t) + 12f_1 \cos(6\pi f_1 t) [/latex]

Peak frequency deviation is the maximum absolute value of [latex] \Delta f(t) [/latex]:
[latex] \Delta f_{\text{peak}} = \max|\Delta f(t)| = 3f_1 + 12f_1 = 15f_1 [/latex]

2025.text: Consider an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel with bandwidth [latex] W [/latex] and noise power spectral density [latex] \frac{N_0}{2} [/latex]. Let [latex] P_{\text{av}} [/latex] denote the average transmit power constraint. Which one of the following plots illustrates the dependence of the channel capacity [latex] C [/latex] on the bandwidth [latex] W [/latex] (keeping [latex] P_{\text{av}} [/latex] and [latex] N_0 [/latex] fixed)?
2025.html:
Consider an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel with bandwidth [latex] W [/latex] and noise power spectral density [latex] \frac{N_0}{2} [/latex]. Let [latex] P_{\text{av}} [/latex] denote the average transmit power constraint.

Which one of the following plots illustrates the dependence of the channel capacity [latex] C [/latex] on the bandwidth [latex] W [/latex] (keeping [latex] P_{\text{av}} [/latex] and [latex] N_0 [/latex] fixed)?
2025.subject: Communication Systems - Random Signals and Noise
2025.explanation_text:
For an AWGN channel, the channel capacity is given by the Shannon?Hartley theorem:[latex] C = W \log_2\left(1 + \frac{P_{\text{av}}}{W N_0}\right) \ \text{bits/sec} [/latex] Let?s analyze this expression:[latex] W [/latex] is in both the linear multiplier and inside the denominator of the SNR. As [latex] W \rightarrow 0 [/latex], capacity [latex] C \rightarrow 0 [/latex] because bandwidth is 0. As [latex] W \rightarrow \infty [/latex], [latex] \frac{P_{\text{av}}}{W N_0} \rightarrow 0 [/latex], and we can use [latex] \log_2(1 + x) \approx x/\ln 2 [/latex] when [latex] x \ll 1 [/latex]. So,
[latex] C \approx W \cdot \frac{P_{\text{av}}}{W N_0 \ln 2} = \frac{P_{\text{av}}}{N_0 \ln 2} [/latex] That is, capacity approaches a finite limit. Conclusion: Capacity increases with [latex] W [/latex], but saturates to a constant as [latex] W [/latex] becomes large. This corresponds to a concave increasing curve that flattens out, which matches Plot (A).
2025.explanation_html:
For an AWGN channel, the channel capacity is given by the Shannon?Hartley theorem:[latex] C = W \log_2\left(1 + \frac{P_{\text{av}}}{W N_0}\right) \ \text{bits/sec} [/latex]

Let?s analyze this expression:[latex] W [/latex] is in both the linear multiplier and inside the denominator of the SNR.

As [latex] W \rightarrow 0 [/latex], capacity [latex] C \rightarrow 0 [/latex] because bandwidth is 0.

As [latex] W \rightarrow \infty [/latex], [latex] \frac{P_{\text{av}}}{W N_0} \rightarrow 0 [/latex], and we can use [latex] \log_2(1 + x) \approx x/\ln 2 [/latex] when [latex] x \ll 1 [/latex].

So, [latex] C \approx W \cdot \frac{P_{\text{av}}}{W N_0 \ln 2} = \frac{P_{\text{av}}}{N_0 \ln 2} [/latex]
That is, capacity approaches a finite limit.

Conclusion:
Capacity increases with [latex] W [/latex], but saturates to a constant as [latex] W [/latex] becomes large.
This corresponds to a concave increasing curve that flattens out, which matches Plot (A).

2025.text: Consider a continuous-time, real-valued signal [latex]f(t)[/latex] whose Fourier transform [latex]F(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \exp (-j \omega t) d t[/latex] exists. Which one of the following statements is always TRUE?
2025.html:
Consider a continuous-time, real-valued signal [latex]f(t)[/latex] whose Fourier transform [latex]F(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \exp (-j \omega t) d t[/latex] exists.

Which one of the following statements is always TRUE?
2025.subject: Signals and Systems - Fourier Transforms, Frequency Response and Correlation
2025.explanation_text: We are given that [latex] F(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) e^{-j\omega t} dt [/latex] exists. This means that [latex] f(t) [/latex] is absolutely integrable, i.e., [latex] \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(t)| dt < \infty [/latex]. To find a general bound on [latex] |F(\omega)| [/latex], we apply the triangle inequality for integrals: [latex] |F(\omega)| = \left| \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) e^{-j\omega t} dt \right| \le \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(t) e^{-j\omega t}| dt = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(t)| dt [/latex] This inequality is always true. Now check the options: (A) [latex] |F(\omega)| \le \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(t)| dt [/latex] -- Correct (B) Strict inequality -- not always true (C) Inequality involving [latex] \int f(t) dt [/latex] -- this can be 0 for symmetric signals (e.g., odd functions), but [latex] |F(\omega)| [/latex] may be nonzero (D) Similar issue -- not always true
2025.explanation_html:
We are given that [latex] F(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) e^{-j\omega t} dt [/latex] exists.
This means that [latex] f(t) [/latex] is absolutely integrable, i.e., [latex] \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(t)| dt < \infty [/latex].

To find a general bound on [latex] |F(\omega)| [/latex], we apply the triangle inequality for integrals:
[latex] |F(\omega)| = \left| \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) e^{-j\omega t} dt \right| \le \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(t) e^{-j\omega t}| dt = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(t)| dt [/latex]

This inequality is always true.

Now check the options:
(A) [latex] |F(\omega)| \le \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(t)| dt [/latex] -- Correct
(B) Strict inequality -- not always true
(C) Inequality involving [latex] \int f(t) dt [/latex] -- this can be 0 for symmetric signals (e.g., odd functions), but [latex] |F(\omega)| [/latex] may be nonzero
(D) Similar issue -- not always true

2025.subject: Control Systems - Root Locus
2025.explanation_text: We are given the root locus plot in Figure (ii), and we are to determine whether a closed-loop pole lies at the complex location [latex] -1 + j1 [/latex] for any [latex] K \geq 0 [/latex]. From control theory, the root locus shows the trajectory of the closed-loop poles as [latex] K [/latex] varies from [latex] 0 [/latex] to [latex] \infty [/latex]. We inspect the root locus diagram in Figure (ii): The root locus branches are symmetric about the real axis. The point [latex] -1 + j1 [/latex] lies outside the plotted root locus path. It is not marked or touched by any of the root locus branches. Hence, the closed-loop poles never pass through the point [latex] -1 + j1 [/latex] for any positive value of [latex] K [/latex].

2025.explanation_text:
(A) The DTFT does not always exist. It exists only if the signal is absolutely summable:
[latex] \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} |x[n]| < \infty [/latex]
So this statement is False. (B) The region of convergence (RoC) contains no poles, but it can include zeros (since zeros do not affect convergence).
So this statement is False. (C) This is True. The DTFT of [latex] x[n] [/latex] exists iff the RoC of [latex] X(z) [/latex] includes the unit circle [latex] |z| = 1 [/latex]. (D) For [latex] x[n] = \alpha \delta[n] [/latex], the [latex] z [/latex]-transform is [latex] X(z) = \alpha [/latex] (a constant), which is defined for all [latex] z \in \mathbb{C} [/latex]. Hence, the RoC is the entire z-plane, so this is True.

2025.text: Consider a message signal [latex]\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{t})[/latex] which is bandlimited to [latex][-\mathrm{W}, \mathrm{W}][/latex], where W is in Hz . Consider the following two modulation schemes for the message signal: Double sideband-suppressed carrier (DSB-SC): [latex]f_{D S B}(t)=A_{c} m(t) \cos \left(2 \pi f_{c} t\right)[/latex] Amplitude modulation (AM): [latex]f_{A M}(t)=A_{c}(1+\mu m(t)) \cos \left(2 \pi f_{c} t\right)[/latex] Here, [latex]A_{c}[/latex] and [latex]f_{c}[/latex] are the amplitude and frequency (in Hz ) of the carrier, respectively. In the case of AM, [latex]\mu[/latex] denotes the modulation index. Consider the following statements: (i) An envelope detector can be used for demodulation in the DSB-SC scheme if [latex]\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{t})>0[/latex] for all t . (ii) An envelope detector can be used for demodulation in the AM scheme only if [latex]\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{t})>0[/latex] for all t . Which of the following options is/are correct?
2025.html:
Consider a message signal [latex]\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{t})[/latex] which is bandlimited to [latex][-\mathrm{W}, \mathrm{W}][/latex], where W is in Hz . Consider the following two modulation schemes for the message signal:

Double sideband-suppressed carrier (DSB-SC):
[latex]f_{D S B}(t)=A_{c} m(t) \cos \left(2 \pi f_{c} t\right)[/latex]

Amplitude modulation (AM):
[latex]f_{A M}(t)=A_{c}(1+\mu m(t)) \cos \left(2 \pi f_{c} t\right)[/latex]

Here, [latex]A_{c}[/latex] and [latex]f_{c}[/latex] are the amplitude and frequency (in Hz ) of the carrier, respectively. In the case of AM, [latex]\mu[/latex] denotes the modulation index.

Consider the following statements:
(i) An envelope detector can be used for demodulation in the DSB-SC scheme if [latex]\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{t})>0[/latex] for all t .
(ii) An envelope detector can be used for demodulation in the AM scheme only if [latex]\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{t})>0[/latex] for all t .

Which of the following options is/are correct?
2025.subject: Communication Systems - Analog Communication Systems
2025.explanation_text:
Even if [latex] m(t) > 0 [/latex] for all [latex] t [/latex], the carrier is suppressed, and therefore envelope detection fails. So, Statement (i) is FALSE. Statement (ii):
In standard AM, the transmitted signal is: [latex] f_{AM}(t) = A_c (1 + \mu m(t)) \cos(2\pi f_c t) [/latex] To ensure proper envelope detection, the envelope [latex] A_c(1 + \mu m(t)) [/latex] must not cross zero, i.e., it must be always positive. So the condition is: [latex] 1 + \mu m(t) > 0 [/latex] for all [latex] t [/latex].
This means not just [latex] m(t) > 0 [/latex], but [latex] m(t) > -1/\mu [/latex]. So even if [latex] m(t) [/latex] is not strictly positive, envelope detection may still work depending on [latex] \mu [/latex]. Therefore, Statement (ii) is FALSE.
2025.explanation_html:
Even if [latex] m(t) > 0 [/latex] for all [latex] t [/latex], the carrier is suppressed, and therefore envelope detection fails.
So, Statement (i) is FALSE.

Statement (ii): In standard AM, the transmitted signal is:
[latex] f_{AM}(t) = A_c (1 + \mu m(t)) \cos(2\pi f_c t) [/latex]
To ensure proper envelope detection, the envelope [latex] A_c(1 + \mu m(t)) [/latex] must not cross zero, i.e., it must be always positive.
So the condition is: [latex] 1 + \mu m(t) > 0 [/latex] for all [latex] t [/latex]. This means not just [latex] m(t) > 0 [/latex], but [latex] m(t) > -1/\mu [/latex]. So even if [latex] m(t) [/latex] is not strictly positive, envelope detection may still work depending on [latex] \mu [/latex].
Therefore, Statement (ii) is FALSE.

2025.explanation_text:
For an ideal operational amplifier, the following properties are defined:Infinite input resistance

2025.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to ideal MOSFET-based DC-coupled single-stage amplifiers having finite load resistors?
2025.html: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to ideal MOSFET-based DC-coupled single-stage amplifiers having finite load resistors?
2025.subject: Analog Circuits - FET and MOSFET Analysis
2025.explanation_text: Let us consider each configuration in the context of ideal MOSFETs (i.e., no body effect, channel-length modulation ignored, etc.) and DC coupling: (A) The common-gate amplifier has an infinite input resistance False. In a common-gate amplifier, the input is applied to the source terminal and the gate is grounded (or biased). The input resistance is low, approximately [latex] \frac{1}{g_m} [/latex]. So, Statement (A) is FALSE. (B) The common-source amplifier has an infinite input resistance True. The input is applied at the gate terminal, which draws no current ideally. Hence, input resistance is infinite. So, Statement (B) is TRUE. (C) The input and output voltages of the common-source amplifier are in phase False. A common-source amplifier introduces a 180? phase shift, i.e., the input and output are out of phase. So, Statement (C) is FALSE. (D) The input and output voltages of the common-drain amplifier are in phase True. A common-drain amplifier (also called source follower) has no phase shift between input and output. So, Statement (D) is TRUE.
2025.explanation_html:
Let us consider each configuration in the context of ideal MOSFETs (i.e., no body effect, channel-length modulation ignored, etc.) and DC coupling:

(A) The common-gate amplifier has an infinite input resistance
False. In a common-gate amplifier, the input is applied to the source terminal and the gate is grounded (or biased).
The input resistance is low, approximately [latex] \frac{1}{g_m} [/latex].
So, Statement (A) is FALSE.

(B) The common-source amplifier has an infinite input resistance
True. The input is applied at the gate terminal, which draws no current ideally.
Hence, input resistance is infinite.
So, Statement (B) is TRUE.

(C) The input and output voltages of the common-source amplifier are in phase
False. A common-source amplifier introduces a 180? phase shift, i.e., the input and output are out of phase.
So, Statement (C) is FALSE.

(D) The input and output voltages of the common-drain amplifier are in phase
True. A common-drain amplifier (also called source follower) has no phase shift between input and output.
So, Statement (D) is TRUE.

2025.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
2025.explanation_text:
We are given a second-order linear homogeneous differential equation:
[latex] t^2 y''(t) - 2t y'(t) + 2y(t) = 0 [/latex] This is a Cauchy-Euler equation. Let us try a solution of the form:
[latex] y(t) = t^r [/latex] Then,
[latex] y'(t) = r t^{r-1},\quad y''(t) = r(r - 1) t^{r-2} [/latex] Substitute into the equation: [latex] t^2 \cdot r(r - 1)t^{r - 2} - 2t \cdot r t^{r - 1} + 2t^r = 0 [/latex] [latex] r(r - 1)t^r - 2r t^r + 2 t^r = 0 [/latex] [latex] \left[r(r - 1) - 2r + 2\right] t^r = 0 [/latex] Simplify the coefficient:
[latex] r^2 - r - 2r + 2 = r^2 - 3r + 2 [/latex] So the auxiliary equation is:
[latex] r^2 - 3r + 2 = 0 [/latex] [latex] (r - 1)(r - 2) = 0 [/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow r = 1, 2 [/latex] So the general solution is:
[latex] y(t) = A t^1 + B t^2 = At + Bt^2 [/latex] Now compute [latex] y'(t) = A + 2Bt [/latex] We are given:
[latex] y'(0) = A = 1 [/latex] [latex] y'(1) = A + 2B = -1 [/latex] From these:
From [latex] y'(0) = 1 \Rightarrow A = 1 [/latex] Then [latex] y'(1) = 1 + 2B = -1 \Rightarrow 2B = -2 \Rightarrow B = -1 [/latex] Thus, the function is:
[latex] y(t) = t - t^2 [/latex] Now find the maximum of [latex] y(t) = t - t^2 [/latex] in [latex] [0, 1] [/latex] This is a downward-opening parabola. Maximum occurs at vertex:
[latex] t = \frac{1}{2} [/latex] [latex] y\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2} - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{4} [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
We are given a second-order linear homogeneous differential equation: [latex] t^2 y''(t) - 2t y'(t) + 2y(t) = 0 [/latex]

This is a Cauchy-Euler equation. Let us try a solution of the form: [latex] y(t) = t^r [/latex]
Then, [latex] y'(t) = r t^{r-1},\quad y''(t) = r(r - 1) t^{r-2} [/latex]
Substitute into the equation:
[latex] t^2 \cdot r(r - 1)t^{r - 2} - 2t \cdot r t^{r - 1} + 2t^r = 0 [/latex]
[latex] r(r - 1)t^r - 2r t^r + 2 t^r = 0 [/latex]
[latex] \left[r(r - 1) - 2r + 2\right] t^r = 0 [/latex]
Simplify the coefficient: [latex] r^2 - r - 2r + 2 = r^2 - 3r + 2 [/latex]
So the auxiliary equation is: [latex] r^2 - 3r + 2 = 0 [/latex]
[latex] (r - 1)(r - 2) = 0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow r = 1, 2 [/latex]
So the general solution is: [latex] y(t) = A t^1 + B t^2 = At + Bt^2 [/latex]
Now compute [latex] y'(t) = A + 2Bt [/latex]
We are given: [latex] y'(0) = A = 1 [/latex]
[latex] y'(1) = A + 2B = -1 [/latex]
From these: From [latex] y'(0) = 1 \Rightarrow A = 1 [/latex]
Then [latex] y'(1) = 1 + 2B = -1 \Rightarrow 2B = -2 \Rightarrow B = -1 [/latex]
Thus, the function is: [latex] y(t) = t - t^2 [/latex]
Now find the maximum of [latex] y(t) = t - t^2 [/latex] in [latex] [0, 1] [/latex]
This is a downward-opening parabola. Maximum occurs at vertex: [latex] t = \frac{1}{2} [/latex]
[latex] y\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2} - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{4} [/latex]

Low-pass cutoff (upper -3dB): [latex] f_H = \frac{1}{2\pi R_{\text{LP}} C_{\text{LP}}} = \frac{1}{2\pi \cdot 2R \cdot 0.1C} = \frac{1}{0.4\pi RC} [/latex] Now plug in [latex] RC = \frac{1}{20\pi \cdot 10^6} [/latex] into this:

2025.text: Consider a continuous-time finite-energy signal [latex]f(t)[/latex] whose Fourier transform vanishes outside the frequency interval [latex]\left[-\omega_{c}, \omega_{c}\right][/latex], where [latex]\omega_{c}[/latex] is in rad/sec. The signal [latex]f(t)[/latex] is uniformly sampled to obtain [latex]y(t)=f(t) p(t)[/latex]. Here, [latex]p(t)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta\left(t-\tau-n T_{s}\right)[/latex], with [latex]\delta(\mathrm{t})[/latex] being the Dirac impulse, [latex]\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{s}}>0[/latex], and [latex]\tau>0[/latex]. The sampled signal [latex]\mathrm{y}(\mathrm{t})[/latex] is passed through an ideal lowpass filter [latex]h(t)=\omega_{c} T_{s} \frac{\sin \left(\omega_{c} t\right)}{\pi \omega_{c} t}[/latex] with cutoff frequency [latex]\omega_{c}[/latex] and passband gain [latex]T_{s}[/latex]. The output of the filter is given by __________ .
2025.html:
Consider a continuous-time finite-energy signal [latex]f(t)[/latex] whose Fourier transform vanishes outside the frequency interval [latex]\left[-\omega_{c}, \omega_{c}\right][/latex], where [latex]\omega_{c}[/latex] is in rad/sec.

The signal [latex]f(t)[/latex] is uniformly sampled to obtain [latex]y(t)=f(t) p(t)[/latex]. Here,

[latex]p(t)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta\left(t-\tau-n T_{s}\right)[/latex],

with [latex]\delta(\mathrm{t})[/latex] being the Dirac impulse, [latex]\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{s}}>0[/latex], and [latex]\tau>0[/latex]. The sampled signal [latex]\mathrm{y}(\mathrm{t})[/latex] is passed through an ideal lowpass filter [latex]h(t)=\omega_{c} T_{s} \frac{\sin \left(\omega_{c} t\right)}{\pi \omega_{c} t}[/latex] with cutoff frequency [latex]\omega_{c}[/latex] and passband gain [latex]T_{s}[/latex].

The output of the filter is given by __________ .
2025.subject: Signals and Systems - Sampling
2025.explanation_text:
We are given that [latex]f(t)[/latex] is bandlimited to [latex][-\omega_c, \omega_c][/latex], meaning its Fourier transform [latex]F(j\omega)[/latex] is zero outside this interval. Step 1: Sampling process
Sampling is done using the impulse train: [latex]
p(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t - \tau - nT_s)
[/latex] Multiplying this with [latex]f(t)[/latex] gives: [latex]
y(t) = f(t) \cdot p(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} f(\tau + nT_s) \cdot \delta(t - \tau - nT_s)
[/latex] This means we are taking samples of [latex]f(t)[/latex] at times [latex]t = \tau + nT_s[/latex]. Step 2: Filtering with ideal LPF The sampled signal [latex]y(t)[/latex] is passed through an ideal lowpass filter with impulse response: [latex]
h(t) = T_s \cdot \text{sinc}\left(\frac{\omega_c t}{\pi}\right)
[/latex] The output of the system is: [latex]
z(t) = y(t) * h(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} f(\tau + nT_s) \cdot h(t - \tau - nT_s)
[/latex] Substitute [latex]h(t)[/latex]: [latex]
z(t) = T_s \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} f(\tau + nT_s) \cdot \text{sinc}\left(\frac{\omega_c (t - \tau - nT_s)}{\pi}\right)
[/latex] This is the reconstruction formula for [latex]f(t)[/latex], but it appears to reconstruct [latex]f(t - \tau)[/latex] at first glance. Step 3: Time-invariance and interpretation Here's the key point:Even though the samples are taken at [latex]t = \tau + nT_s[/latex], the reconstruction system is linear and time-invariant. A shift in sampling time does not affect the shape of the reconstructed signal, because the sinc interpolation is symmetric and consistent. Hence, the filter effectively undoes the delay, and we recover the original signal [latex]f(t)[/latex]. Step 4: Condition for perfect reconstruction Perfect reconstruction using sinc interpolation is possible only if there is no aliasing, which happens when: [latex]
T_s < \dfrac{\pi}{\omega_c}
[/latex] This is the Nyquist condition for bandlimited signals.
2025.explanation_html:
We are given that [latex]f(t)[/latex] is bandlimited to [latex][-\omega_c, \omega_c][/latex], meaning its Fourier transform [latex]F(j\omega)[/latex] is zero outside this interval.

Step 1: Sampling process Sampling is done using the impulse train:
[latex] p(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t - \tau - nT_s) [/latex]
Multiplying this with [latex]f(t)[/latex] gives:
[latex] y(t) = f(t) \cdot p(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} f(\tau + nT_s) \cdot \delta(t - \tau - nT_s) [/latex]
This means we are taking samples of [latex]f(t)[/latex] at times [latex]t = \tau + nT_s[/latex].



Step 2: Filtering with ideal LPF
The sampled signal [latex]y(t)[/latex] is passed through an ideal lowpass filter with impulse response:

[latex] h(t) = T_s \cdot \text{sinc}\left(\frac{\omega_c t}{\pi}\right) [/latex]

The output of the system is:
[latex] z(t) = y(t) * h(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} f(\tau + nT_s) \cdot h(t - \tau - nT_s) [/latex]

Substitute [latex]h(t)[/latex]:
[latex] z(t) = T_s \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} f(\tau + nT_s) \cdot \text{sinc}\left(\frac{\omega_c (t - \tau - nT_s)}{\pi}\right) [/latex]
This is the reconstruction formula for [latex]f(t)[/latex], but it appears to reconstruct [latex]f(t - \tau)[/latex] at first glance.

Step 3: Time-invariance and interpretation
Here's the key point:Even though the samples are taken at [latex]t = \tau + nT_s[/latex], the reconstruction system is linear and time-invariant. A shift in sampling time does not affect the shape of the reconstructed signal, because the sinc interpolation is symmetric and consistent.
Hence, the filter effectively undoes the delay, and we recover the original signal [latex]f(t)[/latex].

Step 4: Condition for perfect reconstruction
Perfect reconstruction using sinc interpolation is possible only if there is no aliasing, which happens when:
[latex] T_s < \dfrac{\pi}{\omega_c} [/latex]
This is the Nyquist condition for bandlimited signals.

2025.text: A source transmits symbol [latex]S[/latex] that takes values uniformly at random from the set [latex]\{-2,0,2\}[/latex]. The receiver obtains [latex]Y=S+N[/latex], where [latex]N[/latex] is a zero-mean Gaussian random variable independent of [latex]S[/latex]. The receiver uses the maximum likelihood decoder to estimate the transmitted symbol [latex]S[/latex]. Suppose the probability of symbol estimation error [latex]\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{e}}[/latex] is expressed as follows: [latex]\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{e}}=\alpha \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{N}>1)[/latex], where [latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{N}>1)[/latex] denotes the probability that [latex]N[/latex] exceeds 1. What is the value of [latex]\alpha[/latex] ?
2025.html:
A source transmits symbol [latex]S[/latex] that takes values uniformly at random from the set [latex]\{-2,0,2\}[/latex]. The receiver obtains [latex]Y=S+N[/latex], where [latex]N[/latex] is a zero-mean Gaussian random variable independent of [latex]S[/latex]. The receiver uses the maximum likelihood decoder to estimate the transmitted symbol [latex]S[/latex].

Suppose the probability of symbol estimation error [latex]\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{e}}[/latex] is expressed as follows:

[latex]\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{e}}=\alpha \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{N}>1)[/latex],

where [latex]\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{N}>1)[/latex] denotes the probability that [latex]N[/latex] exceeds 1.

What is the value of [latex]\alpha[/latex] ?
2025.subject: Communication Systems - Random Signals and Noise
2025.explanation_text: Given: [latex]S \in {-2,\ 0,\ 2}[/latex] uniformly at random [latex]Y = S + N[/latex], where [latex]N \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \sigma^2)[/latex] ML decoder chooses the symbol closest to [latex]Y[/latex], so decision boundaries are at [latex]Y = -1[/latex] and [latex]Y = 1[/latex] Case 1: [latex]S = -2[/latex] [latex]Y = -2 + N[/latex] Error occurs when [latex]Y > -1 \Rightarrow N > 1[/latex] So, [latex]P_e|S = -2 = P(N > 1)[/latex] Case 2: [latex]S = 0[/latex] [latex]Y = N[/latex] Error occurs when [latex]|N| > 1[/latex] So, [latex]P_e|S = 0 = P(N < -1) + P(N > 1) = 2P(N > 1)[/latex] Case 3: [latex]S = 2[/latex] [latex]Y = 2 + N[/latex] Error occurs when [latex]Y < 1 \Rightarrow N < -1[/latex] So, [latex]P_e|S = 2 = P(N < -1) = P(N > 1)[/latex] Average probability of error: [latex]P_e = \frac{1}{3} \left(P(N > 1) + 2P(N > 1) + P(N > 1)\right)[/latex] [latex]P_e = \frac{4}{3} \cdot P(N > 1)[/latex] So, [latex]\alpha = \frac{4}{3}[/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Given: [latex]S \in {-2,\ 0,\ 2}[/latex] uniformly at random
[latex]Y = S + N[/latex], where [latex]N \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \sigma^2)[/latex]
ML decoder chooses the symbol closest to [latex]Y[/latex], so decision boundaries are at [latex]Y = -1[/latex] and [latex]Y = 1[/latex]

Case 1: [latex]S = -2[/latex]
[latex]Y = -2 + N[/latex]
Error occurs when [latex]Y > -1 \Rightarrow N > 1[/latex]
So, [latex]P_e|S = -2 = P(N > 1)[/latex]

Case 2: [latex]S = 0[/latex]
[latex]Y = N[/latex]
Error occurs when [latex]|N| > 1[/latex]
So, [latex]P_e|S = 0 = P(N < -1) + P(N > 1) = 2P(N > 1)[/latex]

Case 3: [latex]S = 2[/latex]
[latex]Y = 2 + N[/latex]
Error occurs when [latex]Y < 1 \Rightarrow N < -1[/latex]
So, [latex]P_e|S = 2 = P(N < -1) = P(N > 1)[/latex]

Average probability of error:
[latex]P_e = \frac{1}{3} \left(P(N > 1) + 2P(N > 1) + P(N > 1)\right)[/latex]
[latex]P_e = \frac{4}{3} \cdot P(N > 1)[/latex]
So, [latex]\alpha = \frac{4}{3}[/latex]

2025.text: Consider a real-valued random process [latex]\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{t})=\sum_{\mathrm{n}=1}^{\mathrm{N}} \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{p}(\mathrm{t}-\mathrm{nT})[/latex], where [latex]\mathrm{T}>0[/latex] and N is a positive integer. Here, [latex]p(t)=1[/latex] for [latex]t \in[0,0.5 T][/latex] and 0 otherwise. The coefficients [latex]\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{n}}[/latex] are pairwise independent, zero-mean unit-variance random variables. Read the following statements about the random process and choose the correct option. (i) The mean of the process [latex]f(t)[/latex] is independent of time t . (ii) The autocorrelation function [latex]\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{t}) \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{t}+\tau)][/latex] is independent of time t for all [latex]\tau[/latex]. (Here, [latex]\mathrm{E}[\cdot][/latex] is the expectation operation.)
2025.html:
Consider a real-valued random process

[latex]\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{t})=\sum_{\mathrm{n}=1}^{\mathrm{N}} \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{p}(\mathrm{t}-\mathrm{nT})[/latex],

where [latex]\mathrm{T}>0[/latex] and N is a positive integer. Here, [latex]p(t)=1[/latex] for [latex]t \in[0,0.5 T][/latex] and 0 otherwise. The coefficients [latex]\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{n}}[/latex] are pairwise independent, zero-mean unit-variance random variables.

Read the following statements about the random process and choose the correct option.

(i) The mean of the process [latex]f(t)[/latex] is independent of time t .
(ii) The autocorrelation function [latex]\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{t}) \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{t}+\tau)][/latex] is independent of time t for all [latex]\tau[/latex].

(Here, [latex]\mathrm{E}[\cdot][/latex] is the expectation operation.)
2025.subject: Communication Systems - Random Signals and Noise
2025.explanation_text: We are given: [latex]f(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} a_n , p(t - nT)[/latex] [latex]a_n[/latex]: zero-mean, unit-variance, pairwise independent [latex]p(t) = 1[/latex] for [latex]t \in [0,\ 0.5T][/latex], and 0 otherwise (i) Mean of [latex]f(t)[/latex]:We use linearity of expectation: [latex]E[f(t)] = \sum_{n=1}^{N} E[a_n] \cdot p(t - nT)[/latex] But [latex]E[a_n] = 0[/latex] for all [latex]n[/latex], so: [latex]E[f(t)] = 0[/latex] for all [latex]t[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex]   Mean is zero and time-independent So, (i) is TRUE (ii) Autocorrelation function [latex]R_f(t, \tau) = E[f(t)f(t + \tau)][/latex]: Expand: [latex]f(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} a_n p(t - nT)[/latex] [latex]f(t + \tau) = \sum_{m=1}^{N} a_m p(t + \tau - mT)[/latex] So: [latex]E[f(t)f(t + \tau)] = E\left[ \sum_{n=1}^{N} \sum_{m=1}^{N} a_n a_m , p(t - nT) p(t + \tau - mT) \right][/latex] Since [latex]a_n[/latex] are zero-mean and pairwise independent: [latex]E[a_n a_m] = 0[/latex] for [latex]n \neq m[/latex], and [latex]E[a_n^2] = 1[/latex] So only diagonal terms survive: [latex]E[f(t)f(t + \tau)] = \sum_{n=1}^{N} p(t - nT) \cdot p(t + \tau - nT)[/latex] Note: [latex]p(t - nT) \cdot p(t + \tau - nT)[/latex] depends on [latex]t[/latex] and [latex]\tau[/latex], so the sum depends on [latex]t[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Autocorrelation is not time-invariant So, (ii) is FALSE
2025.explanation_html:
We are given:
[latex]f(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} a_n , p(t - nT)[/latex]
[latex]a_n[/latex]: zero-mean, unit-variance, pairwise independent
[latex]p(t) = 1[/latex] for [latex]t \in [0,\ 0.5T][/latex], and 0 otherwise

(i) Mean of [latex]f(t)[/latex]:We use linearity of expectation:
[latex]E[f(t)] = \sum_{n=1}^{N} E[a_n] \cdot p(t - nT)[/latex]
But [latex]E[a_n] = 0[/latex] for all [latex]n[/latex], so:
[latex]E[f(t)] = 0[/latex] for all [latex]t[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Mean is zero and time-independent
So, (i) is TRUE

(ii) Autocorrelation function [latex]R_f(t, \tau) = E[f(t)f(t + \tau)][/latex]:
Expand:
[latex]f(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} a_n p(t - nT)[/latex]
[latex]f(t + \tau) = \sum_{m=1}^{N} a_m p(t + \tau - mT)[/latex]
So:
[latex]E[f(t)f(t + \tau)] = E\left[ \sum_{n=1}^{N} \sum_{m=1}^{N} a_n a_m , p(t - nT) p(t + \tau - mT) \right][/latex]
Since [latex]a_n[/latex] are zero-mean and pairwise independent:
[latex]E[a_n a_m] = 0[/latex] for [latex]n \neq m[/latex], and [latex]E[a_n^2] = 1[/latex]
So only diagonal terms survive:
[latex]E[f(t)f(t + \tau)] = \sum_{n=1}^{N} p(t - nT) \cdot p(t + \tau - nT)[/latex]
Note: [latex]p(t - nT) \cdot p(t + \tau - nT)[/latex] depends on [latex]t[/latex] and [latex]\tau[/latex], so the sum depends on [latex]t[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Autocorrelation is not time-invariant
So, (ii) is FALSE

options.html: (i) is TRUE and (ii) is FALSE
(i) is FALSE and (ii) is TRUE

DC analysis (ac input voltages are considered zero)



[latex]\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{D} 1}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{D} 2}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~mA}}{2}=1 \mathrm{~mA}[/latex]
[latex]\mathrm{V}_{3(\mathrm{DC})}=5-1 \mathrm{~m}(1 \mathrm{k})=4 \mathrm{~V}[/latex]

The intrinsic carrier concentration of a semiconductor is [latex]2.5 \times 10^{16} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex] at 300 K.

(Charge of an electron [latex]\mathrm{e}=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}[/latex].)
2025.subject: Electronic Devices - Basic Semiconductor Physics
2025.explanation_text: We are given: [latex]n_i = 2.5 \times 10^{16}\ \text{m}^{-3}[/latex] [latex]\mu_n = 0.15\ \text{m}^2/\text{V?s}[/latex] [latex]\mu_p = 0.05\ \text{m}^2/\text{V?s}[/latex] [latex]e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}[/latex] The intrinsic conductivity is given by: [latex]\sigma = e \cdot n_i \cdot (\mu_n + \mu_p)[/latex] Substitute values: [latex]\sigma = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \cdot 2.5 \times 10^{16} \cdot (0.15 + 0.05)[/latex] [latex]\sigma = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \cdot 2.5 \times 10^{16} \cdot 0.20[/latex] First calculate: [latex]1.6 \times 2.5 = 4.0[/latex] [latex]4.0 \times 0.20 = 0.8[/latex] So: [latex]\sigma = 0.8 \times 10^{-3} = 8 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{S/m}[/latex] Then resistivity is: [latex]\rho = \frac{1}{\sigma} = \frac{1}{8 \times 10^{-4}} = 1250\ \Omega \cdot \text{m} = 1.25\ \text{k}\Omega \cdot \text{m}[/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
We are given:
[latex]n_i = 2.5 \times 10^{16}\ \text{m}^{-3}[/latex]
[latex]\mu_n = 0.15\ \text{m}^2/\text{V?s}[/latex]
[latex]\mu_p = 0.05\ \text{m}^2/\text{V?s}[/latex]
[latex]e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}[/latex]
The intrinsic conductivity is given by:
[latex]\sigma = e \cdot n_i \cdot (\mu_n + \mu_p)[/latex]
Substitute values:
[latex]\sigma = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \cdot 2.5 \times 10^{16} \cdot (0.15 + 0.05)[/latex]
[latex]\sigma = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \cdot 2.5 \times 10^{16} \cdot 0.20[/latex]
First calculate:
[latex]1.6 \times 2.5 = 4.0[/latex]
[latex]4.0 \times 0.20 = 0.8[/latex]
So:
[latex]\sigma = 0.8 \times 10^{-3} = 8 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{S/m}[/latex]
Then resistivity is:
[latex]\rho = \frac{1}{\sigma} = \frac{1}{8 \times 10^{-4}} = 1250\ \Omega \cdot \text{m} = 1.25\ \text{k}\Omega \cdot \text{m}[/latex]

2025.text: Which of the following statements involving contour integrals (evaluated counter-clockwise) on the unit circle C in the complex plane is/are TRUE?
2025.html: Which of the following statements involving contour integrals (evaluated counter-clockwise) on the unit circle C in the complex plane is/are TRUE?
2025.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Variables
2025.explanation_text: Let [latex]f(z)=e^{z}[/latex] Then the function [latex]f(z)[/latex] is every where analytic [latex]\Rightarrow f(z)[/latex] is analytic at every inside and on the given region [latex]|z|=1[/latex] (or) unit circle. [latex]\therefore[/latex] By a Cauchy's theorem, we have [latex]\oint_{C} f(z)=0[/latex] Let [latex]\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{z})=\mathrm{z}^{\mathrm{n}}[/latex], where ' n ' is an even integers Then [latex]f(z)= \begin{cases}z^{n}, & n > 0 \\ \frac{1}{z^{n}}, & n < 0\end{cases}[/latex] for [latex]\mathrm{n}>0, \mathrm{I}_{1}=\oint_{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{z}^{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{dz}=0[/latex] [latex]\therefore\left(f(z)=z^{n}\right.[/latex] is analytic every point inside and on a given region [latex]|z|=1[/latex] ). for [latex]\mathrm{n}<0, \mathrm{I}_{2}=\oint_{\mathrm{C}} \frac{1}{\mathrm{z}^{\mathrm{n}}} \mathrm{dz}[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{2}=\oint_{\mathrm{C}} \frac{1}{(\mathrm{z}-0)^{\mathrm{n}}} \mathrm{dz} \quad\left(\because \int_{\mathrm{C}} \frac{\phi(\mathrm{z})}{\left[\overline{\mathrm{z}}-\mathrm{z}_{0}\right]^{\mathrm{n}}} \mathrm{dz}=\oint_{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{z}) \mathrm{dz}\right)[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{2}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{i}}{(\mathrm{n}-1)!} \frac{\mathrm{d}^{\mathrm{n}-1}}{\mathrm{dz}^{\mathrm{n}-1}}(1)[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{2}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{i}}{(\mathrm{n}-1)!}(0)=0[/latex] Let [latex]\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{z})=\cos (\mathrm{z})[/latex] Then [latex]f(z)[/latex] is every where analytic [latex]\Rightarrow f(z)[/latex] is analytic at every point inside and on the given region [latex]|z|=1[/latex]. [latex]\therefore[/latex] By a Cauchy's theorem, we have [latex]\oint_{C} f(z) d z=0[/latex] Let [latex]f(z)=\sec (z)[/latex] Then [latex]f(z)=\frac{1}{\cos (z)}[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] The singular points of [latex]f(z)[/latex] are given by [latex]\cos (\mathrm{z})=0[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{z}=(2 \mathrm{n}+1) \frac{\pi}{2}, \mathrm{n} \in \mathrm{I}[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow z= \pm \frac{\pi}{2}, \pm \frac{3 \pi}{2},--[/latex] are singular points But all the singular points lie outside the given region [latex]|z|=1[/latex] By a Cauchy's Theorem we have [latex]\oint_{C} f(z) d z=0[/latex] Hence, options A and B are TRUE.
2025.explanation_html:
Let [latex]f(z)=e^{z}[/latex]
Then the function [latex]f(z)[/latex] is every where analytic [latex]\Rightarrow f(z)[/latex] is analytic at every inside and on the given region [latex]|z|=1[/latex] (or) unit circle.
[latex]\therefore[/latex] By a Cauchy's theorem, we have [latex]\oint_{C} f(z)=0[/latex]

Let [latex]\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{z})=\mathrm{z}^{\mathrm{n}}[/latex], where ' n ' is an even integers
Then [latex]f(z)= \begin{cases}z^{n}, & n > 0 \\ \frac{1}{z^{n}}, & n < 0\end{cases}[/latex]
for [latex]\mathrm{n}>0, \mathrm{I}_{1}=\oint_{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{z}^{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{dz}=0[/latex]
[latex]\therefore\left(f(z)=z^{n}\right.[/latex] is analytic every point inside and on a given region [latex]|z|=1[/latex] ).
for [latex]\mathrm{n}<0, \mathrm{I}_{2}=\oint_{\mathrm{C}} \frac{1}{\mathrm{z}^{\mathrm{n}}} \mathrm{dz}[/latex]

[latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{2}=\oint_{\mathrm{C}} \frac{1}{(\mathrm{z}-0)^{\mathrm{n}}} \mathrm{dz} \quad\left(\because \int_{\mathrm{C}} \frac{\phi(\mathrm{z})}{\left[\overline{\mathrm{z}}-\mathrm{z}_{0}\right]^{\mathrm{n}}} \mathrm{dz}=\oint_{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{z}) \mathrm{dz}\right)[/latex]

[latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{2}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{i}}{(\mathrm{n}-1)!} \frac{\mathrm{d}^{\mathrm{n}-1}}{\mathrm{dz}^{\mathrm{n}-1}}(1)[/latex]

[latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{2}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{i}}{(\mathrm{n}-1)!}(0)=0[/latex]

Let [latex]\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{z})=\cos (\mathrm{z})[/latex]
Then [latex]f(z)[/latex] is every where analytic
[latex]\Rightarrow f(z)[/latex] is analytic at every point inside and on the given region [latex]|z|=1[/latex].
[latex]\therefore[/latex] By a Cauchy's theorem, we have [latex]\oint_{C} f(z) d z=0[/latex]

Let [latex]f(z)=\sec (z)[/latex]
Then [latex]f(z)=\frac{1}{\cos (z)}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] The singular points of [latex]f(z)[/latex] are given by [latex]\cos (\mathrm{z})=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \mathrm{z}=(2 \mathrm{n}+1) \frac{\pi}{2}, \mathrm{n} \in \mathrm{I}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow z= \pm \frac{\pi}{2}, \pm \frac{3 \pi}{2},--[/latex] are singular points
But all the singular points lie outside the given region [latex]|z|=1[/latex]

By a Cauchy's Theorem we have
[latex]\oint_{C} f(z) d z=0[/latex]
Hence, options A and B are TRUE.

2025.text: Let [latex]f(t)[/latex] be a periodic signal with fundamental period [latex]\mathrm{T}_{0}>0[/latex]. Consider the signal [latex]\mathrm{y}(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{f}(\alpha \mathrm{t})[/latex], where [latex]\alpha>1[/latex]. The Fourier series expansions of [latex]f(t)[/latex] and [latex]y(t)[/latex] are given by [latex]f(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_{k} e^{j \frac{2 \pi}{T_{0}} k t} \& y(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} d_{k} e^{j \frac{2 \pi}{T_{0}} \alpha k t}[/latex] Which of following statement is/are TRUE?
2025.html:
Let [latex]f(t)[/latex] be a periodic signal with fundamental period [latex]\mathrm{T}_{0}>0[/latex]. Consider the signal [latex]\mathrm{y}(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{f}(\alpha \mathrm{t})[/latex], where [latex]\alpha>1[/latex].

The Fourier series expansions of [latex]f(t)[/latex] and [latex]y(t)[/latex] are given by

[latex]f(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_{k} e^{j \frac{2 \pi}{T_{0}} k t} \& y(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} d_{k} e^{j \frac{2 \pi}{T_{0}} \alpha k t}[/latex]

Which of following statement is/are TRUE?
2025.subject: Signals and Systems - Fourier Series
2025.explanation_text: Let the original signal [latex]f(t)[/latex] have period [latex]T_0[/latex]. Then: [latex]f(t + T_0) = f(t)[/latex] Now consider the time-scaled signal: [latex]y(t) = f(\alpha t)[/latex] To find its period, assume [latex]y(t + T) = y(t)[/latex]: [latex]f(\alpha(t + T)) = f(\alpha t) \Rightarrow [/latex]  [latex]f(\alpha t + \alpha T) = f(\alpha t)[/latex] Since [latex]f(t)[/latex] is periodic with period [latex]T_0[/latex], this implies: [latex]\alpha T = T_0 \Rightarrow T = \frac{T_0}{\alpha}[/latex] Therefore, [latex]y(t)[/latex] is periodic with fundamental period [latex]\frac{T_0}{\alpha}[/latex] So, (D) is TRUE, and (B) is FALSE Fourier Series Comparison: The Fourier series of [latex]f(t)[/latex] is: [latex]f(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_k e^{j \frac{2\pi}{T_0}kt}[/latex] Now [latex]y(t) = f(\alpha t)[/latex] ? [latex]y(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_k e^{j \frac{2\pi}{T_0}k \alpha t} = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} d_k e^{j \frac{2\pi}{T_0/\alpha}k t}[/latex] Hence, [latex]d_k = c_k[/latex] for all [latex]k[/latex] So (A) is TRUE (C) is FALSE
2025.explanation_html:
Let the original signal [latex]f(t)[/latex] have period [latex]T_0[/latex]. Then:
[latex]f(t + T_0) = f(t)[/latex]

Now consider the time-scaled signal:
[latex]y(t) = f(\alpha t)[/latex]
To find its period, assume [latex]y(t + T) = y(t)[/latex]:
[latex]f(\alpha(t + T)) = f(\alpha t) \Rightarrow [/latex] [latex]f(\alpha t + \alpha T) = f(\alpha t)[/latex]
Since [latex]f(t)[/latex] is periodic with period [latex]T_0[/latex], this implies:
[latex]\alpha T = T_0 \Rightarrow T = \frac{T_0}{\alpha}[/latex]
Therefore, [latex]y(t)[/latex] is periodic with fundamental period [latex]\frac{T_0}{\alpha}[/latex]
So, (D) is TRUE, and (B) is FALSE

Fourier Series Comparison:
The Fourier series of [latex]f(t)[/latex] is:
[latex]f(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_k e^{j \frac{2\pi}{T_0}kt}[/latex]
Now [latex]y(t) = f(\alpha t)[/latex] ?
[latex]y(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_k e^{j \frac{2\pi}{T_0}k \alpha t} = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} d_k e^{j \frac{2\pi}{T_0/\alpha}k t}[/latex]
Hence, [latex]d_k = c_k[/latex] for all [latex]k[/latex]
So (A) is TRUE
(C) is FALSE

2025.text: Consider the vectors [latex]\mathbf{a}=\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 1\end{array}\right], \mathbf{b}=\left[\begin{array}{c}0 \\ 3 \sqrt{2}\end{array}\right][/latex] For real-valued scalar variable x , the value of [latex]\min _{x}\|a x-b\|_{2}[/latex] is __________ (rounded off to two decimal places). [latex]\|\cdot\|_{2}[/latex] denotes the Euclidean norm, i.e., if for [latex]\mathbf{y}=\left[\begin{array}{l}\mathrm{y}_{1} \\ \mathrm{y}_{2}\end{array}\right],\|\mathbf{y}\|_{2}=\sqrt{\mathrm{y}_{1}^{2}+\mathrm{y}_{2}^{2}}[/latex].
2025.html:
Consider the vectors

[latex]\mathbf{a}=\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 1\end{array}\right], \mathbf{b}=\left[\begin{array}{c}0 \\ 3 \sqrt{2}\end{array}\right][/latex]

For real-valued scalar variable x , the value of

[latex]\min _{x}\|a x-b\|_{2}[/latex]

is __________ (rounded off to two decimal places).

[latex]\|\cdot\|_{2}[/latex] denotes the Euclidean norm, i.e., if for [latex]\mathbf{y}=\left[\begin{array}{l}\mathrm{y}_{1} \\ \mathrm{y}_{2}\end{array}\right],\|\mathbf{y}\|_{2}=\sqrt{\mathrm{y}_{1}^{2}+\mathrm{y}_{2}^{2}}[/latex].
2025.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Vector Analysis
2025.explanation_text: We are given: [latex] \mathbf{a} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 3\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} [/latex] We need to minimize: [latex] | ax - b |_2 = \left| \begin{bmatrix} x \ x \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 3\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} \right|_2 = \left| \begin{bmatrix} x \ x - 3\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} \right|_2 [/latex] Now compute the square of the norm: [latex] | ax - b |_2^2 = x^2 + (x - 3\sqrt{2})^2 [/latex] Expand: [latex] | ax - b |_2^2 = x^2 + (x^2 - 6\sqrt{2}x + 18) = 2x^2 - 6\sqrt{2}x + 18 [/latex] Minimize this quadratic in [latex] x [/latex]. The minimum occurs at: [latex] x = \frac{6\sqrt{2}}{2 \cdot 2} = \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} [/latex] Now compute the minimum value: [latex] | ax - b |_2 = \left| \begin{bmatrix} x \ x - 3\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} \right|_2 = \sqrt{x^2 + (x - 3\sqrt{2})^2} [/latex] Substitute [latex] x = \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} [/latex] into the expression: First term: [latex] x^2 = \left( \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{9 \cdot 2}{4} = \dfrac{18}{4} = 4.5 [/latex] Second term: [latex] x - 3\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} - 3\sqrt{2} = -\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} [/latex] So, [latex] (x - 3\sqrt{2})^2 = \left( -\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \right)^2 = 4.5 [/latex] Therefore, the minimum norm is: [latex] \sqrt{4.5 + 4.5} = \sqrt{9} = 3 [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
We are given:
[latex] \mathbf{a} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 3\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

We need to minimize:
[latex] | ax - b |_2 = \left| \begin{bmatrix} x \ x \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 3\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} \right|_2 = \left| \begin{bmatrix} x \ x - 3\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} \right|_2 [/latex]

Now compute the square of the norm:
[latex] | ax - b |_2^2 = x^2 + (x - 3\sqrt{2})^2 [/latex]

Expand:
[latex] | ax - b |_2^2 = x^2 + (x^2 - 6\sqrt{2}x + 18) = 2x^2 - 6\sqrt{2}x + 18 [/latex]

Minimize this quadratic in [latex] x [/latex]. The minimum occurs at:
[latex] x = \frac{6\sqrt{2}}{2 \cdot 2} = \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} [/latex]

Now compute the minimum value:
[latex] | ax - b |_2 = \left| \begin{bmatrix} x \ x - 3\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} \right|_2 = \sqrt{x^2 + (x - 3\sqrt{2})^2} [/latex]
Substitute [latex] x = \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} [/latex] into the expression:

First term:
[latex] x^2 = \left( \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{9 \cdot 2}{4} = \dfrac{18}{4} = 4.5 [/latex]

Second term:
[latex] x - 3\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} - 3\sqrt{2} = -\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} [/latex]
So, [latex] (x - 3\sqrt{2})^2 = \left( -\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \right)^2 = 4.5 [/latex]

Therefore, the minimum norm is:
[latex] \sqrt{4.5 + 4.5} = \sqrt{9} = 3 [/latex]

2025.text:
X and Y are Bernoulli random variables taking values in [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex]. The joint probability mass function of the random variables is given by: [latex]
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=0, \mathrm{Y}=0)=0.06
& \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=0, \mathrm{Y}=1)=0.14
& \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=1, \mathrm{Y}=0)=0.24
& \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=1, \mathrm{Y}=1)=0.56
\end{aligned}
[/latex] The mutual information [latex]\mathrm{I}(\mathrm{X} ; \mathrm{Y})[/latex] is __________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
2025.html:
X and Y are Bernoulli random variables taking values in [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex]. The joint probability mass function of the random variables is given by:

[latex] \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=0, \mathrm{Y}=0)=0.06 & \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=0, \mathrm{Y}=1)=0.14 & \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=1, \mathrm{Y}=0)=0.24 & \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{X}=1, \mathrm{Y}=1)=0.56 \end{aligned} [/latex]

The mutual information [latex]\mathrm{I}(\mathrm{X} ; \mathrm{Y})[/latex] is __________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
2025.subject: Communication Systems - Information Theory and Coding
2025.explanation_text:
The mutual information is given by: [latex]
I(X;Y) = \sum_{x,y} P(x,y) \log_2 \left( \frac{P(x,y)}{P(x)P(y)} \right)
[/latex] Step 1: Compute marginals [latex]
\begin{aligned}
P(X=0) &= 0.06 + 0.14 = 0.20 \\
P(X=1) &= 0.24 + 0.56 = 0.80 \\
P(Y=0) &= 0.06 + 0.24 = 0.30 \\
P(Y=1) &= 0.14 + 0.56 = 0.70
\end{aligned}
[/latex] Step 2: Compute mutual information We compute [latex] P(x,y) \log_2 \left( \frac{P(x,y)}{P(x)P(y)} \right) [/latex] for each combination: (i) [latex] x=0,\ y=0 [/latex]: [latex]
P = 0.06,\quad P(X=0) = 0.20,\quad P(Y=0) = 0.30 \
\Rightarrow \frac{0.06}{0.20 \cdot 0.30} = 1.0,\quad \log_2(1) = 0 \
\Rightarrow \text{term} = 0.06 \cdot 0 = 0
[/latex] (ii) [latex] x=0,\ y=1 [/latex]: [latex]
P = 0.14,\quad P(X=0) = 0.20,\quad P(Y=1) = 0.70 \
\Rightarrow \frac{0.14}{0.20 \cdot 0.70} = 1.0,\quad \log_2(1) = 0 \
\Rightarrow \text{term} = 0.14 \cdot 0 = 0
[/latex] (iii) [latex] x=1,\ y=0 [/latex]: [latex]
P = 0.24,\quad P(X=1) = 0.80,\quad P(Y=0) = 0.30 \
\Rightarrow \frac{0.24}{0.80 \cdot 0.30} = 1.0,\quad \log_2(1) = 0 \
\Rightarrow \text{term} = 0.24 \cdot 0 = 0
[/latex] (iv) [latex] x=1,\ y=1 [/latex]: [latex]
P = 0.56,\quad P(X=1) = 0.80,\quad P(Y=1) = 0.70 \
\Rightarrow \frac{0.56}{0.80 \cdot 0.70} = 1.0,\quad \log_2(1) = 0 \
\Rightarrow \text{term} = 0.56 \cdot 0 = 0
[/latex] So:
[latex] I(X;Y) = 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 0 [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
The mutual information is given by:
[latex] I(X;Y) = \sum_{x,y} P(x,y) \log_2 \left( \frac{P(x,y)}{P(x)P(y)} \right) [/latex]

Step 1: Compute marginals
[latex] \begin{aligned} P(X=0) &= 0.06 + 0.14 = 0.20 \\ P(X=1) &= 0.24 + 0.56 = 0.80 \\ P(Y=0) &= 0.06 + 0.24 = 0.30 \\ P(Y=1) &= 0.14 + 0.56 = 0.70 \end{aligned} [/latex]

Step 2: Compute mutual information
We compute [latex] P(x,y) \log_2 \left( \frac{P(x,y)}{P(x)P(y)} \right) [/latex] for each combination:

(i) [latex] x=0,\ y=0 [/latex]:
[latex] P = 0.06,\quad P(X=0) = 0.20,\quad P(Y=0) = 0.30 \ \Rightarrow \frac{0.06}{0.20 \cdot 0.30} = 1.0,\quad \log_2(1) = 0 \ \Rightarrow \text{term} = 0.06 \cdot 0 = 0 [/latex]

(ii) [latex] x=0,\ y=1 [/latex]:
[latex] P = 0.14,\quad P(X=0) = 0.20,\quad P(Y=1) = 0.70 \ \Rightarrow \frac{0.14}{0.20 \cdot 0.70} = 1.0,\quad \log_2(1) = 0 \ \Rightarrow \text{term} = 0.14 \cdot 0 = 0 [/latex]

(iii) [latex] x=1,\ y=0 [/latex]:
[latex] P = 0.24,\quad P(X=1) = 0.80,\quad P(Y=0) = 0.30 \ \Rightarrow \frac{0.24}{0.80 \cdot 0.30} = 1.0,\quad \log_2(1) = 0 \ \Rightarrow \text{term} = 0.24 \cdot 0 = 0 [/latex]

(iv) [latex] x=1,\ y=1 [/latex]:
[latex] P = 0.56,\quad P(X=1) = 0.80,\quad P(Y=1) = 0.70 \ \Rightarrow \frac{0.56}{0.80 \cdot 0.70} = 1.0,\quad \log_2(1) = 0 \ \Rightarrow \text{term} = 0.56 \cdot 0 = 0 [/latex]

So: [latex] I(X;Y) = 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 0 [/latex]

2025.subject: Digital Circuits - Sequential Circuits
2025.explanation_text:
Setup time constraint: Total data delay from one flip-flop to the next must arrive before the next clock edge minus setup time. Total data path delay =
Clock-to-Q delay (2 ns) + AND gate delay (1 ns) = 3 ns Setup time = 2 ns Required clock period:
[latex] T_{\text{clk}} \geq \text{Data path delay} + \text{Setup time} [/latex]
[latex] T_{\text{clk}} \geq 3\ \text{ns} + 2\ \text{ns} = 5\ \text{ns} [/latex] Maximum clock frequency:

2025.explanation_text:
[latex] I = I_s \left( e^{\frac{eV}{k_BT}} - 1 \right) [/latex] Where:

[latex] I \approx I_s e^{\frac{eV}{k_BT}} [/latex] Taking natural logarithm on both sides:
[latex] \frac{eV}{k_BT} = \ln\left(\frac{I}{I_s}\right) [/latex] [latex] V = \frac{k_BT}{e} \ln\left(\frac{I}{I_s}\right) [/latex] Now plug in the values:
[latex] \frac{k_BT}{e} = \frac{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 0.025875\ \text{V} [/latex] [latex] \ln\left(\frac{0.1}{10 \times 10^{-6}}\right) = \ln(10000) = \ln(10^4) = 4 \ln(10) \approx 4 \times 2.3026 = 9.2104 [/latex] So,

2025.text: A [latex]50 \Omega[/latex] lossless transmission line is terminated with a load [latex]\mathrm{Z}_{\mathrm{L}}[/latex] of [latex](50-\mathrm{j} 75) \Omega[/latex]. If the average incident power on the line is 10 mW , then the average power delivered to the load (in mW , rounded off to one decimal place) is __________ .
2025.html:
A [latex]50 \Omega[/latex] lossless transmission line is terminated with a load [latex]\mathrm{Z}_{\mathrm{L}}[/latex] of [latex](50-\mathrm{j} 75) \Omega[/latex].

If the average incident power on the line is 10 mW , then the average power delivered to the load (in mW , rounded off to one decimal place) is __________ .
2025.subject: Electromagnetics - Transmission Lines
2025.explanation_text:
Step 1: Characteristic Impedance
Given:
[latex] Z_0 = 50\ \Omega [/latex] (lossless line) [latex] Z_L = 50 - j75\ \Omega [/latex] Incident power = [latex] P_{\text{inc}} = 10\ \text{mW} [/latex] Step 2: Reflection Coefficient
Reflection coefficient [latex] \Gamma = \frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0} [/latex] First compute:
[latex] Z_L + Z_0 = (50 - j75) + 50 = 100 - j75 [/latex] [latex] Z_L - Z_0 = (50 - j75) - 50 = -j75 [/latex] So:
[latex] \Gamma = \frac{-j75}{100 - j75} [/latex] Multiply numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator:
[latex] \Gamma = \frac{-j75 \cdot (100 + j75)}{(100 - j75)(100 + j75)} [/latex] Numerator:
[latex] -j75(100 + j75) = -j7500 - j^2 75 \cdot 75 = -j7500 + 5625 [/latex] Denominator:
[latex] 100^2 + 75^2 = 10000 + 5625 = 15625 [/latex] So:
[latex] \Gamma = \frac{5625 - j7500}{15625} = 0.36 - j0.48 [/latex] Step 3: Reflected Power
[latex] |\Gamma|^2 = (0.36)^2 + (0.48)^2 = 0.1296 + 0.2304 = 0.36 [/latex] So, reflected power = [latex] P_{\text{ref}} = |\Gamma|^2 \cdot P_{\text{inc}} = 0.36 \cdot 10 = 3.6\ \text{mW} [/latex] Step 4: Delivered Power
[latex] P_{\text{delivered}} = P_{\text{inc}} - P_{\text{ref}} = 10 - 3.6 = \boxed{6.4\ \text{mW}} [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Step 1: Characteristic Impedance Given: [latex] Z_0 = 50\ \Omega [/latex] (lossless line)
[latex] Z_L = 50 - j75\ \Omega [/latex]
Incident power = [latex] P_{\text{inc}} = 10\ \text{mW} [/latex]

Step 2: Reflection Coefficient Reflection coefficient [latex] \Gamma = \frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0} [/latex]
First compute: [latex] Z_L + Z_0 = (50 - j75) + 50 = 100 - j75 [/latex]
[latex] Z_L - Z_0 = (50 - j75) - 50 = -j75 [/latex]

So: [latex] \Gamma = \frac{-j75}{100 - j75} [/latex]
Multiply numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator: [latex] \Gamma = \frac{-j75 \cdot (100 + j75)}{(100 - j75)(100 + j75)} [/latex]
Numerator: [latex] -j75(100 + j75) = -j7500 - j^2 75 \cdot 75 = -j7500 + 5625 [/latex]
Denominator: [latex] 100^2 + 75^2 = 10000 + 5625 = 15625 [/latex]
So: [latex] \Gamma = \frac{5625 - j7500}{15625} = 0.36 - j0.48 [/latex]

Step 3: Reflected Power [latex] |\Gamma|^2 = (0.36)^2 + (0.48)^2 = 0.1296 + 0.2304 = 0.36 [/latex]
So, reflected power = [latex] P_{\text{ref}} = |\Gamma|^2 \cdot P_{\text{inc}} = 0.36 \cdot 10 = 3.6\ \text{mW} [/latex]

Step 4: Delivered Power [latex] P_{\text{delivered}} = P_{\text{inc}} - P_{\text{ref}} = 10 - 3.6 = \boxed{6.4\ \text{mW}} [/latex]

2025.text: Two resistors are connected in a circuit loop of area [latex]5 \mathrm{~m}^{2}[/latex], as shown in the figure below. The circuit loop is placed on the [latex]x-y[/latex] plane. When a time-varying magnetic flux, with fluxdensity [latex]\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{t})=0.5 \mathrm{t}[/latex] (in Tesla), is applied along the positive z-axis, the magnitude of current I (in Amperes, rounded off to two decimal places) in the loop is __________ .
2025.html:
Two resistors are connected in a circuit loop of area [latex]5 \mathrm{~m}^{2}[/latex], as shown in the figure below. The circuit loop is placed on the [latex]x-y[/latex] plane.

When a time-varying magnetic flux, with fluxdensity [latex]\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{t})=0.5 \mathrm{t}[/latex] (in Tesla), is applied along the positive z-axis, the magnitude of current I (in Amperes, rounded off to two decimal places) in the loop is __________ .
2025.subject: Electromagnetics - Miscellaneous Topics
2025.explanation_text:
Given: Loop area, [latex] A = 5\ \text{m}^2 [/latex] Magnetic field, [latex] B(t) = 0.5t\ \text{T} [/latex] Total resistance in the loop = [latex]2\ \Omega + 2\ \Omega = 4\ \Omega[/latex] We use Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction:
[latex] \mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt} [/latex]
where [latex] \Phi = B(t) \cdot A [/latex] is the magnetic flux. So,
[latex] \Phi(t) = B(t) \cdot A = 0.5t \cdot 5 = 2.5t [/latex] [latex] \frac{d\Phi}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(2.5t) = 2.5\ \text{V} [/latex] So, the induced EMF is:
[latex] \mathcal{E} = -2.5\ \text{V} [/latex] (The negative sign indicates direction, but we are interested in magnitude of current) Now, using Ohm's Law:
[latex] I = \frac{|\mathcal{E}|}{R} = \frac{2.5}{4} = 0.625\ \text{A} [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Given:
Loop area, [latex] A = 5\ \text{m}^2 [/latex]
Magnetic field, [latex] B(t) = 0.5t\ \text{T} [/latex]
Total resistance in the loop = [latex]2\ \Omega + 2\ \Omega = 4\ \Omega[/latex]

We use Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction: [latex] \mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt} [/latex] where [latex] \Phi = B(t) \cdot A [/latex] is the magnetic flux.
So, [latex] \Phi(t) = B(t) \cdot A = 0.5t \cdot 5 = 2.5t [/latex]
[latex] \frac{d\Phi}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(2.5t) = 2.5\ \text{V} [/latex]

So, the induced EMF is: [latex] \mathcal{E} = -2.5\ \text{V} [/latex]
(The negative sign indicates direction, but we are interested in magnitude of current)

Now, using Ohm's Law: [latex] I = \frac{|\mathcal{E}|}{R} = \frac{2.5}{4} = 0.625\ \text{A} [/latex]

A stick of length one meter is broken at two locations at distances of [latex]b_1[/latex] and [latex]b_2[/latex] from the origin (0), as shown in the figure. Note that [latex]0 < b_1 < b_2 < 1[/latex]. Which one of the following is not a necessary condition for forming a triangle using the three pieces?

Note: All lengths are in meter. The figure shown is representative.
2025.subject: General Aptitude - Numerical Ability
2025.explanation_text:
The stick is broken at positions [latex]b_1[/latex] and [latex]b_2[/latex], where [latex]0 < b_1 < b_2 < 1[/latex]. This creates three segments: [latex]L_1 = b_1[/latex] (from 0 to [latex]b_1[/latex]) [latex]L_2 = b_2 - b_1[/latex] (from [latex]b_1[/latex] to [latex]b_2[/latex]) [latex]L_3 = 1 - b_2[/latex] (from [latex]b_2[/latex] to 1) To form a triangle with these three segments, the triangle inequality must be satisfied: Sum of any two sides must be greater than the third. 1. [latex]L_1 + L_2 > L_3[/latex] [latex]b_1 + (b_2 - b_1) > 1 - b_2[/latex]
[latex]b_2 > 1 - b_2[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow b_2 > 0.5[/latex] 2. [latex]L_2 + L_3 > L_1[/latex] [latex](b_2 - b_1) + (1 - b_2) > b_1[/latex]
[latex]1 - b_1 > b_1[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow b_1 < 0.5[/latex] 3. [latex]L_1 + L_3 > L_2[/latex] [latex]b_1 + (1 - b_2) > b_2 - b_1[/latex]
[latex]b_1 + 1 - b_2 > b_2 - b_1[/latex]
[latex]2b_1 + 1 - b_2 > b_2[/latex]
[latex]2b_1 + 1 > 2b_2[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow b_2 < b_1 + 0.5[/latex] Now check each option: (A) [latex]b_1 < 0.5[/latex] - this is a necessary condition (B) [latex]b_2 > 0.5[/latex] - this is a necessary condition (C) [latex]b_2 < b_1 + 0.5[/latex] - this is a necessary condition (D) [latex]b_1 + b_2 < 1[/latex] - this is not required by any triangle inequality
2025.explanation_html:
The stick is broken at positions [latex]b_1[/latex] and [latex]b_2[/latex], where [latex]0 < b_1 < b_2 < 1[/latex].
This creates three segments:
[latex]L_1 = b_1[/latex] (from 0 to [latex]b_1[/latex])
[latex]L_2 = b_2 - b_1[/latex] (from [latex]b_1[/latex] to [latex]b_2[/latex])
[latex]L_3 = 1 - b_2[/latex] (from [latex]b_2[/latex] to 1)

To form a triangle with these three segments, the triangle inequality must be satisfied:
Sum of any two sides must be greater than the third.

1. [latex]L_1 + L_2 > L_3[/latex]
[latex]b_1 + (b_2 - b_1) > 1 - b_2[/latex] [latex]b_2 > 1 - b_2[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow b_2 > 0.5[/latex]

2. [latex]L_2 + L_3 > L_1[/latex]
[latex](b_2 - b_1) + (1 - b_2) > b_1[/latex] [latex]1 - b_1 > b_1[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow b_1 < 0.5[/latex]

3. [latex]L_1 + L_3 > L_2[/latex]
[latex]b_1 + (1 - b_2) > b_2 - b_1[/latex] [latex]b_1 + 1 - b_2 > b_2 - b_1[/latex] [latex]2b_1 + 1 - b_2 > b_2[/latex] [latex]2b_1 + 1 > 2b_2[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow b_2 < b_1 + 0.5[/latex]

Now check each option:
(A) [latex]b_1 < 0.5[/latex] - this is a necessary condition
(B) [latex]b_2 > 0.5[/latex] - this is a necessary condition
(C) [latex]b_2 < b_1 + 0.5[/latex] - this is a necessary condition
(D) [latex]b_1 + b_2 < 1[/latex] - this is not required by any triangle inequality

So top three by total medals: USA (125), Canada (90), France (64) (A is correct)(B) USA: 125, Canada: 90. No other nation has more than 90. So, order remains same
(B is correct)(C) USA + Canada: [latex]125 + 90 = 215[/latex] Check 50% of 376: [latex]\frac{376}{2} = 188[/latex] 215 is more than 188 (C is incorrect)(D) Canada: 90, Japan: 45 [latex]90 = 2 \times 45[/latex]

2025.text: An organization allows its employees to work independently on consultancy projects but charges an overhead on the consulting fee. The overhead is 20% of the consulting fee, if the fee is up to Rs. 5,00,000. For higher fees, the overhead is Rs. 1,00,000 plus 10% of the amount by which the fee exceeds Rs. 5,00,000. The government charges a Goods and Services Tax of 18% on the total amount (the consulting fee plus the overhead). An employee of the organization charges this entire amount, i.e., the consulting fee, overhead, and tax, to the client. If the client cannot pay more than Rs. 10,00,000, what is the maximum consulting fee that the employee can charge?
2025.html: An organization allows its employees to work independently on consultancy projects but charges an overhead on the consulting fee. The overhead is 20% of the consulting fee, if the fee is up to Rs. 5,00,000. For higher fees, the overhead is Rs. 1,00,000 plus 10% of the amount by which the fee exceeds Rs. 5,00,000. The government charges a Goods and Services Tax of 18% on the total amount (the consulting fee plus the overhead). An employee of the organization charges this entire amount, i.e., the consulting fee, overhead, and tax, to the client. If the client cannot pay more than Rs. 10,00,000, what is the maximum consulting fee that the employee can charge?
2025.subject: General Aptitude - Numerical Ability
2025.explanation_text: Let the consulting fee be [latex] x [/latex]. Case 1: [latex] x \leq 5{,}00{,}000 [/latex] Overhead = [latex] 0.2x [/latex] Total before tax = [latex] x + 0.2x = 1.2x [/latex] Total with GST (18%) = [latex] 1.18 \times 1.2x = 1.416x [/latex] We want: [latex] 1.416x \leq 10{,}00{,}000 [/latex] [latex] x \leq \frac{10{,}00{,}000}{1.416} \approx 7{,}06{,}199 [/latex] But this value of [latex] x [/latex] is greater than Rs. 5,00,000, so this case is invalid. Case 2: [latex] x > 5{,}00{,}000 [/latex] Overhead = [latex] 1{,}00{,}000 + 0.1(x - 5{,}00{,}000) [/latex] [latex] = 1{,}00{,}000 + 0.1x - 50{,}000 = 0.1x + 50{,}000 [/latex] Total before tax = [latex] x + 0.1x + 50{,}000 = 1.1x + 50{,}000 [/latex] Total with GST = [latex] 1.18(1.1x + 50{,}000) = 1.298x + 59{,}000 [/latex] We want: [latex] 1.298x + 59{,}000 \leq 10{,}00{,}000 [/latex] [latex] 1.298x \leq 9{,}41{,}000 [/latex] [latex] x \leq \frac{9{,}41{,}000}{1.298} \approx 7{,}24{,}961 [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Let the consulting fee be [latex] x [/latex].

Case 1: [latex] x \leq 5{,}00{,}000 [/latex]
Overhead = [latex] 0.2x [/latex]
Total before tax = [latex] x + 0.2x = 1.2x [/latex]
Total with GST (18%) = [latex] 1.18 \times 1.2x = 1.416x [/latex]
We want: [latex] 1.416x \leq 10{,}00{,}000 [/latex]
[latex] x \leq \frac{10{,}00{,}000}{1.416} \approx 7{,}06{,}199 [/latex]
But this value of [latex] x [/latex] is greater than Rs. 5,00,000, so this case is invalid.

Case 2: [latex] x > 5{,}00{,}000 [/latex]
Overhead = [latex] 1{,}00{,}000 + 0.1(x - 5{,}00{,}000) [/latex]
[latex] = 1{,}00{,}000 + 0.1x - 50{,}000 = 0.1x + 50{,}000 [/latex]
Total before tax = [latex] x + 0.1x + 50{,}000 = 1.1x + 50{,}000 [/latex]
Total with GST = [latex] 1.18(1.1x + 50{,}000) = 1.298x + 59{,}000 [/latex]
We want: [latex] 1.298x + 59{,}000 \leq 10{,}00{,}000 [/latex]
[latex] 1.298x \leq 9{,}41{,}000 [/latex]
[latex] x \leq \frac{9{,}41{,}000}{1.298} \approx 7{,}24{,}961 [/latex]

2024.html:
In the feedback control system shown in the figure below [latex]G(s)=\frac{6}{s(s+1)(s+2)}[/latex].

[latex]R(s), Y(s)[/latex], and [latex]E(s)[/latex] are the Laplace transforms of [latex]r(t), y(t)[/latex], and [latex]e(t)[/latex], respectively. If the input [latex]r(t)[/latex] is a unit step function, then _____
2024.subject: Control Systems - Stability Analysis
2024.explanation_text:
Given system is [latex]
G(s)=\frac{6}{s(s+1)(s+2)}
[/latex] The characteristic equation, [latex]
\begin{aligned}
1+G(s) & =0 \\
1+\frac{6}{s(s+1)(s+2)} & =0 \\
s(s+1)(s+2)+6 & =0 \\
s^{3}+3 s^{2}+2 s+6 & =0
\end{aligned}
[/latex] Clearly, here the internal coefficient product is equal to external coefficient product i.e., [latex]
3 \times 2=6 \times 1
[/latex] Hence, the given system is marginally stable system. [latex]\therefore e(t)[/latex] not exist because system is oscillatory system.

Clearly, here the internal coefficient product is equal to external coefficient product i.e.,
[latex] 3 \times 2=6 \times 1 [/latex]
Hence, the given system is marginally stable system.

2024.text: Let [latex]\hat{i}[/latex] and [latex]\hat{j}[/latex] be the unit vectors along [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] axes, respectively and let [latex]A[/latex] be a positive constant. Which one of the following statements is true for the vector fields [latex]\vec{F}_{1}=A(\hat{i} y+\hat{j} x)[/latex] and [latex]\vec{F}_{2}=A(\hat{i} y-\hat{j} x) ?[/latex]
2024.html: Let [latex]\hat{i}[/latex] and [latex]\hat{j}[/latex] be the unit vectors along [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] axes, respectively and let [latex]A[/latex] be a positive constant. Which one of the following statements is true for the vector fields [latex]\vec{F}_{1}=A(\hat{i} y+\hat{j} x)[/latex] and [latex]\vec{F}_{2}=A(\hat{i} y-\hat{j} x) ?[/latex]
2024.subject: Electromagnetics - Basics of Electromagnetics
2024.explanation_text:
For an electrostatic field, [latex]\nabla \times \bar{F}=0[/latex] [latex]
\begin{aligned}
& \bar{F}_{1}=A[y \hat{i}+x \hat{j}] \\
& \Rightarrow \\
& \Delta \times \bar{F}_{1}=A\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\
\partial / \partial x & \partial / \partial y & \partial / \partial z \\
y & x & 0
\end{array}\right| \\
& =A[0 \hat{i}-0 \hat{j}+(1-1) \hat{k}] \\
& =0 \\
& \bar{F}_{2}=A[y \hat{i}-x \hat{j}] \\
& \Rightarrow \\
& \Delta \times \bar{F}_{2}=A\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\
\partial / \partial x & \partial / \partial y & \partial / \partial z \\
y & -x & 0
\end{array}\right| \\
& =A[0 \hat{i}-0 \hat{j}+(-1-1) \hat{k}] \\
& =-2 A \hat{k}
\end{aligned}
[/latex] Hence, [latex]\bar{F}_{1}[/latex] is electrostatic, [latex]\bar{F}_{2}[/latex] is not electrostatic.
2024.explanation_html:
For an electrostatic field, [latex]\nabla \times \bar{F}=0[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & \bar{F}_{1}=A[y \hat{i}+x \hat{j}] \\ & \Rightarrow \\ & \Delta \times \bar{F}_{1}=A\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \partial / \partial x & \partial / \partial y & \partial / \partial z \\ y & x & 0 \end{array}\right| \\ & =A[0 \hat{i}-0 \hat{j}+(1-1) \hat{k}] \\ & =0 \\ & \bar{F}_{2}=A[y \hat{i}-x \hat{j}] \\ & \Rightarrow \\ & \Delta \times \bar{F}_{2}=A\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \partial / \partial x & \partial / \partial y & \partial / \partial z \\ y & -x & 0 \end{array}\right| \\ & =A[0 \hat{i}-0 \hat{j}+(-1-1) \hat{k}] \\ & =-2 A \hat{k} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence, [latex]\bar{F}_{1}[/latex] is electrostatic, [latex]\bar{F}_{2}[/latex] is not electrostatic.

[latex] \begin{aligned} E[n(t)] & =E[W(t)] \cdot H(0) \\ E[n(t)] & =0 \\ E\left[n^{2}(t)\right] & =\left\{E(n(t)\}^{2}+\operatorname{var}[n(t)]\right. \\ \operatorname{var}[n(t)] & =E\left[n^{2}(t)\right] \end{aligned} [/latex]
at [latex]t=t_{k}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left.\operatorname{var}[n(t)]\right|_{t=t_{k}} & =E\left[n^{2}\left(t_{k}\right)\right]=E\left[n\left(t_{k}\right) \cdot n\left(t_{k}\right)\right]=R_{n}(0) \\ S_{n}(f) & =S_{W}(f) \cdot|H(f)|^{2} \\ & =\frac{N_{0}}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{1+(\omega R C)^{2}} \\ R_{n}(\tau) & =\operatorname{IFT}\left[S_{n}(f)\right]=\frac{N_{0}}{4 R C} \cdot e^{\frac{-|\tau|}{R C}} \\ R_{n}(0) & =\frac{N_{0}}{4 R C} \end{aligned} [/latex]

2024.html:
For a causal discrete-time LTI system with transfer function

[latex] H(z)=\frac{2 z^{2}+3}{\left(z+\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(z-\frac{1}{3}\right)} [/latex]

which of the following statements is/are true?
2024.subject: Signals and Systems - LTI Systems Continuous and Discrete
2024.explanation_text:
Given: [latex]H(z)=\frac{2 z^{2}+3}{\left(z+\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(z-\frac{1}{3}\right)}[/latex] System is non-minimum phase system. Since zero are lying outside the unit circle. Final value: [latex]
h(\infty)=\lim _{z \rightarrow 1}(z-1) \frac{2 z^{2}+3}{\left(z+\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(z-\frac{1}{3}\right)}=0
[/latex] Initial value: [latex]
\begin{aligned}
h(0) & =\lim _{z \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\left(2 z^{2}+3\right)}{\left(z+\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(z-\frac{1}{3}\right)}=\lim _{z \rightarrow \infty} \frac{z^{2}\left[2+\frac{3}{z^{2}}\right]}{z^{2}\left[1+\frac{1}{3 z}\right]\left[1-\frac{1}{3 z}\right]} \\
& =\lim _{z \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\left[2+\frac{3}{z^{2}}\right]}{\left[1+\frac{1}{3 z}\right]\left[1-\frac{1}{3 z}\right]}=\frac{2}{1 \times 1}=2 \\
|z| & =\frac{1}{3}=0.33
\end{aligned}
[/latex] [latex]z=-\frac{1}{3}, z=\frac{1}{3}[/latex] System is stable. Since [latex]\mid[/latex] pole [latex]\mid \lt 1[/latex] i.e. pole are lying inside the unit circle.

System is non-minimum phase system. Since zero are lying outside the unit circle.
Final value:
[latex] h(\infty)=\lim _{z \rightarrow 1}(z-1) \frac{2 z^{2}+3}{\left(z+\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(z-\frac{1}{3}\right)}=0 [/latex]
Initial value:
[latex] \begin{aligned} h(0) & =\lim _{z \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\left(2 z^{2}+3\right)}{\left(z+\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(z-\frac{1}{3}\right)}=\lim _{z \rightarrow \infty} \frac{z^{2}\left[2+\frac{3}{z^{2}}\right]}{z^{2}\left[1+\frac{1}{3 z}\right]\left[1-\frac{1}{3 z}\right]} \\ & =\lim _{z \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\left[2+\frac{3}{z^{2}}\right]}{\left[1+\frac{1}{3 z}\right]\left[1-\frac{1}{3 z}\right]}=\frac{2}{1 \times 1}=2 \\ |z| & =\frac{1}{3}=0.33 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]z=-\frac{1}{3}, z=\frac{1}{3}[/latex]
System is stable. Since [latex]\mid[/latex] pole [latex]\mid \lt 1[/latex] i.e. pole are lying inside the unit circle.

[latex] \begin{array}{ll} & \Gamma=-1 \\ \Rightarrow & \Gamma=1 \mid \pi \end{array} [/latex]
As we know that [latex]H_{\min }[/latex] occurs at [latex]E_{\max }[/latex]. Hence,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & E_{\max }=E_{0}[1+|\Gamma|] \\ & H_{\min }=\frac{E_{0}}{\eta}[1-|\Gamma|] \text { at } 2 \beta x_{\max }=2 n \pi+\theta_{\Gamma} \end{aligned} [/latex]
So,
[latex] 2 \beta x_{\max }=2 n \pi+\theta_{\Gamma} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{4 \pi}{\lambda} x_{\max }=2 n \pi+\pi[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad x_{\max }=(2 n+1) \frac{\lambda}{4} ; n=0,1,2,3 \ldots [/latex]
So, for [latex]1^{\text {st }}[/latex] value of [latex]x[/latex] for [latex]\mathrm{H}[/latex]-field to be zero is
[latex] x_{\max }=\frac{\lambda}{4} \quad[\text { at } n=0] [/latex]
Now, from the equation given,
[latex] \begin{array}{rlrl} \beta & =\frac{2 \pi}{3} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} & =\frac{2 \pi}{3} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \lambda & =3 \end{array} [/latex]
Hence,
[latex] x_{\max }=\frac{3}{4} [/latex]
If the reference is not at interference then [latex]x=-\frac{3}{4}[/latex].
