2024.explanation_text:
[latex]\because[/latex] Given integral is independent of contour ' [latex]C[/latex] ' [latex]\int_{C}\left(F_{1} d x+F_{2} d y+F_{3} d z\right)=\int_{C} \bar{F} \cdot \overline{d r}[/latex] is independent of ' [latex]C[/latex] ' Then [latex]\bar{F}[/latex] is conservative field [latex]
\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore & \bar{F}=\overline{\nabla \phi} \\
\Rightarrow & F_{1}=\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}, F_{2}=\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}, F_{3}=\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z}
\end{array}
[/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex] Option is true. [latex]\because \bar{F}[/latex] is conservative Then, [latex]
\nabla \times \bar{F}=0
[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \quad\left|\begin{array}{ccc}i & j & K \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ F_{1} & F_{2} & F_{3}\end{array}\right|=\overrightarrow{0}[/latex] [latex]=i\left(\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial z}\right)-j\left(\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial z}\right)+K\left(\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial y}\right)=0 \hat{i}+0 \hat{j}+0 \hat{k}[/latex] Equate on both sides, We get, [latex]
\frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial z}, \quad \frac{\partial F_{3}}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial z}, \quad \frac{\partial F_{2}}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial F_{1}}{\partial y}
[/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex] Option is true. If [latex]\bar{F}[/latex] is irrotational then, [latex]
\oint_{C} F_{1} d x+F_{2} d y+F_{3} d z=0
[/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex] Option is also true.
But, [latex]
\bar{\nabla} \cdot \bar{F}=\bar{\nabla} \cdot(\bar{\nabla} \phi) \neq 0
[/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex] Option is false.

[latex]9 V_{1}-6 I_{1}-4 I_{2}=0[/latex]
but [latex]\quad I_{1}=\frac{V_{1}-0}{2} \Rightarrow \frac{V_{1}}{2}=I_{1}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad 9 V_{1}-6\left(\frac{V_{1}}{2}\right)-4 I_{2}=0[/latex]
[latex]6 V_{1}=4 I_{2}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad \frac{I_{2}}{V_{1}}=\frac{6}{4}=\frac{3}{2}=1.5 \mathrm{~S}[/latex]

2024.text: A non-degenerate n-type semiconductor has 5\% neutral dopant atoms. Its Fermi level is located at [latex]0.25 \mathrm{eV}[/latex] below the conduction band [latex]\left(E_{C}\right)[/latex] and the donor energy level [latex]\left(E_{D}\right)[/latex] has a degeneracy of 2. Assuming the thermal voltage to be [latex]20 \mathrm{mV}[/latex]. The difference between [latex]E_{C}[/latex] and [latex]E_{D}[/latex] (in [latex]\mathrm{eV}[/latex], rounded off to two decimal places) is ______
2024.html: A non-degenerate n-type semiconductor has 5\% neutral dopant atoms. Its Fermi level is located at [latex]0.25 \mathrm{eV}[/latex] below the conduction band [latex]\left(E_{C}\right)[/latex] and the donor energy level [latex]\left(E_{D}\right)[/latex] has a degeneracy of 2. Assuming the thermal voltage to be [latex]20 \mathrm{mV}[/latex]. The difference between [latex]E_{C}[/latex] and [latex]E_{D}[/latex] (in [latex]\mathrm{eV}[/latex], rounded off to two decimal places) is ______
2024.subject: Electronic Devices - Basic Semiconductor Physics
2024.explanation_html:
[latex]5 \%[/latex] neutral donor atoms/dopant atoms means [latex]95 \%[/latex] donor atoms are ionized.
Concentration of electrons occupying the donor level is given as
[latex] n_{d}=\frac{N_{d}}{1+\frac{1}{g} \exp \left(\frac{E_{D}-E_{F}}{k T}\right)} [/latex]
and [latex]n_{d}=N_{d}-N_{d}^{+}[/latex]where [latex]N_{d}^{+}[/latex]is ionized donor atoms concentration.
according to question
[latex] \begin{aligned} n_{d} & =5 \% \text { of } N_{d} \\ g & =2 \text { degeneracy factor } \end{aligned} [/latex]

[latex] \frac{5}{100} N_{d}=\frac{N_{d}}{1+\frac{1}{g} \exp \left(\frac{E_{D}-E_{F}}{k T}\right)} [/latex]

[latex] \frac{1}{20}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{g} \exp \left(\frac{E_{D}-E_{F}}{k T}\right)} [/latex]

[latex] 1+\frac{1}{g} \exp \left(\frac{E_{D}-E_{F}}{k T}\right)=20 [/latex]

[latex] \exp \left(\frac{E_{D}-E_{F}}{k T}\right)=38 [/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{E_{D}-E_{F}}{k T} & =\ln (38) \quad\left\{\text { given } V_{T}=\frac{k T}{q}=20 \mathrm{mV}\right\} \\ E_{D}-E_{F} & =\ln (38) \times 0.020 \\ & =0.07275 \mathrm{eV} \end{aligned} [/latex]
given: [latex]\quad E_{C}-E_{F}=0.25 \mathrm{eV}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad E_{C}-E_{D}+E_{D}-E_{F}=0.25 \mathrm{eV}[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} E_{C}-E_{D} & =0.25 \mathrm{eV}-\left(E_{D}-E_{F}\right) \\ & =0.25 \mathrm{eV}-0.07275 \mathrm{eV} \\ & =0.17725 \mathrm{eV} \simeq 0.18 \mathrm{eV} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Keeping [latex]V_{G S}[/latex] constant, the [latex]V_{D S}[/latex] is increased to [latex]1.5 \mathrm{~V}[/latex]. Given that [latex]\mu_{n} C_{o x} \frac{W}{L}=50 \mu \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{V}^{2}[/latex], the transconductance at the new operating point (in [latex]\mu \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{V}[/latex], rounded off to two decimal places) is ________

An NMOS transistor operating in the linear region has [latex]I_{D S}[/latex] of [latex]5 \mu \mathrm{A}[/latex] at [latex]V_{D S}[/latex] of [latex]0.1 \mathrm{~V}[/latex]. Keeping [latex]V_{G S}[/latex] constant, the [latex]V_{D S}[/latex] is increased to [latex]1.5 \mathrm{~V}[/latex].
Given that [latex]\mu_{n} C_{o x} \frac{W}{L}=50 \mu \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{V}^{2}[/latex], the transconductance at the new operating point (in [latex]\mu \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{V}[/latex], rounded off to two decimal places) is ________
2024.subject: Electronic Devices - BJT and FET Basics
2024.explanation_html:
For linear region of MOS,
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{D} & =\mu_{n} C_{O X}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)\left[\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) V_{D S}-\frac{1}{2} V_{D S}^{2}\right] \\ 5 \times 10^{-6} & =50 \times 10^{-6}\left[\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) 0.1-\frac{1}{2}(0.1)^{2}\right] \\ \frac{1}{10} & =\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) 0.1-\frac{1}{2} \times 0.1^{2} \\ 0.1+0.5(0.1)^{2} & =\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) 0.1 \\ 1+0.5(0.1) & =\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) \\ 1.05 \text { volt } & =V_{G S}-V_{T} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Now: [latex]V_{G S} \rightarrow[/latex] fix
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{D S} & =1.5 \\ V_{D S} & >V_{G S}-V_{T} \Rightarrow \mathrm{MOS} \text { is in saturation } \\ g_{m \text { (sat) }} & =\mu_{n} C_{o x}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)\left(V_{G S}-V_{T}\right) \\ & =50 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.05 \\ & =52.5 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{V}=52.5 \mu \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{V} \end{aligned} [/latex]

2023.explanation_text:
[latex]\int_{P}^{Q} z^{2} d x+3 y^{2} d y+2 x z d z[/latex] along the line joining the points [latex]P(1,1,2)[/latex] and [latex]Q(2,3,1)[/latex] is [latex]

& =\int_{P(1,2)}^{P(2,1)} z^{2} d x+2 x y d z+\int_{y=1}^{3} 3 y^{2} d y \\

2023.explanation_html:
Given,

Let
[latex] \begin{aligned} (x)_{n \times 1} & =\left[\begin{array}{l} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \\ \vdots \\ x_{n} \end{array}\right] \\ l & =\sqrt{x^{T} x}=\sqrt{x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2}+\ldots x_{n}^{2}} \\ P & =x x^{T} \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{l} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \\ \cdot \\ x_{n} \end{array}\right]\left[x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} \ldots x_{n}\right]\\ P&=\left[ \begin{array}{lllll} x_{1}^{2} & & & & \\ & x_{1}^{2} & & & \\ & & - & & \\ & & & - & \\ & & & & x_{n}^{2} \end{array} \right] \end{aligned} [/latex]
Trace of [latex]P=x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+ . . .+ x_{n}^{2}=l^2[/latex]

[latex] Y(s)=\underbrace{G_{1}(s) R(s)}_{Y_{1}(s)}+\underbrace{G_{2}(s) D(s)}_{Y_{2}(s)} [/latex] Considering first [latex]R(s)[/latex] only, then [latex]Y(s)[/latex] is [latex]Y_{1}(s)[/latex]



[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{Y_{1}(s)}{R(s)}&=\frac{\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s) H(s)}}{1+\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s) H(s)}} \\ \frac{Y_{1}(s)}{R(s)}&=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s) H(s)+G(s)} \\ Y_{1}(s)&=\left[\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)+G(s) H(s)}\right] R(s) \\ G_{1}(s)&=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)+G(s) H(s)} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Now considering [latex]D(s)[/latex] only, then [latex]Y(s)[/latex] is [latex]Y_{2}(s)[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{Y_{2}(s)}{D(s)} & =\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)[1+H(s)]} \\ Y_{2}(s) & =\left[\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)+G(s) H(s)}\right] D(s) \\ G_{2}(s) & =\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)+G(s) H(s)} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence, [latex]G_{1}(s)[/latex] and [latex]G_{2}(s)[/latex] both are equal.

2023.explanation_html:
[latex] x(t)=A \cos \left[\omega_{c} t+K_{f} \int_{-\infty}^{t} m(\lambda) d \lambda\right] [/latex]
B.W. [latex][x(t)] \rightarrow B T=2[\Delta f+\omega][/latex]

[latex] \left.x^{2}(t) \rightarrow \begin{array}{c} \Delta f^{\prime}=2 \Delta f \\ \omega_{c}^{\prime}=2 \omega_{c} \end{array}\right\} [/latex]

[latex]\mathrm{BW}\left[x^{2}(t)\right]=2\left[\Delta f^{\prime}+\omega\right][/latex] [latex]=2[2 \Delta f+\omega]=B T+2 \Delta f[/latex]
[latex]y(t)=2x(t)+5x^2(t) [/latex]

To recover [latex]x(t) \rightarrow \quad 2 \omega_{C}-\frac{B_{T}}{2}-\Delta f \gt \omega_{C}+\frac{B_{T}}{2}[/latex]
[latex]\omega_{c} \gt \Delta f+B T[/latex]
[latex]\omega_{c} \gt \Delta f+2 \Delta f+2 \omega[/latex]
[latex]\omega_{c} \gt 3 \Delta f+2 \omega[/latex]
[latex]\omega_{c} \gt \frac{3}{2}\{2[\Delta f+\omega]\}-\omega[/latex]
[latex]\omega_{c} \gt \frac{3}{2} B_{T}-\omega[/latex]
Compared to FM BW, message BW is very small. So, that it can be ignored.
[latex] \begin{aligned} \omega_{C} & \gt \frac{3}{2} B_{T} \\ \left[\omega_{C}\right]_{min } & =\frac{3}{2} B_{T} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Let the discrete-time Fourier series (DTFS) representation be [latex]x[n]=\sum_{k=0}^{4} a_{k} e^{\frac{j k 2 \pi n}{5}}[/latex], where [latex]a_{0}=1, a_{1}=3 j, a_{2}=2 j[/latex], [latex]a_{3}=-2 j[/latex] and [latex]a_{4}=-3 j[/latex]. 2023.subject: Signals and Systems - DTFS, DTFT and DFT
2023.explanation_html:
Let, [latex]I=\sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \sin \frac{4 \pi n}{5}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2 j} \sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot\left[e^{j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}-e^{-j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}\right] \\ & =\frac{1}{2 j}\left[\sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) e^{j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}-\sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot e^{-j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}\right] \quad (i) \end{aligned} [/latex]
As we know, [latex]\quad a_{k}=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot e^{-j k \cdot \frac{2 \pi}{N} n}[/latex] [latex] =\frac{1}{5} \sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot e^{-j \frac{2 \pi}{N} k n} [/latex]

Put [latex]K=2 ; \quad a_{2}=\frac{1}{5} \sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot e^{-j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}[/latex]

Put [latex]K=-2 ; \quad a_{-2}=\frac{1}{5} \sum_{n=0}^{4} x(n) \cdot e^{j \frac{4 \pi n}{5}}[/latex]

From equation (i),

[latex] \begin{aligned} I&=\frac{1}{2 j}\left[5 a_{-2}-5 a_{2}\right] & =\frac{5}{2 j}\left[a_{3}-a_{2}\right] \\ I & =\frac{5}{2 j}[-2 j-2 j]=-10 \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{rl} a_{-2} & =a_{-2+N} \\ \because \quad & =a_{-2+5} \\ & =a_{3} \end{array} [/latex]

The S-parameters of a two port network is given as

[latex] [S]=\left[\begin{array}{ll} S_{11} & S_{12} \\ S_{21} & S_{22} \end{array}\right] [/latex]

with reference to [latex]Z_{0}[/latex]. Two lossless transmission line sections of electrical lengths [latex]\theta_{1}=\beta l_{1}[/latex] and [latex]\theta_{2}=\beta l 2[/latex] are added to the input and output ports for measurement purposes, respectively. The S-parameters [latex]\left[S^{\prime}\right][/latex] of the resultant two port network is
2023.subject: Network Theory - Two Port Networks
2023.explanation_html:
Let us evaluate [latex]S_{11}[/latex] and [latex]S_{21}[/latex] first at [latex]V_{2}^{+}=0[/latex]

(A) [latex]S11:[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{1}&=V_{1}^{+}+V_{1}^{-}=\left(V_{1}^{+}\right)^{\prime} e^{-j \beta l_{1}}+\left(V_{1}^{-}\right) e^{+j \beta l_{1}} \\ \therefore \quad V_{1}^{+}&=\left(V_{1}^{+}\right)^{\prime} e^{-j \beta l_{1}} \\ V_{1}^{-}&=\left(V_{1}^{-}\right) e^{+j \beta l_{1}} \\ S_{11}&=\frac{V_{1}^{-}}{V_{1}^{+}}=\frac{\left(V_{1}^{-}\right) e^{+j \beta l_{1}}}{\left(V_{1}^{+}\right)^{\prime} e^{-j \beta l_{1}}}=S_{11}^{\prime} e^{+j 2 \beta l_{1}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad S_{11}^{\prime}&=S_{11} e^{-j 2 \beta l_{1}}=S_{11} e^{-j 2 \theta_{1}} \\ \therefore \quad S_{11}^{\prime}&=S_{11} e^{-j 2 \theta_{1}} \end{aligned} [/latex]

(B) [latex]S_{21}[/latex] :
[latex] V_{2}=V_{2}^{+} e^{+j \beta l_{2}}+V_{2}^{-} e^{-j \beta l_{2}}=\left(V_{2}^{+}\right)^{\prime}+\left(V_{2}^{-}\right)^{\prime} [/latex]
Here, [latex]V_{2}^{+}=0[/latex]
Hence,
[latex] V_{2}=\left(V_{2}^{-}\right)^{\prime}=V_{2}^{-} e^{-j \beta l_{2}} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad V_{2}^{-}=\left(V_{2}^{-}\right)^{\prime} e^{+j \beta l_{2}} [/latex]

From previous discussion in [latex]S_{11}[/latex],
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{1}^{+}&=\left(V_{1}^{+}\right) e^{-j l_{1}} \\ \therefore \quad S_{21}&=\frac{V_{2}^{-}}{V_{1}^{+}}=\frac{\left(V_{2}^{-}\right)^{\prime} e^{+j \beta l_{2}}}{\left(V_{1}^{+}\right)^{\prime} e^{-j \beta l_{1}}}=S_{21}^{\prime} e^{+j\left(\beta l_{2}+\beta l_{1}\right)} \\ \Rightarrow S_{21}^{\prime}&=S_{21} e^{-j\left(\beta l_{2}+\beta l_{1}\right)} \\ \Rightarrow \quad S_{21}^{\prime}&=S_{21} e^{-j\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\right)} \end{aligned} [/latex]

The distance between successive voltage minima is [latex]30 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex] and the first minimum is located at [latex]10 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex] from the load. [latex]Z_{L}[/latex] can be replaced by an equivalent length [latex]l_{m}[/latex] and terminating resistance [latex]R_{m}[/latex] of the same line. The value of [latex]R_{m}[/latex] and [latex]l_{m}[/latex], respectively, are
2023.subject: Electromagnetics - Transmission Lines
2023.explanation_html:
Given [latex]S=2, Z_{\min }=10 \mathrm{~cm}, Z_{0}=50 \Omega[/latex]
As we know that, [latex]\quad|\Gamma|=\frac{S-1}{S+1}=\frac{2-1}{2+1}=\frac{1}{3}[/latex]
Now, distance between successive voltage minima [latex]=30 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\lambda}{2}=30 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \lambda=60 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]

Also, for minima,
[latex] 2 \beta Z_{\min }=(2 n+1) \pi+\theta_{\Gamma} [/latex]

At [latex]n=0,1 \mathrm{st}[/latex] minima, [latex]Z_{\text {min }}=10 \mathrm{~cm}[/latex]
[latex] \frac{4 \pi}{\lambda} Z_{\min }=\pi+\theta_{\Gamma} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{4 \pi}{60} * 10=\pi+\theta_{\Gamma}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{2 \pi}{3}-\pi=\theta_{\Gamma}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \theta_{\Gamma}=\frac{-\pi}{3} \quad \therefore \Gamma=\frac{1}{3} \angle-60^{\circ}[/latex]

Now, [latex] \Gamma=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}} [/latex]


[latex]\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow \quad & Z_{L}=Z_{0}\left[\frac{1+\Gamma}{1-\Gamma}\right] \\ \Rightarrow & Z_{L}=50\left[\frac{1+0.33 e^{-j \frac{\pi}{3}}}{1-0.33 e^{-j \frac{\pi}{3}}}\right]\end{array}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad Z_{L}=67.97 \angle-32.67^{\circ}[/latex]
Now [latex]Z_{\text {in }}=Z_{0}\left[\frac{Z_{L}+j Z_{0} \tan \beta l}{Z_{0}+j Z_{L} \tan \beta l}\right][/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad Z_{\text {in }}=50\left[\frac{R_{m}+j 50 \tan \beta l_{m}}{50+j R_{m} \tan \beta l_{m}}\right][/latex]
Here, [latex]\quad Z_{\text {in }}=Z_{L}=67.97 \angle-32.67^{\circ}[/latex]
Going through options,
[latex]\left.\begin{array}{l}R_{m}=100 \Omega \text { and } L_{m}=5 \mathrm{~cm} \\ R_{m}=25 \Omega \text { and } L_{m}=20 \mathrm{~cm}\end{array}\right\}[/latex] satisfy this identity, hence option (B) and (C) are correct.

2023.text: The electric field of a plane electromagnetic wave is [latex]E=a_{x} C_{1 x} \cos (\omega t-\beta z)+a_{y} C_{1 y} \cos (\omega t-\beta z+\theta) \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{m}[/latex] Which of the following combination(s) will give rise to a left handed elliptically polarized (LHEP) wave?
2023.html:
The electric field of a plane electromagnetic wave is

[latex]E=a_{x} C_{1 x} \cos (\omega t-\beta z)+a_{y} C_{1 y} \cos (\omega t-\beta z+\theta) \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{m}[/latex]

Which of the following combination(s) will give rise to a left handed elliptically polarized (LHEP) wave?
2023.subject: Electromagnetics - Uniform Plane Waves
2023.explanation_html:
Given, [latex]\quad \vec{E}=\hat{a}_{x} C_{1 x} \cos (\omega t-\beta z)+\hat{a}_{y} C_{1 y} \cos (\omega t-\beta z+\theta)[/latex]
at [latex]z=0[/latex]
[latex] \vec{E}=C_{1 x} \cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+C_{1 y} \cos (\omega t+\theta) \hat{a}_{y} [/latex]
Going by options,

Option (A) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=\cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+\cos (\omega t+\pi / 4) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \omega t=0, \vec{E}=\hat{a}_{x}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=0-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is LHEP.



Option (B) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=2 \cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+\cos (\omega t+\pi / 2) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \omega t=0, \vec{E}=2 \hat{a}_{x}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=-1 \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is LHEP.



Option (C) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=\cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+2 \cos (\omega t+3 \pi / 2) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \quad \quad \omega t=0, \vec{E}=\hat{a}_{x}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=2 \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is RHEP.



Option (D) [latex]\quad \vec{E}=2 \cos \omega t \hat{a}_{x}+\cos (\omega t+3 \pi / 4) \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=0, \omega t=0, \vec{E}=2 \hat{a}_{x}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
at [latex]t=T / 4, \omega t=\pi / 2, \vec{E}=0-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{2}} \hat{a}_{y}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] Hence, it is LHEP.


[latex]\therefore[/latex] Option (A), (B) and (D) are correct.

The ratio of electron to hole mobility for equal hole and electron drift current is given as  ___ (rounded off to two decimal places).
2023.html:
In an extrinsic semiconductor, the hole concentration is given to be [latex]1.5 n_{i}[/latex] where [latex]n_{i}[/latex] is the intrinsic carrier concentration of [latex]1 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]. The ratio of electron to hole mobility for equal hole and electron drift current is given as ___
(rounded off to two decimal places).
2023.subject: Electronic Devices - Basic Semiconductor Physics
2023.explanation_html:
Given, intrinsic carrier concentration [latex]n_{i}=1 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]
Hole concentration,
[latex]\quad p=1.5 \times n_{i}[/latex]
[latex] p=1.5 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} [/latex]

Given, electron and hole current are equal
[latex] \begin{aligned} I_{p \text { dritt }} & =I_{n \text { dritt }} \\ p q \mu_{p} E A & =n q \mu_{n} E A \\ 1.5 \times 10^{10} \mu_{p} & =n \mu_{n} \quad ...(i) \end{aligned} [/latex]

But according to mass action law,
[latex] \begin{aligned} n p & =n_{i}^{2} \\ n & =\frac{n_{i}}{1.5}=\frac{10^{10}}{1.5} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Put in equation (i)
[latex]\therefore \quad 1.5 \times 10^{10} \mu_{p}=\frac{10^{10}}{1.5} \times \mu_{n}[/latex]
[latex] \frac{\mu_{n}}{\mu_{p}}=2.25 [/latex]

2023.subject: Signals and Systems - LTI Systems Continuous and Discrete
2023.explanation_html:
[latex]h(t)=e^{-t} u(t)[/latex]
Given: Input PSD
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad S_{x}(f)=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{Hz}[/latex]

We know output PSD,
[latex] \begin{aligned} S_{Y}(f) & =S_{X}(f)|H(f)|^{2} \\ S_{Y}(f) & =\frac{1}{2}|H(f)|^{2} \\ \text { Power }[y(t)] & =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} S_{Y}(f) d f=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2}|H(f)|^{2} d f \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h^{2}(t) d t=\frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-2 t} d t \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4}=0.25 \mathrm{~W} \end{aligned} [/latex]

2023.html: A transparent dielectric coating is applied to glass [latex]\left(\epsilon_{r}=4, \mu_{r}=1\right)[/latex] to eliminate the reflection of red light [latex]\left(\lambda_{0}=0.75 \mu \mathrm{m}\right)[/latex]. The minimum thickness of the dielectric coating, in [latex]\mu \mathrm{m}[/latex], that can be used is ____ (rounded off to two decimal places).
2023.subject: Electromagnetics - Basics of Electromagnetics
2023.explanation_html:
For no reflection, impedance must be matched.
Hence, [latex]\eta_{2}[/latex] acts like a quarter wave impedance transformer.

So,
[latex] (i) \quad \eta_{2}=\sqrt{\eta_{1} \cdot \eta_{3}} \Rightarrow \epsilon_{r_{2}}=\sqrt{\epsilon_{r_{1}} \cdot \epsilon_{r_{3}}} \Rightarrow \epsilon_{r_{2}}=2 [/latex]

(ii) For impedance matching,
[latex] \begin{aligned} & d=(2 n+1) \frac{\lambda}{4} ; n=0,1,2 \ldots \\ & \lambda=\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r}}}=\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r_{2}}}} \\ Here \;\;& \lambda=\frac{0.75 \times 10^{-6}}{\sqrt{2}}=0.53 \times 10^{-6} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Hence, for minimum distance, [latex]n=0[/latex]
So, [latex] d=\frac{\lambda}{4}=\frac{0.53 \times 10^{-6}}{4}=0.133 \mu \mathrm{m} [/latex]

2023.html:
In a semiconductor device, the Fermi-energy level is [latex]0.35 \mathrm{eV}[/latex] above the valence band energy. The effective density of states in the valence band at [latex]T=300 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] is [latex]1 \times 10^{19} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]. The thermal equilibrium hole concentration in silicon at [latex]400 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] is ___ [latex]\_\times 10^{13} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}[/latex]. (rounded off to two decimal places).
Given [latex]\mathrm{kT}[/latex] at [latex]300 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] is [latex]0.026 \mathrm{eV}[/latex].
2023.subject: Electronic Devices - Basic Semiconductor Physics
2023.explanation_html:
Given,
[latex] E_{F}-E_{V}=0.35 \mathrm{eV} \quad \text { [Considering it is given at } 400 \mathrm{~K} \text { ] } [/latex]
Also, [latex]V_{T_{1}}=K T_{1}=0.026 \mathrm{eV}[/latex] at [latex]T_{1}=300 \mathrm{~K}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] [latex]\frac{V_{T_{1}}}{V_{T_{2}}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}} \Rightarrow V_{T_{2}}=\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}} \times V_{T_{1}}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] [latex]V_{T_{2}}=\frac{400}{300} \times 0.026[/latex]
[latex]V_{T_{2}}=0.03466 \mathrm{eV}[/latex] at [latex]T_{2}=400 \mathrm{~K}[/latex]

Now, [latex]N_{v}=1 \times 10^{19} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}[/latex] at [latex]T_{1}=300 \mathrm{~K}[/latex]
[latex]N_{v} \propto T^{3 / 2}[/latex]
[latex]\frac{N_{V_{2}}}{N_{V_{1}}}=\left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)^{3 / 2}[/latex]
[latex]N_{V_{2}}=\left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)^{3 / 2} N V_{1}[/latex]
[latex]\left(\because T_{2}=400 \mathrm{~K}\right)[/latex] [latex]=\left(\frac{400}{300}\right)^{3 / 2} N_{V_{1}}[/latex]
[latex]N_{V_{2}}=1.5396 \times 10^{19} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}[/latex]

Now, hole concentration at [latex]400 \mathrm{~K}[/latex] is given as
[latex] \begin{aligned} & p=N_{V} e^{-\left(E_{F}-E_{V}\right) / k T_{2}}=1.5396 \times 10^{19} \times e^{-0.35 \mathrm{eV} / 0.03466 \mathrm{eV}} \\ & p=63.36 \times 10^{13} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3} \end{aligned} [/latex]

2023.text: A sample and hold circuit is implemented using a resistive switch and a capacitor with a time constant of [latex]1 \mu \mathrm{s}[/latex]. The time for sampling switch to stay closed to charge a capacitor adequately to a full scale voltage of [latex]1 \mathrm{~V}[/latex] with 12-bit accuracy is ____ [latex]\mu \mathrm{s}[/latex]. (rounded off to two decimal places)
2023.html: A sample and hold circuit is implemented using a resistive switch and a capacitor with a time constant of [latex]1 \mu \mathrm{s}[/latex]. The time for sampling switch to stay closed to charge a capacitor adequately to a full scale voltage of [latex]1 \mathrm{~V}[/latex] with 12-bit accuracy is ____ [latex]\mu \mathrm{s}[/latex]. (rounded off to two decimal places)
2023.subject: Network Theory - Transient Analysis
2023.explanation_html:
Given: Time constant [latex](\tau)[/latex] of [latex]1 \mu \mathrm{sec}[/latex].
Full scale voltage [latex]=1 \mathrm{~V}[/latex]

The voltage across capacitor is given as
[latex]\quad \quad V_{c}(t)=V_{\text {in }}\left(1-e^{-t / \tau}\right)[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad V_{c}(t)=\left(1-e^{-t / 1 \mu \mathrm{sec}}\right) \quad ...(i)[/latex]
To calculate the voltage to stay closed to charge capacitor adequately to a full scale voltage with 12-bit accuracy is given by
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{c}(t) & =V_{\text {ref }}\left[1-\frac{1}{2^{n}}\right] \\ n & =\text { Number of bit }=12 \\ V_{c}(t) & =\left[1-\frac{1}{4096}\right] \quad ...(ii) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Comparing equations (i) and (ii), we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} e^{-t / 1 \mu \mathrm{sec}} & =\frac{1}{4096} \\ -\frac{t}{1 \mu \mathrm{sec}} & =\ln \left\{\frac{1}{4096}\right\} \\ t & =8.3177 \mu \mathrm{sec} \end{aligned} [/latex]

How many students in the class like romantic movies?
2023.html:
In a class of 100 students,

(i) there are 30 students who neither like romantic movies nor comedy movies,
(ii) the number of students who like romantic movies is twice the number of students who like comedy movies, and
(iii) the number of students who like both romantic movies and comedy movies is 20.

How many students in the class like romantic movies?
2023.subject: General Aptitude - Numerical Ability
2023.explanation_text:
Let students who like Romantic Movies [latex]=R[/latex]. Students who like Comedy Movies [latex]=C[/latex]. Given [latex]R=2 C[/latex] Also, 30 students do not like Romantic and Comedy Movies both. [latex]
\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad 100-30&=70=n(R \cap C) \\
\text{and  } n(C \cap R)&=20 \\
n(R \cap C)&=n(R)+n(C)-n(C \cap R)\\
70&=2 C+C-20 
3 C & =90 \\
C & =30 \\
R & =2 C=60
\end{aligned}
[/latex]

equilibrium hole density is [latex]10^{17}cm^{-3}[/latex] and the intrinsic carrier concentration is [latex]10^{10}cm^{-3}[/latex]. Electron and hole diffusion lengths are [latex]2\mu m[/latex]and [latex]1\mu m[/latex], respectively.
The left side of the bar ([latex]x=0[/latex]) is uniformly illuminated with a laser having photon
energy greater than the bandgap of the semiconductor. Excess electron-hole pairs
are generated ONLY at [latex]x=0[/latex] because of the laser. The steady state electron density
at [latex]x=0[/latex] is [latex]10^{14}cm^{-3}[/latex]
 due to laser illumination. Under these conditions and ignoring
electric field, the closest approximation (among the given options) of the steady state
electron density at [latex]x=2 \mu m[/latex], is _____
2022.html: Consider a long rectangular bar of direct bandgap p-type semiconductor. The equilibrium hole density is [latex]10^{17}cm^{-3}[/latex] and the intrinsic carrier concentration is [latex]10^{10}cm^{-3}[/latex]. Electron and hole diffusion lengths are [latex]2\mu m[/latex]and [latex]1\mu m[/latex], respectively. Excess electron-hole pairs are generated ONLY at [latex]x=0[/latex] because of the laser. The steady state electron density at [latex]x=0[/latex] is [latex]10^{14}cm^{-3}[/latex] due to laser illumination. Under these conditions and ignoring electric field, the closest approximation (among the given options) of the steady state electron density at [latex]x=2 \mu m[/latex], is _____
2022.subject: Electronic Devices - Basic Semiconductor Physics
2022.explanation_text:
From continuity equation of electrons [latex]\frac{dn}{dt}=n\mu _n\frac{dE}{dx}+\mu _nE\frac{dn}{dx}+G_n-R_n+x_n\frac{d^2x}{dx^2} \;\;\;...(i)[/latex] [Because 
 [latex]\vec{E}[/latex] is not mentioned hence [latex]\frac{dE}{dx}=0[/latex] For 
 [latex] x \gt 0, G_n[/latex]  is also zero [latex]n=\frac{n_i^2}{N_A}=\frac{10^{20}}{10^{17}}=10^3[/latex] [latex]n=n_0+\delta n=10^3+10^{14}=10^{14}[/latex] at steady state, 
[latex]\frac{db}{dt}=0[/latex] Hence equation (i) becomes: [latex]O=D_n\frac{d^2\delta n}{dx^2}-\frac{\delta n}{\tau _n}[/latex] [latex]\frac{d^2\delta n}{dx^2}=\frac{\delta n}{L_n^2} \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex] From solving equation (ii) [latex]\delta _n(x)=\delta _n(0)e^{-x/L_n}[/latex] at  
[latex]x=2\mu m[/latex] [latex]\delta _n(2\mu m)=10^{14}e^{-2/2}=10^{14}e^{-1}=0.37 \times 10^{14}[/latex]
2022.explanation_html:
From continuity equation of electrons
[latex]\frac{dn}{dt}=n\mu _n\frac{dE}{dx}+\mu _nE\frac{dn}{dx}+G_n-R_n+x_n\frac{d^2x}{dx^2} \;\;\;...(i)[/latex]
[Because [latex]\vec{E}[/latex] is not mentioned hence
[latex]\frac{dE}{dx}=0[/latex]
For [latex] x \gt 0, G_n[/latex] is also zero
[latex]n=\frac{n_i^2}{N_A}=\frac{10^{20}}{10^{17}}=10^3[/latex]
[latex]n=n_0+\delta n=10^3+10^{14}=10^{14}[/latex]
at steady state, [latex]\frac{db}{dt}=0[/latex]
Hence equation (i) becomes:
[latex]O=D_n\frac{d^2\delta n}{dx^2}-\frac{\delta n}{\tau _n}[/latex]
[latex]\frac{d^2\delta n}{dx^2}=\frac{\delta n}{L_n^2} \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
From solving equation (ii)
[latex]\delta _n(x)=\delta _n(0)e^{-x/L_n}[/latex]
at [latex]x=2\mu m[/latex]
[latex]\delta _n(2\mu m)=10^{14}e^{-2/2}=10^{14}e^{-1}=0.37 \times 10^{14}[/latex]

2022.explanation_text:
Here we have to find the value of
[latex]E_c-E_{fn}[/latex] As we know, [latex]E_C-E_F=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n} \right ) \;\;\;...(i)[/latex] [latex]E_C-E_{F1}=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n_1} \right ) \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex] [latex]E_C-E_{F2}=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n_2} \right ) \;\;\;...(iii)[/latex] Equation (ii) - Equation (iii) [latex](E_C-E_{F1})-(E_C-E_{F2})=kT \ln \left ( \frac{\frac{N_c}{n_1}}{\frac{N_c}{n_2}} \right )=kT \ln \frac{n_2}{n_1}[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow 200meV-(E_C-E_{F2})=26meV \times \ln \left ( \frac{0.5 \times 10^{16}}{1 \times 10^{16}} \right )[/latex] [latex] 200meV-(E_C-E_{F2})=+26meV \ln (0.5)=-18[/latex] [latex](E_C-E_{F2})=200+8=218meV[/latex]
2022.explanation_html:
Here we have to find the value of [latex]E_c-E_{fn}[/latex]
As we know,
[latex]E_C-E_F=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n} \right ) \;\;\;...(i)[/latex]
[latex]E_C-E_{F1}=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n_1} \right ) \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
[latex]E_C-E_{F2}=kT \ln\left ( \frac{N_c}{n_2} \right ) \;\;\;...(iii)[/latex]
Equation (ii) - Equation (iii)
[latex](E_C-E_{F1})-(E_C-E_{F2})=kT \ln \left ( \frac{\frac{N_c}{n_1}}{\frac{N_c}{n_2}} \right )=kT \ln \frac{n_2}{n_1}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow 200meV-(E_C-E_{F2})=26meV \times \ln \left ( \frac{0.5 \times 10^{16}}{1 \times 10^{16}} \right )[/latex]
[latex] 200meV-(E_C-E_{F2})=+26meV \ln (0.5)=-18[/latex]
[latex](E_C-E_{F2})=200+8=218meV[/latex]

Consider the following partial differential equation (PDE)
[latex]a\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2} +b\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2}=f(x,y)[/latex]
, where [latex]a[/latex]and [latex]b[/latex] are distinct positive real numbers. Select the combination(s) of values of the real parameters [latex]\xi [/latex] and [latex]\eta [/latex] such that [latex]f(x,y)=e^{(\xi x+\eta y)} [/latex] is a solution of the given PDE.
2022.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
2022.explanation_text:
Given [latex] \begin{aligned}
 f(x,y)&=e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\
\frac{\partial f(x,y)}{\partial x}&=\xi \cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\
\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2}&=\xi ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\
\end{aligned}[/latex] Similarly, [latex] \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2}=\eta ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}[/latex] Now, as given [latex]a \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2}+b\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2}=f(x,y)[/latex] or [latex]a \times \xi ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}+b \times  \eta  ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}= e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}[/latex] [latex] a\cdot \xi ^2+b\cdot \eta ^2=1[/latex] Thus,  
[latex]\xi =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2a}}, \eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2b}}[/latex] [latex](\xi =\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}, \eta = 0)[/latex] and [latex](\xi =0, \eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{b}})[/latex] satisfy the above result.
2022.explanation_html:
Given
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(x,y)&=e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\ \frac{\partial f(x,y)}{\partial x}&=\xi \cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\ \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2}&=\xi ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Similarly,
[latex] \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2}=\eta ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}[/latex]
Now, as given
[latex]a \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2}+b\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2}=f(x,y)[/latex]
or
[latex]a \times \xi ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}+b \times \eta ^2\cdot e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}= e^{(\xi x+\eta y)}[/latex]
[latex] a\cdot \xi ^2+b\cdot \eta ^2=1[/latex]
Thus, [latex]\xi =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2a}}, \eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2b}}[/latex]
[latex](\xi =\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}, \eta = 0)[/latex] and [latex](\xi =0, \eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{b}})[/latex] satisfy the above result.

2022.subject: Digital Circuits - Logic Gates
2022.explanation_text:
[latex] \begin{aligned}
y &=A+\bar{B} =\overline{\bar{A}\cdot B}\\ 
 f(A,B)&=A+\bar{B} \\ 
f(0,B) &=0+\bar{B}=\bar{B}\Rightarrow NOT\; Gate \\ 
f(A,\bar{B}) &=A+\bar{\bar{B}} =A+B\Rightarrow OR \;Gate\\ 
 f(0,f(A,\bar{B}))&=0+(\overline{A+B})\Rightarrow NOR \; Gate \\ 
f(\bar{A},B) &= \bar{A}+\bar{B}=\overline{A\cdot B}\Rightarrow NAND\; Gate\\ 
 f(0,f(\bar{A},B))&=0+\overline{\overline{A\cdot B}} =A\cdot B\Rightarrow AND \; Gate
\end{aligned}[/latex] Since, we can implement NOT Gate we can
also implement OR, AND, NOR and NAND Gate.

2022.explanation_text:
[latex] \begin{aligned}

electronic charge, [latex] q=-1.6 \times 10^{-19}C[/latex]. The profiles of photo-generation rate of
carriers and the recombination rate of excess minority carriers (R) are shown. Under
these conditions, the magnitude of the current density due to the photo-generated

2022.html: A p-type semiconductor with zero electric field is under illumination (low level injection) in steady state condition. Excess minority carrier density is zero at [latex] x=\pm 2l_n[/latex], where [latex] l_n=10^{-4} cm[/latex] is the diffusion length of electrons. Assume electronic charge, [latex] q=-1.6 \times 10^{-19}C[/latex]. The profiles of photo-generation rate of carriers and the recombination rate of excess minority carriers (R) are shown. Under these conditions, the magnitude of the current density due to the photo-generated electrons at [latex] x=+2l_n[/latex] is _________ [latex] mA/cm^2[/latex] (rounded off to two decimal places).
2022.subject: Electronic Devices - PN-Junction Diodes and Special Diodes
2022.explanation_text:
Given, [latex] \begin{aligned}
\delta _n(x)&=R\tau _n=10^{20}e^{-|x|/l_n}\cdot \tau _n\\
\delta (l_n)&=10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n \;\;\;...(i)\\
for \;\; l_n\leq x\leq 2l_n
\end{aligned}[/latex] Continuity equation is given by [latex] D_n\frac{\partial^2 \delta _n}{\partial x^2}+G-R \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex] G and R both are zero - for
[latex] [l_n\leq x\leq 2l_n][/latex] Hence Equation (i) reduced to 
[latex] D_n \frac{\partial^n \delta _n }{\partial x^2}=0[/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow \delta _n(x)=Ax+B[/latex] For calculating A and B we use Boundary
condition [latex] \delta _n(2l_n)=0\; \Rightarrow A=\frac{-B}{2l_n}[/latex] [latex] \therefore \delta _n(x)=\frac{-B}{2l_n}x+B=B\left [ 1-\frac{x}{2l_n} \right ] \;\;\;...(iii)[/latex] At 
[latex]x=l_n [/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned}
 10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n&=B\left [ 1-\frac{l_n}{2l_n} \right ] \\ 
 B&= 2 \times 10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n\\ 
\therefore \; \delta _n(x) &=2 \times 10^{20} e^{-1}\tau _n\left [ 1-\frac{x}{2l_n} \right ]
\end{aligned} [/latex] for [latex]l_n \leq x \leq 2l_n [/latex] Electron diffusion current density is given by
[latex] |J_n|_{diff}=qD_n\frac{d\eta }{dx}=qD_n \times 2 \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1} \times \tau _n\left [ 0-\frac{1}{2l_n} \right ][/latex] [latex] =\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times l_n ^2 \times 2 \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1}}{2l_n}[/latex] [latex]=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times l_n  \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1} [/latex] [latex] =1.6 \times 10 \times 1 \times 10^{-4} \times e^{-1}[/latex] [latex] =0.59mA/cm^2[/latex]
2022.explanation_html:
Given,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \delta _n(x)&=R\tau _n=10^{20}e^{-|x|/l_n}\cdot \tau _n\\ \delta (l_n)&=10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n \;\;\;...(i)\\ for \;\; l_n\leq x\leq 2l_n \end{aligned}[/latex]
Continuity equation is given by
[latex] D_n\frac{\partial^2 \delta _n}{\partial x^2}+G-R \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
G and R both are zero - for [latex] [l_n\leq x\leq 2l_n][/latex]
Hence Equation (i) reduced to [latex] D_n \frac{\partial^n \delta _n }{\partial x^2}=0[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \delta _n(x)=Ax+B[/latex]
For calculating A and B we use Boundary condition
[latex] \delta _n(2l_n)=0\; \Rightarrow A=\frac{-B}{2l_n}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \delta _n(x)=\frac{-B}{2l_n}x+B=B\left [ 1-\frac{x}{2l_n} \right ] \;\;\;...(iii)[/latex]
At [latex]x=l_n [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} 10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n&=B\left [ 1-\frac{l_n}{2l_n} \right ] \\ B&= 2 \times 10^{20}e^{-1}\tau _n\\ \therefore \; \delta _n(x) &=2 \times 10^{20} e^{-1}\tau _n\left [ 1-\frac{x}{2l_n} \right ] \end{aligned} [/latex]
for [latex]l_n \leq x \leq 2l_n [/latex]
Electron diffusion current density is given by [latex] |J_n|_{diff}=qD_n\frac{d\eta }{dx}=qD_n \times 2 \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1} \times \tau _n\left [ 0-\frac{1}{2l_n} \right ][/latex]
[latex] =\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times l_n ^2 \times 2 \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1}}{2l_n}[/latex]
[latex]=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times l_n \times 10^{20} \times e^{-1} [/latex]
[latex] =1.6 \times 10 \times 1 \times 10^{-4} \times e^{-1}[/latex]
[latex] =0.59mA/cm^2[/latex]

Channel capacity, [latex]C_s=Max[I(X:Y)] [/latex] [latex]I[(X:Y)]=H(Y)-H\left ( \frac{Y}{X} \right ) [/latex] Where, [latex] H\left ( \frac{Y}{X} \right )=-\sum_{i=1}^{3}\sum_{i=1}^{3}P(x_i,y_i) \log_2P\left ( \frac{y_i}{x_i} \right )[/latex] [latex] P\left ( \frac{Y}{X} \right )=\begin{matrix}
 &y_1  & y_2 & y_3\\ 
x_1 &1-\alpha   & \alpha  & 0\\ 
x_2 &0  &1-\alpha   &\alpha  \\ 
x_3 & \alpha  & 0 & 1-\alpha 
\end{matrix}[/latex] For simplication convenience, let

1-\alpha  & \alpha  &0 \\ 
 0&  0&0 \\ 
0 & 0 &0 
\end{bmatrix}\\
H\left ( \frac{Y}{X} \right )&=-((1-\alpha ) \log_2 (1-\alpha )+\alpha  \log _2 \alpha )\\

C_s&=MAX\left \{ (X:Y) \right \}\\
&=MAX\left \{ H(Y)+(1-\alpha ) \log_2 (1-\alpha )+ \log _2 \alpha \right \}\\
&=log_2 3+(1-\alpha ) \log_2 (1-\alpha )+\alpha  \log _2 \alpha

[latex] \alpha \in [0.25,1][/latex] Hence, [latex]\alpha =1 [/latex] is correct answer.

[latex]X_A [/latex] For

2021.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x}+\frac{x}{1-x^{2}} y&=x \sqrt{y}, \quad \text { IF }=?\\ \text{Divided by }\sqrt{y}\\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \frac{d y}{d x}+\frac{x}{1-x^{2}} \sqrt{y}&=x \\ 2 \frac{d u}{d x}+\frac{x}{1-x^{2}} u&=x\\ \text{Let }\qquad x \sqrt{y}&=u\\ \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{v}} \frac{d y}{d x}&=\frac{d u}{d x}\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \frac{d u}{d x}+\frac{x}{2\left(1-x^{2}\right)} u&=\frac{x}{2} \rightarrow \text{ lines diff. equ.} \\ \text { I. } F&=e^{\int \frac{x}{2\left(1-x^{2}\right)} d x}=e^{-\frac{1}{4} \log \left(1-x^{2}\right)}&=e^{\log \left(1-x^{2}\right) \frac{-1}{4}} \\ \text { I.F }&=\frac{1}{\left(1-x^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2021.explanation_text: Let [latex]\quad P\left(H_{2}\right)=[/latex] Probability of getting head in second toss [latex] P\left(H_{1}\right)=[/latex] Probability of getting head in first toss [latex] \begin{aligned} P\left(\frac{H_{2}}{H_{1}}\right) &=\frac{P\left(H_{2} \cap H_{1}\right)}{P\left(H_{1}\right)} \\ P\left(H_{1}\right) &=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3} \times 1+\frac{1}{3} \times 0=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] To get head in second toss when head came in first toss, following cases can be made 1. Fair coin : [latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Both head coin }=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times 1=\frac{1}{12} \\ \text { Both tail coin }=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times 0=0 \end{aligned}[/latex] 2. Both head coin : [latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Fair coin }&=\frac{1}{3} \times 1 \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{12}\\ \text{Both tail coin }&=0\\ \therefore \qquad P\left(H_{2} \cap H_{1}\right)&=\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{6} \\ \therefore \qquad P\left(H_{2} / H_{1}\right)&=\frac{1 / 6}{1 / 2}=\frac{1}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2021.explanation_text: [latex]A=\left[\begin{array}{cc} x & -3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right][/latex] Characteristic equation [latex] \begin{aligned} |A-\lambda I| &=\left|\begin{array}{cc} x-\lambda & -3 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{array}\right|=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \lambda^{2}-(4+x) \lambda+(4 x+9)&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex] Roots are repeating [latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \qquad b^{2}-4 a c&=0\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \left(4+x^{2}\right)-4(4 x+9) &=0 \\ 16+x^{2}+8 x-16 x-20 &=0 \\ x &=10 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad x^{2}-8 x+20 &=0\\ x&=\frac{8 \pm \sqrt{64+80}}{2} \\ &=\frac{8 \pm 12}{2}=-2,10 \end{aligned}[/latex] Since, x is positive [latex] \therefore x=10[/latex]

Since, x is positive

2021.explanation_html:
Method 1: [latex]\vec{D}=\rho \cos ^{2} \phi \hat{a}_{\rho}+z^{2} \sin ^{2} \phi \hat{a}_{\phi}[/latex]
Electric flux crossing the closed surface is
[latex] \begin{aligned} \psi &=\oiint \vec{D} \cdot \overrightarrow{d S}=\iiint(\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{D}) d v \\ \vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{D} &=\frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial}{\partial p}\left(\rho D_{\rho}\right)+\frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial D_{\phi}}{\partial \phi}+\frac{\partial D_{z}}{\partial z} \\ &=\frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial}{\partial p}\left(\rho \rho \cos ^{2} \phi\right)+\frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial}{\partial \phi}\left(z^{2} \sin ^{2} \phi\right)+0 \\ &=\frac{1}{\rho}(2 \rho) \cos ^{2} \phi+\frac{1}{\rho} z^{2} 2 \sin \phi \cos \phi=2 \cos ^{2} \phi+\frac{z^{2}}{\rho} \sin 2 \phi\\ \iiint(\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{D}) d v &=\iiint 2 \cos ^{2} \phi(\rho d \rho d \phi d z)+\iiint\left(\frac{z^{2}}{\rho} \sin 2 \phi\right) \rho d \rho d \phi d z \\ &=2 \int_{\rho=0}^{3} \rho d \rho \int_{\phi=0}^{2 \pi}\left(\frac{1+\cos 2 \phi}{2}\right) d \phi \int_{z=0}^{2} d z+\int_{\rho=0}^{2} d \rho \int_{\phi=0}^{2 \pi} \sin 2 \phi d \phi \int_{z=0}^{2} z^{2} d z \\ &=2\left(\frac{\rho^{2}}{-2}\right)_{\rho=0}^{3} \frac{1}{2}(2 \pi)(z)_{z=0}^{2}+0 \\ &=2\left(\frac{3^{2}}{2}\right) \pi(2)=18 \pi(\text { Coulomb })=56.55(\text { Coulomb }) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Method 2: Electric flux crossing the closed surface is
[latex] \psi=\oiint \vec{D} \cdot \overrightarrow{d S}[/latex]
Electric flux crossing \rho=3 cylindrical surface is
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left.\psi\right|_{\rho=3} &=\oiint\left(\rho \cos ^{2} \phi \hat{a}_{p}\right) \cdot(\rho d \phi d z) \hat{a}_{p} \\ &=3^{2} \int_{\phi=0}^{2 \pi} \cos ^{2} \phi d \phi \int_{z=0}^{2} d z \\ &=9 \frac{1}{2}(2 \pi)(2)=18 \pi(\text { coulomb })=56.55(\text { coulomb }) \end{aligned}[/latex]

2021.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} x[n] &=2^{n-1} u[-n+2] \\ y[n] &=2^{-n+2} u[n+1] \\ y[-n] &=2^{n+2} u[-n+1] \\ V &=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} X\left(e^{j \omega}\right) Y\left(e^{-j \omega}\right) d \omega &\ldots(i)\\ z[n] &=x[n] * y[-n] \\ z[n] & \rightarrow Z\left(e^{j \omega}\right) \\ z[n] &=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} Z\left(e^{j \omega}\right) e^{j \omega n} d \omega \\ \text { Put } n=0, \qquad z[0] &=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{0}^{2 \pi} Z\left(e^{j \omega}\right) d \omega &\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex] Compare equations (i) and (ii) [latex] \begin{aligned} z[0] &=V \\ Z\left(e^{j \omega}\right) &=X\left(e^{j \omega}\right) Y\left(e^{-j \omega}\right) \\ \text{Apply IDTFT},\qquad Z[n] &=x[n] * y[-n]=x[n] * p[n]\\ \because \qquad p[n]&=y[-n]=2^{n+2} u[-n+1]\\ z[n] &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{+\infty} 2^{k-1} u[-k+2] 2^{n-k+2} u[-n+k+1] \\ &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{2} 2^{k-1} 1 \cdot 2^{n-k+2} u[k+1-n] \\ &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{2} 2^{k-1+n-k+2} u[k+1-n] \\ z[n] &=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{2} 2^{n+1} u[k-n+1] \\ \text { Put } n=0,\qquad \qquad V &=z[0]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{2} 2^{1} \cdot u[k+1]=2 \sum_{k=-1}^{2} 1=2[1+1+1+1] \\ V &=8 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2021.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
2021.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given,}\qquad P(G)&=\frac{1}{2} \text { and } P(B)=\frac{1}{2} \\ P(C)&=\frac{1}{4} \text { and } P(S)=\frac{3}{4} \end{aligned}[/latex] Let probability of selected science student is a boy is [latex]P(B/S) = x[/latex] Given that Commerce students are two time more likely to be a boy than are Science students. Then, probability of selected Commerce student is a boy [latex] P\left(\frac{B}{C}\right)=2 x[/latex] We have to find probability of randomly selected girl studies Commerce i.e. [latex] \begin{aligned} P\left(\frac{C}{G}\right)&=\frac{P(C \cap G)}{P(G)}=\frac{P(C) P(G / C)}{P(G)} \\ P\left(\frac{C}{G}\right)&=\frac{\frac{1}{4} \times P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right)}{\frac{1}{2}} &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex] To find [latex]P(G / C)[/latex], first we have to find [latex]P(B/C).[/latex] The probability of selected student is a boy [latex]\begin{aligned} P(B) &=P(S) P(B / S)+P(C) \times P(B / C) \\ \frac{1}{2} &=\frac{3}{4} \times x+\frac{1}{4} \times 2 x \\ \Rightarrow\qquad\qquad x &=\frac{2}{5}\\ \text{Then},\qquad \qquad P(B / C)&=2 x=\frac{4}{5}\\ \text{We know that},\qquad \\ P\left(\frac{B}{C}\right)+P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right)&=1    \\ P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right) =1- \frac{4}{5}&=\frac{1}{5} \\ \text{From  equation (i),} \\ P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right) = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{\frac{5}{1/2}} &= \frac{1}{10} \end{aligned}[/latex] The amount of information gained in knowing that a randomly selected girl student studies Commerce [latex]I\left ( \frac{C}{G} \right )=\log _2 \frac{1}{P\left ( \frac{C}{G} \right )}= \log _2 10=3.32[/latex]
2021.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given,}\qquad P(G)&=\frac{1}{2} \text { and } P(B)=\frac{1}{2} \\ P(C)&=\frac{1}{4} \text { and } P(S)=\frac{3}{4} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Let probability of selected science student is a boy is [latex]P(B/S) = x[/latex]
Given that Commerce students are two time more likely to be a boy than are Science students.
Then, probability of selected Commerce student is a boy
[latex] P\left(\frac{B}{C}\right)=2 x[/latex]
We have to find probability of randomly selected girl studies Commerce i.e.
[latex] \begin{aligned} P\left(\frac{C}{G}\right)&=\frac{P(C \cap G)}{P(G)}=\frac{P(C) P(G / C)}{P(G)} \\ P\left(\frac{C}{G}\right)&=\frac{\frac{1}{4} \times P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right)}{\frac{1}{2}} &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
To find [latex]P(G / C)[/latex], first we have to find [latex]P(B/C).[/latex]
The probability of selected student is a boy
[latex]\begin{aligned} P(B) &=P(S) P(B / S)+P(C) \times P(B / C) \\ \frac{1}{2} &=\frac{3}{4} \times x+\frac{1}{4} \times 2 x \\ \Rightarrow\qquad\qquad x &=\frac{2}{5}\\ \text{Then},\qquad \qquad P(B / C)&=2 x=\frac{4}{5}\\ \text{We know that},\qquad \\ P\left(\frac{B}{C}\right)+P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right)&=1 \\ P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right) =1- \frac{4}{5}&=\frac{1}{5} \\ \text{From equation (i),} \\ P\left(\frac{G}{C}\right) = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{\frac{5}{1/2}} &= \frac{1}{10} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The amount of information gained in knowing that a randomly selected girl student studies Commerce
[latex]I\left ( \frac{C}{G} \right )=\log _2 \frac{1}{P\left ( \frac{C}{G} \right )}= \log _2 10=3.32[/latex]

2020.text: For a vector field [latex]\vec{A}[/latex], which one of the following is False?

2020.explanation_text: Divergence and curl operator is performed on a vector field [latex]\vec{A}[/latex] Curl operation provides a vector orthogonal to the given vector field [latex] \vec{A} [/latex] [latex]\bigtriangledown \times(\bigtriangledown \times \vec{A})=\bigtriangledown (\bigtriangledown \cdot \vec{A})-\bigtriangledown ^2 \vec{A}[/latex] If a vector field is irrortational then  [latex]\bigtriangledown \times \vec{A}=0[/latex] If a vector field is solenoidal then [latex]\bigtriangledown \cdot \vec{A}=0[/latex] If a field is scalar A, then [latex]\bigtriangledown ^2  \vec{A}=0[/latex], is a laplacian equation. Divergence and curl operator is performed on a vector field [latex]\vec{A}[/latex]
Curl operation provides a vector orthogonal to the given vector field [latex] \vec{A} [/latex]
[latex]\bigtriangledown \times(\bigtriangledown \times \vec{A})=\bigtriangledown (\bigtriangledown \cdot \vec{A})-\bigtriangledown ^2 \vec{A}[/latex]
If a vector field is irrortational then [latex]\bigtriangledown \times \vec{A}=0[/latex]
If a vector field is solenoidal then [latex]\bigtriangledown \cdot \vec{A}=0[/latex]
If a field is scalar A, then [latex]\bigtriangledown ^2 \vec{A}=0[/latex], is a laplacian equation.
Hence option (C) is incorrect

2020.text: The partial derivative of the function [latex]f(x,y,z)=e^{1-x \cos y}+xze^{-1/(1+y^2)}[/latex] with respect to x at the point (1,0,e) is
2020.html:
The partial derivative of the function

[latex]f(x,y,z)=e^{1-x \cos y}+xze^{-1/(1+y^2)}[/latex]

with respect to x at the point (1,0,e) is
2020.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2020.explanation_text:

2020.explanation_text: s={(H,H),(H,T),(T,H),(T,T)} [latex]M=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ H & H & T & T \end{bmatrix}[/latex] of first toss [latex]N=\begin{bmatrix} H & T & H& T \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] of second toss Now,X=Min{M,N} [latex]\therefore[/latex] X=Min{H,H}=Min{1,1}=1 X=Min{H,T}=Min{1,0}=0 X=Min{T,H}=Min{0,1}=0 X=Min(T,T)=Min(0,0)=0 [latex]\therefore[/latex]P(X=1)=[latex]\frac{1}{4}[/latex],P(x=0)=[latex]\frac{3}{4}[/latex] We Know that, [latex]E(X)=\sum_{i}X_{i}P(x_{i})=1\times \frac{1}{4}+0\times \frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{4}=0.25[/latex]

2020.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty }^{\infty }\left | X(\omega ) \right |^{2}d\omega &=2\pi \int_{-\infty }^{\infty }\left | x(t) \right |^{2}dt \\ &=2\pi \int_{-\infty }^{\infty }\left | y(t) \right |^{2}\\      &=2\times 2\pi \int_{-2}^{0}\left | y(t) \right |^{2}dt\\      &=2\times 2\pi\left [ \int_{-2}^{-1}(t+2)^{2}dt+\int_{-1}^{0}(2t+3)^{2}dt \right ]\\&=4\pi \left [\left \{ \frac{(t+2)^{3}}{3} \right \} _{-1}^{-2}+\left \{ \frac{(2t+3)^3}{3\times 2} \right \}_{0}^{-1} \right ]\\&=4\pi \left [ \frac{1-0}{3}+\frac{3^{3}-1}{6} \right ]\\&=4\pi \left [ \frac{1}{3}+\frac{26}{6} \right ]\\&=     4\pi \times \left [ \frac{1}{3}+\frac{26}{6} \right ] \\ &=4\pi \times \left [ \frac{1}{3}+\frac{13}{3} \right ]\\&=4\pi \times \frac{14}{3} \\&=\frac{56\pi }{3}=58.61\end{aligned} [/latex]

2020.text: X is a random variable with uniform probability density function in the interval [-2,10]. For Y = 2X-6, the conditional probability [latex]P(Y \leq 7|X \geq 5)[/latex] (rounded off to three decimal places) is _____.

2020.subject: Communication Systems - Random Processes
2020.explanation_text: [latex]x[/latex] follows uniform distribution over [-2, 10] [latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \; f(x)&=\frac{1}{b-a}=\frac{1}{10-(-2)}=\frac{1}{12}\\ \text{Given: } y &= 2x - 6\\ \Rightarrow \; x&=\frac{y+6}{2}\\ \text{For } y = 7 \\ x&=\frac{7+6}{2}=\frac{13}{2}=6.5\\ P\left [ \frac{y\lt7}{x\gt 5} \right ]&=P\left [ \frac{x\lt6.5}{x\gt 5} \right ] \\ &=\frac{P\left [ x\gt 5\, and\, x\lt6.5 \right ]}{P\left [ x\gt 5 \right ]} \\ &=\frac{P\left [ 5\lt x \lt 6.5 \right ]}{P[x\gt 5]} \\ &=\frac{\int_{5}^{6.5}f(x)dx}{\int_{5}^{10}F(x)dx} \\ &=\frac{\int_{5}^{6.5}\frac{1}{12}dx}{\int_{5}^{10}\frac{1}{12}dx} \\ &=\frac{(x)_{6.5}^{5}}{(x)_{5}^{10}}=\frac{1.5}{5}=0.3\end{aligned}[/latex]

2020.explanation_text: Open loop transfer function for the system [latex]=C(s)\times G(s)=\frac{K(s+1)}{ (s+3)}\times \frac{1}{s(s+1)}[/latex] Since the system is type-1, so far a given unit ramp input steady state [latex]e_{ss}=\frac{1}{K_{V}} [/latex] where,  [latex]K_{V}=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}S\times \frac{K}{S(S+3)}=\frac{K}{3} [/latex] so, [latex]\; e_{ss}=\frac{1}{K/3}=\frac{3}{K}[/latex] Given that,  [latex]\; e_{ss}=0.1 [/latex] So, [latex]0.1=\frac{3}{K}\Rightarrow K=30[/latex]

Since the system is type-1, so far a given unit ramp input steady state
[latex]e_{ss}=\frac{1}{K_{V}} [/latex]

2019.text: Let H(z) be the z-transform of a real-valued discrete-time signal h[n]. If [latex]P(z)=H(z)H\left (\frac{1}{z} \right )[/latex] has a zero at [latex]z=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}j[/latex], and P(z) has a total of four zeros, which one of the following plots represents all the zeros correctly?
2019.html: Let H(z) be the z-transform of a real-valued discrete-time signal h[n]. If [latex]P(z)=H(z)H\left (\frac{1}{z} \right )[/latex] has a zero at [latex]z=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}j[/latex], and P(z) has a total of four zeros, which one of the following plots represents all the zeros correctly?
2019.subject: Signals and Systems - Z-Transform
2019.explanation_text: [latex]P(Z)=H(Z)H\left ( \frac{1}{Z} \right )[/latex] (i) [latex]h(n)[/latex] is real. Som [latex]p(n)[/latex] will be also real (ii) [latex]P(z)=P(z^{-1})[/latex] From (i) : if [latex]z_1[/latex] is a zero of [latex]P(z)[/latex], then [latex]z_1^*[/latex] will be also a zero of [latex]P(z)[/latex]. From (ii): If [latex]z_1[/latex] is a zero of [latex]P(z)[/latex], then [latex]\frac{1}{z_1}[/latex] will be also a zero of [latex]P(z)[/latex]. So, the 4 zeros are, [latex]\begin{aligned} z_1&= \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}j\\ z_2&= z_1^*=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}j\\ z_3&=\frac{1}{z_1}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}j}=1-j \\ z_4&=\left ( \frac{1}{z_1} \right )^*=z_3^*=1+j \end{aligned}[/latex]
2019.explanation_html:
[latex]P(Z)=H(Z)H\left ( \frac{1}{Z} \right )[/latex]
(i) [latex]h(n)[/latex] is real. Som [latex]p(n)[/latex] will be also real
(ii) [latex]P(z)=P(z^{-1})[/latex]
From (i) : if [latex]z_1[/latex] is a zero of [latex]P(z)[/latex], then [latex]z_1^*[/latex] will be also a zero of [latex]P(z)[/latex].
From (ii): If [latex]z_1[/latex] is a zero of [latex]P(z)[/latex], then [latex]\frac{1}{z_1}[/latex] will be also a zero of [latex]P(z)[/latex].
So, the 4 zeros are,
[latex]\begin{aligned} z_1&= \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}j\\ z_2&= z_1^*=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}j\\ z_3&=\frac{1}{z_1}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}j}=1-j \\ z_4&=\left ( \frac{1}{z_1} \right )^*=z_3^*=1+j \end{aligned}[/latex]

2019.explanation_text: Given, [latex]\quad G(s)=\frac{3-s}{(s+1)(s+3)} [/latex] [latex] \therefore \quad Y(s)=\frac{G(s)}{s}=\frac{3-s}{s(s+1)(s+3)} [/latex] Using partial fractions, we get, [latex] \begin{aligned} Y(s)&=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{(s+1)}+\frac{C}{(s+3)} \\ A\left(s^{2}+4 s+3\right)&+B\left(s^{2}+3 s\right)+C\left(s^{2}+s\right)=3-s \\ A+B+C&=0\\ 4 A+3 B+C&=-1 \\ \text{and }3 A&=3 \\ \text{Therefore, }&\text{we get,}\\ A=1, B&=-2 \text { and } C=1\\ \text{So, }\quad Y(s)&=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{2}{(s+1)}+\frac{1}{(s+3)} \\ \text{and}\quad \mathrm{y}(t)&=u(t)-2 e^{-t} u(t)+e^{-3 t} u(t) \\ \end{aligned}[/latex] Forced response, [latex] y_{t}(t)=u(t) \Rightarrow \text { option }(D)[/latex]

[latex] \therefore \quad Y(s)=\frac{G(s)}{s}=\frac{3-s}{s(s+1)(s+3)} [/latex]
Using partial fractions, we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Y(s)&=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{(s+1)}+\frac{C}{(s+3)} \\ A\left(s^{2}+4 s+3\right)&+B\left(s^{2}+3 s\right)+C\left(s^{2}+s\right)=3-s \\ A+B+C&=0\\ 4 A+3 B+C&=-1 \\ \text{and }3 A&=3 \\ \text{Therefore, }&\text{we get,}\\ A=1, B&=-2 \text { and } C=1\\ \text{So, }\quad Y(s)&=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{2}{(s+1)}+\frac{1}{(s+3)} \\ \text{and}\quad \mathrm{y}(t)&=u(t)-2 e^{-t} u(t)+e^{-3 t} u(t) \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Forced response,
[latex] y_{t}(t)=u(t) \Rightarrow \text { option }(D)[/latex]

2019.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given that, }&\left|f^{\prime}(x)\right| \leq 2 ; &f(-1)=0 \\ &-2 \leq f^{\prime}(x) \leq 2\\ x \in[-2,2] &\rightarrow 2 \leq x \leq 2 \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex] \therefore [/latex] By applying mean value theorem in [-1,2] [latex] \begin{array}{l} -2 \leq f^{\prime}(x) \leq 2 \\ -2 \leq \frac{f(2)-f(-1)}{2-(-1)} \leq 2 \\ -2 \leq \frac{f(2)-f(-1)}{3} \leq 2 \\ -6 \leq f(2)-0 \leq 6 \\ -6 \leq f(2) \leq 6 \end{array}[/latex] It is satisfied by only option (B).
2019.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given that, }&\left|f^{\prime}(x)\right| \leq 2 ; &f(-1)=0 \\ &-2 \leq f^{\prime}(x) \leq 2\\ x \in[-2,2] &\rightarrow 2 \leq x \leq 2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] By applying mean value theorem in [-1,2]
[latex] \begin{array}{l} -2 \leq f^{\prime}(x) \leq 2 \\ -2 \leq \frac{f(2)-f(-1)}{2-(-1)} \leq 2 \\ -2 \leq \frac{f(2)-f(-1)}{3} \leq 2 \\ -6 \leq f(2)-0 \leq 6 \\ -6 \leq f(2) \leq 6 \end{array}[/latex]
It is satisfied by only option (B).

[latex]x[n]=c_1 \; exp\left ( -\frac{j\pi n}{2} \right )+c_2 \; exp\left ( \frac{j\pi n}{2} \right )[/latex]

where [latex]c_1 \; and \; c_2[/latex] are arbitrary real numbers. The desired three-tap filter is given by

and

2019.html:
Consider a causal second-order system with the transfer function

[latex]G(s)=\frac{1}{1+2s+s^2}[/latex]

with a unit-step [latex]R(s)=\frac{1}{s}[/latex] as an input. Let C(s) be the corresponding output. The time taken by the system output c(t) to reach 94% of its steady-state value [latex]\lim_{t \to \infty }c(t)[/latex], rounded off to two decimal places, is
2019.subject: Control Systems - Time Response Analysis
2019.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{1}{s^{2}+2 s+1}=\frac{1}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ R(s)&=\frac{1}{s} \\ \alpha (s)&=G(s) R(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+1)^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex] Using partial fraction expansion, we get, [latex] \begin{aligned} C(s) & =\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{(s+1)}+\frac{C}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ A\left(s^{2}+2 s+1\right)&+B\left(s^{2}+s\right)+C s=1 \\ A&=1 \\ A+B & =0 \Rightarrow B=-1 \\ 2 A+B+C & =0 \Rightarrow C=-1 \\ \therefore \quad C(s) & =\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{(s+1)}-\frac{1}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ \text{and}\quad c(t) & =\left(1-e^{-t}-t e^{-t}\right) u(t) \\ \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} c(t) & =1 \end{aligned}[/latex] In order to reach 94 % of its steady-state value, [latex] \left(1-e^{-t}-t e^{-t}\right)=0.94[/latex] By trial and error, we get, [latex] t \approx 4.50 \mathrm{sec}[/latex]
2019.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{1}{s^{2}+2 s+1}=\frac{1}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ R(s)&=\frac{1}{s} \\ \alpha (s)&=G(s) R(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+1)^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using partial fraction expansion, we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} C(s) & =\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{(s+1)}+\frac{C}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ A\left(s^{2}+2 s+1\right)&+B\left(s^{2}+s\right)+C s=1 \\ A&=1 \\ A+B & =0 \Rightarrow B=-1 \\ 2 A+B+C & =0 \Rightarrow C=-1 \\ \therefore \quad C(s) & =\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{(s+1)}-\frac{1}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ \text{and}\quad c(t) & =\left(1-e^{-t}-t e^{-t}\right) u(t) \\ \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} c(t) & =1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
In order to reach 94 % of its steady-state value,
[latex] \left(1-e^{-t}-t e^{-t}\right)=0.94[/latex]
By trial and error, we get,
[latex] t \approx 4.50 \mathrm{sec}[/latex]

Let [latex]B=[0\;0\;1]^T[/latex] and d=0. Which one of the following options for A and C will ensure that the transfer function of this LTI system is
[latex]H(s)=\frac{1}{s^3+3s^2+2s+1}[/latex]?
2019.subject: Control Systems - State Space Analysis
2019.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} X(t) &=A x(t)+B u(t) \\ y(t) &=C x(t) \\ B &=\left[\begin{array}{l} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right] \\ \frac{\gamma(s)}{U(s)} &=\\ \frac{\gamma(s)}{X_{1}(s)} \times \frac{X_{1}(s)}{U(s)}=& 1 \times \frac{1}{s^{3}+3 s^{2}+2 s+1} \\ x_{1}(s)\left(s^{3}+3 s^{2}+2 s+1\right]&=U(s) \\ x_{2} &=\dot{x}_{1}(t) \\ x_{2}(s) &=s x_{1}(s) \\ x_{3} &=\dot{x}_{2}(t) \\ \Rightarrow \quad x_{3}(s) &=s x_{2}(s)=s^{2} X_{1}(s) \\ \text { So, } \quad s x_{3}(s) &=-x_{1}(s)-2 x_{2}(s)-3 x_{3}(s)+u(s) \\ \dot{x}_{3}(t) &=-x_{1}(t)-2 r_{2}(t)-3 x_{3}(t)+u(t) \\ y(t) &=x_{1}(t) \\ \dot{x}(t) &=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2 & -3\end{array}\right] x(t)+\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right] u(t) \\ y(t) &=[1 \quad 0 \quad 0] x(t) \end{aligned}[/latex]
2019.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} X(t) &=A x(t)+B u(t) \\ y(t) &=C x(t) \\ B &=\left[\begin{array}{l} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right] \\ \frac{\gamma(s)}{U(s)} &=\\ \frac{\gamma(s)}{X_{1}(s)} \times \frac{X_{1}(s)}{U(s)}=& 1 \times \frac{1}{s^{3}+3 s^{2}+2 s+1} \\ x_{1}(s)\left(s^{3}+3 s^{2}+2 s+1\right]&=U(s) \\ x_{2} &=\dot{x}_{1}(t) \\ x_{2}(s) &=s x_{1}(s) \\ x_{3} &=\dot{x}_{2}(t) \\ \Rightarrow \quad x_{3}(s) &=s x_{2}(s)=s^{2} X_{1}(s) \\ \text { So, } \quad s x_{3}(s) &=-x_{1}(s)-2 x_{2}(s)-3 x_{3}(s)+u(s) \\ \dot{x}_{3}(t) &=-x_{1}(t)-2 r_{2}(t)-3 x_{3}(t)+u(t) \\ y(t) &=x_{1}(t) \\ \dot{x}(t) &=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2 & -3\end{array}\right] x(t)+\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{array}\right] u(t) \\ y(t) &=[1 \quad 0 \quad 0] x(t) \end{aligned}[/latex]

2019.text: In the circuit shown, the breakdown voltage and the maximum current of the Zener diode are 20 V and 60 mA, respectively. The values of [latex]R_1 \; and \; R_L[/latex] are [latex]200\Omega \; and \; 1k\Omega[/latex], respectively. The values of [latex]R_1 \; and \; R_L[/latex] are [latex]200\Omega \; and \; 1k\Omega[/latex], respectively. 2019.subject: Analog Circuits - Diodes Applications
2019.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} V_{z} &=20 \mathrm{V} \\ I_{z \max } &=60 \mathrm{mA} \end{aligned}[/latex] Set zener diode be OFF [latex] V_{o}=\frac{V_{i} \times 1}{0.2+1}=\frac{V_{i}}{1.2}[/latex] Zener diode can become ON i.e. it goes into breakdown, when [latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{V_{i}}{1.2} & \gt 20 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{i} & \gt 24 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex] When Zener diode is in breakdown region, [latex] \begin{array}{l} I_{1}=\frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2 \mathrm{k} \Omega}=\frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2} \mathrm{mA}\\ I_{L}=\frac{V_{0}}{R_{L}}=\frac{20}{1 \mathrm{k} \Omega}=20 \mathrm{mA} \\ I_{z}=I_{1}-I_{L}=\frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2}-20 \end{array}[/latex] For safe operation, [latex]I_{z} \leq I_{z \max } [/latex] [latex] \frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2}-20 \leq 60[/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow V_{i} \leq 36 \mathrm{V}[/latex] Hence, [latex]24 \lt V_{i} \lt 36 V[/latex]
2019.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{z} &=20 \mathrm{V} \\ I_{z \max } &=60 \mathrm{mA} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Set zener diode be OFF
[latex] V_{o}=\frac{V_{i} \times 1}{0.2+1}=\frac{V_{i}}{1.2}[/latex]
Zener diode can become ON i.e. it goes into
breakdown, when
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{V_{i}}{1.2} & \gt 20 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{i} & \gt 24 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]
When Zener diode is in breakdown region,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} I_{1}=\frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2 \mathrm{k} \Omega}=\frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2} \mathrm{mA}\\ I_{L}=\frac{V_{0}}{R_{L}}=\frac{20}{1 \mathrm{k} \Omega}=20 \mathrm{mA} \\ I_{z}=I_{1}-I_{L}=\frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2}-20 \end{array}[/latex]
For safe operation, [latex]I_{z} \leq I_{z \max } [/latex]
[latex] \frac{V_{i}-20}{0.2}-20 \leq 60[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow V_{i} \leq 36 \mathrm{V}[/latex]
Hence, [latex]24 \lt V_{i} \lt 36 V[/latex]

2019.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{array}{c} T=3 R_{0} C=3 \mathrm{sec} \\ R(t)=\left(1-\frac{t}{3}\right) ; 0 \leq t \leq 3 \mathrm{sec} \end{array}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} R(t) i(t)+\frac{1}{C} \int i(t) d t&=1 \\ \left(1-\frac{t}{3}\right) i(t)+\int i(t) d t&=1 \end{aligned}[/latex] Differentiating both sides, we get [latex] \begin{aligned} \left(1-\frac{t}{3}\right) \frac{d i}{d t}-\frac{i}{3}+i &=0 \\ (3-t) \frac{d i}{d t}+2 i &=0 \\ \frac{d i}{i} &=-\frac{2}{(3-t)} d t \end{aligned}[/latex] Integrating on both sides, we get, [latex] \begin{aligned} \ln (i)&=2 \ln (3-t)+\ln (c)\\ i(t)&=c(3-t)^{2} ; t \geq 0\\ \text{Given that,} i(0)&=1 A.\\ \text{So,}\quad c(3-0)^{2} &=1 \mathrm{A} \\ c &=\frac{1}{9} \mathrm{A} \\ i(t) &=\frac{1}{9}(3-t)^{2} \mathrm{A}\\ \text{At }t&=\frac{T}{2}=1.5 \mathrm{sec} \\ i(1.5)&=\frac{1}{9}(1.5)^{2}=0.25 A \end{aligned}[/latex]

Differentiating both sides, we get

Integrating on both sides, we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \ln (i)&=2 \ln (3-t)+\ln (c)\\ i(t)&=c(3-t)^{2} ; t \geq 0\\ \text{Given that,} i(0)&=1 A.\\ \text{So,}\quad c(3-0)^{2} &=1 \mathrm{A} \\ c &=\frac{1}{9} \mathrm{A} \\ i(t) &=\frac{1}{9}(3-t)^{2} \mathrm{A}\\ \text{At }t&=\frac{T}{2}=1.5 \mathrm{sec} \\ i(1.5)&=\frac{1}{9}(1.5)^{2}=0.25 A \end{aligned}[/latex]

2019.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
2019.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \left(x^{2} D^{2}-3 x D+3\right)&=0 \\ (0(0-1)-30+3) y&=0 \\ \left(0^{2}-40+3\right) y&=0 \\ \text { AE is }\quad m^{2}-4 m+3&=0 \\ m&=1.3 \\ CF&=C_{1}x+C_{2}x^{3} \\ \text { Solution is } \quad y&=C_{1}x+C_{2}x^{3} \\ y(1)=1\quad 1&=C_{1}+C_{2} \\ y(2)=14\quad 14&=2 C_{1}+8 C_{2} \\ \text{From (il) and (ii). }C_{1}&=-1, \quad C_{2}=2 \\ \therefore\quad y&=-x+2 x^{3} \\ y(1.5)&=-1.5+2(1.5)^{3}=5.25 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2019.explanation_text: From Parseval's theorem, [latex] \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}|x[n]|^{2}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\left|X\left(e^{j \omega}\right)\right|^{2} d \omega[/latex] So, [latex] \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\left|H\left(e^{j \omega}\right)-G\left(e^{j \omega}\right)\right|^{2} d \omega=2 \pi \sum_{n=-3}^{3}|h(n)-g(n)|^{2} [/latex] The solution of g(n) that minimizes E(h, g) also minimizes [latex]\sum_{n=-3}^{3}|h(n)-g(n)|^{2} [/latex] [latex] \sum_{n=-3}^{3}|h(n)-g(n)|^{2}[/latex] [latex] =|4-g(0)|^{2}+|3-g(1)|^{2}+|-3-g(-1)|^{2}+10 [/latex] The solution of g(n) that minimizes the above equation is [latex] g(n)=(-3,4,3\}[/latex] [latex] So, 10 g(-1)+g(1)=10(-3)+3=-27[/latex]
2019.explanation_html:
From Parseval's theorem,
[latex] \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}|x[n]|^{2}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\left|X\left(e^{j \omega}\right)\right|^{2} d \omega[/latex]
So,
[latex] \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\left|H\left(e^{j \omega}\right)-G\left(e^{j \omega}\right)\right|^{2} d \omega=2 \pi \sum_{n=-3}^{3}|h(n)-g(n)|^{2} [/latex]
The solution of g(n) that minimizes E(h, g) also
minimizes [latex]\sum_{n=-3}^{3}|h(n)-g(n)|^{2} [/latex]
[latex] \sum_{n=-3}^{3}|h(n)-g(n)|^{2}[/latex]
[latex] =|4-g(0)|^{2}+|3-g(1)|^{2}+|-3-g(-1)|^{2}+10 [/latex]
The solution of g(n) that minimizes the above
equation is
[latex] g(n)=(-3,4,3\}[/latex]
[latex] So, 10 g(-1)+g(1)=10(-3)+3=-27[/latex]

2019.text: A voice signal m(t) is in the frequency range 5 kHz to 15 kHz. The signal is amplitude-modulated to generate an AM signal [latex]f(t)=A(1+m(t))cos 2\pi f_c t[/latex], where [latex]f_c[/latex]=600kHz. The AM signal f(t) is to be digitized and archived. This is done by first sampling f(t) at 1.2 times the Nyquist frequency, and then quantizing each sample using a 256-level quantizer. Finally, each quantized sample is binary coded using K bits, where K is the minimum number of bits required for the encoding. The rate, in Megabits per second (rounded off to 2 decimal places), of the resulting stream of coded bits is _______ Mbps.

2019.text: A random variable X takes values  -1 and +1 with probabilities 0.2 and 0.8, respectively. It is transmitted across a channel which adds noise N, so that the random variable at the channel output is Y=X+N. The noise N is independent of X, and is uniformly distributed over the interval [-2,2]. The receiver makes a decision [latex]\hat{X}=\left\{\begin{matrix} -1 & if & Y\leq \theta \\ +1& if & Y> \theta \end{matrix}\right.[/latex] where the threshold [latex]\theta \in [-1,1][/latex] is chosen so as to minimize the probability of error [latex]Pr[\hat{X}\neq X][/latex]. The minimum probability of error, rounded off to 1 decimal place, is ______.
2019.html:
A random variable X takes values -1 and +1 with probabilities 0.2 and 0.8, respectively. It is transmitted across a channel which adds noise N, so that the random variable at the channel output is Y=X+N. 2018.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x, y) &=\frac{a x^{2}+b y^{2}}{x y}=a\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)+b\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \\\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|_{(1,2)} &=\left.\left[\frac{a}{y}-\frac{b y}{x^{2}}\right]\right|_{(12)}-\frac{a}{2}-2 b \\\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right|_{(1,2)} &=\left.\left[-\frac{a x}{y^{2}}+\frac{b}{x}\right]\right|_{(1,2)}=-\frac{a}{4}+b \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} &=\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \\ \text{So,}\quad \frac{a}{2}-2 b &=-\frac{a}{4}+b \\ \frac{3 a}{4}&=3 b \\ a&=4 b \end{aligned}[/latex]

2018.text:
Consider a binary channel code in which each codeword has a fixed length of 5 bits. The
Hamming distance between any pair of distinct codewords in this code is at least 2. The
maximum number of codewords such a code can contain is _________.
2018.html: Consider a binary channel code in which each codeword has a fixed length of 5 bits. The Hamming distance between any pair of distinct codewords in this code is at least 2. The maximum number of codewords such a code can contain is _________.
2018.subject: Communication Systems - Information Theory and Coding
2018.explanation_text: According to the Plotkin bound. [latex] \begin{aligned} d_{\min } &\leq \frac{n 2^{k-1}}{2^{k}-1}\\ n&= \text{ Length of each code word }\\ k&= \text{ Length of each message word} \\ \text{Given that.}\\ d_{\min }&=2 \text { and } n=5\\ \text{So, } \frac{2^{k}}{2\left(2^{k}-1\right)} &\geq \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2^{k}}{2^{k}-1} &\geq \frac{4}{5} \end{aligned}[/latex] For any value of k, the above bound will be  satisfied. But as [latex]n > k[/latex] and n is fixed at 5. The maximum value of k that can be selected is 4. So, the maximum number of codewords possible is [latex]2_{4} = 16[/latex].
2018.explanation_html:
According to the Plotkin bound.
[latex] \begin{aligned} d_{\min } &\leq \frac{n 2^{k-1}}{2^{k}-1}\\ n&= \text{ Length of each code word }\\ k&= \text{ Length of each message word} \\ \text{Given that.}\\ d_{\min }&=2 \text { and } n=5\\ \text{So, } \frac{2^{k}}{2\left(2^{k}-1\right)} &\geq \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2^{k}}{2^{k}-1} &\geq \frac{4}{5} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For any value of k, the above bound will be satisfied. But as [latex]n > k[/latex] and n is fixed at 5. The maximum value of k that can be selected is 4.
So, the maximum number of codewords possible is [latex]2_{4} = 16[/latex].

Probability of error, [latex] \begin{aligned} P_{e} &=P\left(s_{1}\right) P\left(r_{0} \mid s_{1}\right)+P\left(s_{0}\right) P\left(r_{1} \mid s_{0}\right) \\ P\left(r_{0} \mid s_{1}\right) &=P\left(r_{1} \mid s_{0}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{8}\\ \text{Given that,}\\ P\left(s_{0}\right)&=P\left(s_{1}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\\ \text{So}\quad P_{e}&=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{8}\right)=\frac{1}{8}=0.125 \end{aligned}[/latex]

A lossy transmission line has resistance per unit length R = 0.05 [latex]\Omega [/latex] /m. The line is
distortionless and has characteristic impedance of 50 [latex]\Omega [/latex]. The attenuation constant (in Np/m, correct to three decimal places) of the line is _______.

2018.subject: Electromagnetics - Transmission Lines
2018.explanation_text: For a distortionless transmission line, [latex] \frac{L}{R}=\frac{C}{G}[/latex] Propagation constant, [latex] \begin{aligned} \gamma &=\alpha+j \beta=\sqrt{(R+j \omega L)(G+j \omega C)} \\ &=\sqrt{R G}\left(1+j \omega \frac{L}{R}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex] Attenuation constant, [latex] \alpha=\sqrt{R G}[/latex] Characteristic impedance, [latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{0} &=\sqrt{\frac{(R+j \omega L)}{(G+j \omega C)}}=\sqrt{\frac{R}{G}} \\ \sqrt{G} &=\frac{\sqrt{R}}{Z_{0}} \\ \text{So,}\quad\alpha &=\sqrt{R} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{R}}{Z_{0}}=\frac{R}{Z_{0}} \\ &=\frac{0.05}{50}=\frac{0.01}{10}=0.001 \mathrm{Np} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]
2018.explanation_html:
For a distortionless transmission line,
[latex] \frac{L}{R}=\frac{C}{G}[/latex]
Propagation constant,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \gamma &=\alpha+j \beta=\sqrt{(R+j \omega L)(G+j \omega C)} \\ &=\sqrt{R G}\left(1+j \omega \frac{L}{R}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Attenuation constant,
[latex] \alpha=\sqrt{R G}[/latex]
Characteristic impedance,
[latex] \begin{aligned} Z_{0} &=\sqrt{\frac{(R+j \omega L)}{(G+j \omega C)}}=\sqrt{\frac{R}{G}} \\ \sqrt{G} &=\frac{\sqrt{R}}{Z_{0}} \\ \text{So,}\quad\alpha &=\sqrt{R} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{R}}{Z_{0}}=\frac{R}{Z_{0}} \\ &=\frac{0.05}{50}=\frac{0.01}{10}=0.001 \mathrm{Np} / \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2018.text: A curve passes through the point (x =1, y = 0) and satisfies the differential equation [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{2y} + \frac{y}{x}[/latex]. The equation that describes the curve is
2018.html: A curve passes through the point (x =1, y = 0) and satisfies the differential equation [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{2y} + \frac{y}{x}[/latex]. The equation that describes the curve is
2018.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2018.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x} &=\frac{x^{2}}{2 y}+\frac{y}{2}+\frac{y}{x} \\ \text { Put. } \frac{y}{x}=t \\ \frac{d y}{d x}&=t+x \frac{d t}{d x} \\ t+x \frac{d t}{d x} &=\frac{x}{2 t}+\frac{t x}{2}+t \\ x \frac{d t}{d x} &=x\left(\frac{1}{2 t}+\frac{t}{2}\right) \\ x \frac{d t}{d x} &=x\left(\frac{1+t^{2}}{2 t}\right) \\ \frac{2 t}{1+t^{2}} d t &=\int d x+C \\ \ln \left(1+t^{2}\right) &=x+c \\ t &=\frac{y}{x}\\ \text{So, }\ln \left(1+\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)&=x+C \\ \text{At }x=1, y=0 \\ \ln \left(1+\frac{0}{1}\right) &=\ln (1)=0=1+C \\ C &=-1 \\ \text{So,} \ln \left(1+\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)&=x-1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
2018.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x} &=\frac{x^{2}}{2 y}+\frac{y}{2}+\frac{y}{x} \\ \text { Put. } \frac{y}{x}=t \\ \frac{d y}{d x}&=t+x \frac{d t}{d x} \\ t+x \frac{d t}{d x} &=\frac{x}{2 t}+\frac{t x}{2}+t \\ x \frac{d t}{d x} &=x\left(\frac{1}{2 t}+\frac{t}{2}\right) \\ x \frac{d t}{d x} &=x\left(\frac{1+t^{2}}{2 t}\right) \\ \frac{2 t}{1+t^{2}} d t &=\int d x+C \\ \ln \left(1+t^{2}\right) &=x+c \\ t &=\frac{y}{x}\\ \text{So, }\ln \left(1+\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)&=x+C \\ \text{At }x=1, y=0 \\ \ln \left(1+\frac{0}{1}\right) &=\ln (1)=0=1+C \\ C &=-1 \\ \text{So,} \ln \left(1+\frac{y^{2}}{x^{2}}\right)&=x-1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2018.explanation_text: The small-signal equivalent model of the given circuit can be drawn as shown below. [latex] \begin{aligned} \text{Given that, }\omega&=2 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \\ C_{j} &=0.5 \mathrm{nF} \\ I_{\mathrm{DC}} &=26 \mu \mathrm{A} \\ V_{T} &=26 \mathrm{mV} \\ \eta &=1\\ \mathrm{So} \quad r_{d} &=\frac{\eta V_{T}}{I_{\mathrm{DC}}}=\frac{26 \mathrm{mV}}{26 \mu \mathrm{A}}=1 \mathrm{k} \Omega \\ \frac{1}{\omega C_{j}} &=\frac{1}{2 \times 10^{6} \times 0.5 \times 10^{-9}} \Omega=1 \mathrm{k} \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex] So, total impedance of the circuit will be, [latex] \begin{aligned} Z &=\left(r_{d} \| \frac{1}{j \omega C_{j}}\right)+100 \Omega \\\left(r_{d} \| \frac{1}{j \omega C_{j}}\right) &=\frac{(1000)(-j 1000)}{1000-j 1000} \Omega \\ &=\frac{-j(1+j)}{2} \mathrm{k} \Omega \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(1-j) \mathrm{k} \Omega=(500-j 500) \Omega \\ \therefore \quad Z &=600-j 500 \Omega \\|Z| &=100 \sqrt{36+25}=100 \sqrt{61} \Omega \\ I_{m} &=\frac{V_{m}}{|Z|} \\ &=\frac{5 \mathrm{mV}}{100 \sqrt{61} \Omega}=\frac{50}{\sqrt{61}} \mu \mathrm{A}=6.40 \mu \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2018.explanation_text: Hilbert transform does not alter the amplitude spectrum of the signal. [latex] \begin{aligned} \text{So, }\quad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|y(t)|^{2} d t&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^{2} d t=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|X(f)|^{2} d f \\ x(t)&=4 \sin \mathrm{c}(2 t) \\ \text{sinc}(t) &\stackrel{CTFT}{\longleftrightarrow} \text{rect}(f) \\ 4 \text{sinc}(2 t) &\stackrel{CTFT}{\longleftrightarrow}+\frac{4}{2} \text{rect}\left(\frac{f}{2}\right)=2 \text{rect}\left(\frac{f}{2}\right) \end{aligned}\\ \begin{aligned} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|X(f)|^{2} d f &=2 \times(2)^{2}=8 \\ \text { So. } \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|y(t)|^{2} d t &=8 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2018.text: For a unity feedback control system with the forward path transfer function [latex]G(s)=\frac{K}{s(s+2)}[/latex] The peak resonant magnitude [latex]M_{r}[/latex], of the closed-loop frequency response is 2. The corresponding value of the gain K (correct to two decimal places) is _________.
2018.html:
For a unity feedback control system with the forward path transfer function

[latex]G(s)=\frac{K}{s(s+2)}[/latex]

The peak resonant magnitude [latex]M_{r}[/latex], of the closed-loop frequency response is 2. The corresponding value of the gain K (correct to two decimal places) is _________.
2018.subject: Control Systems - Frequency Response Analysis
2018.explanation_text: Maximum resonant peak, [latex]\begin{aligned} M_{r} &=\frac{1}{2 \xi \sqrt{1-\xi^{2}}}=2 \\ 2 \xi \sqrt{1-\xi^{2}} &=\frac{1}{2} \\ \xi^{2}\left(1-\xi^{2}\right) &=\frac{1}{16} \\ \xi^{4}-\xi^{2}+\frac{1}{16} &=0 \\ \xi^{2}&=\frac{1}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{1-\frac{1}{4}}{4}}=\frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \\ \text { As } M_{r}=2 \gt 1, \xi& \lt \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text { and } \xi^{2} \lt \frac{1}{2} \\ \text { So. } \quad\xi^{2}&=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\\ Given, \quad G(s)&=\frac{K}{s(s+2)}=\frac{\omega_{n}^{2}}{s\left(s+2 \xi \omega_{n}\right)} \\ \text{So} \quad\omega_{n} &=\sqrt{K} \\ 2 \xi \sqrt{K} &=2\\ \sqrt{K} &=\frac{1}{\xi} \\ K &=\frac{1}{\xi^{2}}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right)} \\ &=\frac{4}{2-\sqrt{3}}=14.928 \end{aligned}[/latex]

The threshold voltage [latex]V_{T}[/latex] for both transistors is 1.0V. Note that [latex] V_{GS} \; for M_{2} [/latex] must be [latex]\gt[/latex] 1.0 V.
The voltage (in volts, accurate to two decimal places) at [latex] V_{x} [/latex] is _______.
2018.subject: Analog Circuits - FET and MOSFET Analysis
2018.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Let},\quad K_{n}&=\frac{\mu_{n} C_{o x}}{2}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)\\ \text{Given that,}\\ \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{2} &=2\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{1} \\ \text{So,}\quad K_{n 2} &=2 K_{n 1}\\ \text{For }M_{1}, \quad V_{G S 1}-V_{T}&=2-1=1 V \\ \text{For }M_{2}, \quad V_{G S 2}-V_{T}&=2-V_{x}-1=1 \mathrm{V}-V_{x}<1 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{D S 2}&=\left(3.3-V_{x}\right)>\left(V_{G S 2}-V_{T}\right) \end{aligned}[/latex] So, [latex]M_{1}[/latex] will be in linear region and [latex]M_{2}[/latex] will be in saturation region. [latex]\begin{aligned} I_{D_{1}}&=I_{D_{2}} \\ K_{n 1}\left[2\left(V_{G S 1}-V_{T}\right) V_{D S 1}-V_{D S 1}^{2}\right]&=K_{n 2}\left(V_{G S 2}-V_{T}\right)^{2} \\ K_{n 1}\left[2(2-1) V_{x}-V_{x}^{2}\right]&=2 K_{n 1}\left(2-V_{x}-1\right)^{2} \\ 2 V_{x}-V_{x}^{2} &=2\left(1+V_{x}^{2}-2 V_{x}\right) \\ &=2 V_{x}^{2}-4 V_{x}+2\\ 3V_{x}^{2}-6 V_{x}+2 &=0 \\ V_{x}^{2}-2 V_{x}+\frac{2}{3} &=0 \\ V_{x} &=1 \pm \sqrt{\frac{4-\frac{8}{3}}{4}}=1 \pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} V \\ V_{GS2}&=\left(2-V_{x}\right) \geq V_{T}\\ \Rightarrow \quad \left(1-V_{x}\right) &\geq0\\ \text{So, valid value,} \quad V_{x}&=1-\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}=0.4226 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2018.subject: Electronic Devices - PN-Junction Diodes and Special Diodes
2018.explanation_text: For solar cell, [latex] \begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{OC}} &=V_{T} \ln \left(\frac{I_{S C}}{I_{O}}\right) \\ V_{\mathrm{OC} 2}-V_{\mathrm{OC} 1} &=V_{T} \ln \left(\frac{I_{S C 2}}{I_{S C}}\right)=V_{T} \ln \left(\frac{0.20}{1.0}\right) \\ V_{\mathrm{OC} 2} &=V_{\mathrm{OC} 1}-0.026 \mathrm{ln}(5) \\ &=0.65-0.041845=0.608 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2018.text:
The logic gates shown in the digital circuit below use strong pull-down nMOS transistors for
LOW logic level at the outputs. When the pull-downs are off, high-value resistors set the
output logic levels to HIGH (i.e. the pull-ups are weak). Note that some nodes are
intentionally shorted to implement "wired logic". Such shorted nodes will be HIGH only if
the outputs of all the gates whose outputs are shorted are HIGH. The number of distinct values of [latex]X_{3}X_{2}X_{1}X_{0}[/latex] (out of the 16 possible values) that give Y = 1 is _______.
2018.html:
The logic gates shown in the digital circuit below use strong pull-down nMOS transistors for LOW logic level at the outputs. When the pull-downs are off, high-value resistors set the output logic levels to HIGH (i.e. the pull-ups are weak). Note that some nodes are intentionally shorted to implement "wired logic". Such shorted nodes will be HIGH only if the outputs of all the gates whose outputs are shorted are HIGH.

The number of distinct values of [latex]X_{3}X_{2}X_{1}X_{0}[/latex] (out of the 16 possible values) that give Y = 1 is _______.

2018.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} A&=\left(X_{1} \oplus X_{2}\right) \bar{X}_{3} \\ B&=\left[\left(X_{1} \oplus X_{2}\right) \bar{X}_{3} X_{0}\right] \cdot \bar{X}_{0}=0\\ Y&=B+X_{3}=0+X_{3}=X_{3} \end{aligned}[/latex] Out of 16 possible combinations of [latex]x_{3} x_{2} x_{1} x_{0} x_{3} ,[/latex] will be high for 8 combinations. So, Y will be high for 8 combinations.
