2014-set-3.text:
A fair coin is tossed repeatedly till both head and tail appear at least once. The
average number of tosses required is____.
2014-set-3.html: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly till both head and tail appear at least once. The average number of tosses required is____.
2014-set-3.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
2014-set-3.explanation_text: To get both head and Tail atleast once. We have to toss minimum two times. The random variable x represents first toss starting  with Head. [latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{|r|r|r|r|r|r|} \hline x & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots \\ \hline(x) & \frac{1}{2^{2}} & \frac{1}{2^{3}} & \frac{1}{2^{4}} & \frac{1}{2^{5}} & \cdots\\ \hline \end{array} \\ E(x) &=\Sigma x \cdot P(x) & \\ &=2 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{4}}+\cdots \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots-1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(4-1)=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] Y represents first toss starting with Tail. [latex] \begin{aligned} &\begin{array}{|r|r|r|r|r|r|} \hline y & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots \\ \hline(y) & \frac{1}{2^{2}} & \frac{1}{2^{3}} & \frac{1}{2^{4}} & \frac{1}{2^{5}} & \cdots\\ \hline \end{array} \\ &=2 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{4}}+\cdots \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}+3 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \frac{1}{2^{2}}+4 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3}}+\cdots-1\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right]=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-2}-1\right] \\ &=\frac{1}{2}(4-1)=\frac{3}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex] \therefore \quad[/latex] The average number of tosses required [latex] =E(x)+E(y)=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=3[/latex]

2014-set-3.html: Let [latex]H_{1}(z)=(1-pz^{-1})^{-1}[/latex], [latex]H_{2}(z)=(1-qz^{-1})^{-1}[/latex], [latex]H(z)=H_{1}(z)+rH_{2}(z)[/latex]. 2014-set-3.subject: Signals and Systems - Z-Transform

2014-set-3.subject: Control Systems - State Space Analysis
2014-set-3.explanation_text: Given [latex]\dot{x}(t)=A x(t), \quad x(0)=x_{0} [/latex] Taking the Laplace transform [latex] \begin{aligned} s X(s)-x(0) &=A X(s) \\ [s I-A] X(s) &=x(0) \\ X(s) &=[s I-A]^{-1} x(0) \\ x(t) &=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x(0) &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex] Condition given are [latex] \begin{aligned} For x_{0}&=\left[\begin{array}{c}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right], x(t)=\left[\begin{array}{c}e^{-t} \\ -e^{-t}\end{array}\right] \\ For x_{0}&=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right], x(t)=\left[\begin{array}{l}e^{-t}-e^{-2 t} \\ -e^{-t}+2 e^{-2 t}\end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex] Using the linearity property in equation (i) [latex] K_{1} x_{1}(t)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x_{1}(0) K_{1} [/latex] [latex] K_{2} x_{2}(t)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x_{2}(0) K_{2} [/latex] Using the linearity property as [latex] \begin{aligned} K_{1} x_{1}(t)+K_{2} x_{2}(t)&=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} \\  \left[K_{1} x_{1}(0)+K_{2} x_{2}(0)\right] & \quad \ldots(ii)\\ \text { Also } \quad X_{3}(s)&=[s I-A]^{-1} x_{3}(0) \\ \text{So, } \quad K_{1}\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right]+&K_{2}\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 5\end{array}\right] \\ \left[\begin{array}{l}K_{1}+O K_{2} \\ -K_{1}+K_{2}\end{array}\right]&=\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 5\end{array}\right] \\ \Rightarrow \quad K_{1}&=3 \\ K_{2}&=8 \end{aligned}[/latex] So, from equation (ii), we get x(t) [latex]\begin{aligned} x(t) &=K_{1} x_{1}(t)+K_{2} x_{2}(t) \\ &=3\left[\begin{array}{c} e^{-t} \\ -e^{-t} \end{array}\right]+8\left[\begin{array}{c} e^{-t}-e^{-2 t} \\ -e^{-t}+2 e^{-2 t} \end{array}\right] \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{c} 11 e^{-t}-8 e^{-2 t} \\ -1 t e^{-t}+16 e^{-2 t} \end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-3.explanation_html:
Given [latex]\dot{x}(t)=A x(t), \quad x(0)=x_{0} [/latex]
Taking the Laplace transform
[latex] \begin{aligned} s X(s)-x(0) &=A X(s) \\ [s I-A] X(s) &=x(0) \\ X(s) &=[s I-A]^{-1} x(0) \\ x(t) &=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x(0) &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Condition given are
[latex] \begin{aligned} For x_{0}&=\left[\begin{array}{c}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right], x(t)=\left[\begin{array}{c}e^{-t} \\ -e^{-t}\end{array}\right] \\ For x_{0}&=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right], x(t)=\left[\begin{array}{l}e^{-t}-e^{-2 t} \\ -e^{-t}+2 e^{-2 t}\end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Using the linearity property in equation (i)
[latex] K_{1} x_{1}(t)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x_{1}(0) K_{1} [/latex]
[latex] K_{2} x_{2}(t)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} x_{2}(0) K_{2} [/latex]
Using the linearity property as
[latex] \begin{aligned} K_{1} x_{1}(t)+K_{2} x_{2}(t)&=\mathcal{L}^{-1}[s I-A]^{-1} \\ \left[K_{1} x_{1}(0)+K_{2} x_{2}(0)\right] & \quad \ldots(ii)\\ \text { Also } \quad X_{3}(s)&=[s I-A]^{-1} x_{3}(0) \\ \text{So, } \quad K_{1}\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1\end{array}\right]+&K_{2}\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 5\end{array}\right] \\ \left[\begin{array}{l}K_{1}+O K_{2} \\ -K_{1}+K_{2}\end{array}\right]&=\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 5\end{array}\right] \\ \Rightarrow \quad K_{1}&=3 \\ K_{2}&=8 \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, from equation (ii), we get x(t)
[latex]\begin{aligned} x(t) &=K_{1} x_{1}(t)+K_{2} x_{2}(t) \\ &=3\left[\begin{array}{c} e^{-t} \\ -e^{-t} \end{array}\right]+8\left[\begin{array}{c} e^{-t}-e^{-2 t} \\ -e^{-t}+2 e^{-2 t} \end{array}\right] \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{c} 11 e^{-t}-8 e^{-2 t} \\ -1 t e^{-t}+16 e^{-2 t} \end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-3.html: A binary random variable X takes the value of 1 with probability 1/3. X is input to a cascade of 2 independent identical binary symmetric channels (BSCs) each with crossover probability 1/2. The output of BSCs are the random variables [latex]Y_{1}[/latex] and [latex]Y_{2}[/latex] as shown in the figure. The value of [latex]H(Y_{1})+ H(Y_{2})[/latex] in bits is ____.
2014-set-3.subject: Communication Systems - Random Processes
2014-set-3.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} P(X=1) &=\frac{1}{3} \text { and } P(X=0)=\frac{2}{3} \\ \text { and } \quad H\left(Y_{1}\right) &=P\left(Y_{1}\right) \log _{2} \frac{1}{P\left(Y_{1}\right)} \\ H\left(Y_{2}\right) &=P\left(Y_{2}\right) \log \frac{1}{P\left(Y_{2}\right)} \\ \text { where, } P\left(Y_{1}\right.&=1)=P\left(Y_{1}=0\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] Similarly, [latex] \begin{aligned} P\left(Y_{2}=1\right)&=P\left(Y_{2}=0\right)=\frac{1}{2} \\ \text { Here } H\left(Y_{1}\right)+H\left(Y_{2}\right)&=\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 2+\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 2 \\ &\quad+\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 2+\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 2 \\ H\left(Y_{1}\right)+H\left(Y_{2}\right)&=2 \text { bits } \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-3.text: Given the vector [latex]A=(cos x)(sin y)\hat{a}_{x}+(sin x)(cos y)\hat{a}_{y} [/latex], where [latex] \hat{a}_{x},\hat{a}_{y}[/latex] denotes unit vectors along x , y directions, respectively. The magnitude of curl of A is____.
2014-set-3.html: Given the vector [latex]A=(cos x)(sin y)\hat{a}_{x}+(sin x)(cos y)\hat{a}_{y} [/latex], where [latex] \hat{a}_{x},\hat{a}_{y}[/latex] denotes unit vectors along x , y directions, respectively. The magnitude of curl of A is____.
2014-set-3.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2014-set-3.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{A}&=(\cos x)(\sin y) \hat{a}_{x}+(\sin x)(\cos y) \hat{a}_{y} \\ \vec{A}&=(\cos x)(\sin y) \hat{a}_{x}+(\sin x)(\cos y) \hat{a}_{y}+0 \hat{a}_{z} & \hat{a}_{y} & \hat{a}_{z} \\ \nabla \times \vec{A}&=\left|\begin{array}{cccc} \hat{a}_{x} & \hat{a}_{y}&\hat{a}_{z}\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ \cos x \sin y & \sin x \cos y & 0 \end{array}\right| \\ &=\hat{a}_{z}[\cos x \cos y-\cos x \cos y]=0 \\ \therefore|\nabla \times \vec{A}| &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-2.text:
The capacity of a band-limited additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel
is given by [latex]C=Wlog_{2}(1+\frac{P}{\sigma ^{2}W})[/latex] bits per second (bps), where W is the channel bandwidth, P is the average power received and [latex]{\sigma^{2}}[/latex] is the one sided power spectral density of the AWGN. For a fixed [latex]\frac{P}{\sigma ^{2}}=1000[/latex], the channel capacity (in kbps) with infinite bandwidth [latex](W\rightarrow \infty )[/latex] is approximately.
2014-set-2.html:
The capacity of a band-limited additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel is given by [latex]C=Wlog_{2}(1+\frac{P}{\sigma ^{2}W})[/latex] bits per second (bps), where W is the channel bandwidth, P is the average power received and [latex]{\sigma^{2}}[/latex] is the one sided power spectral density of the AWGN.
For a fixed [latex]\frac{P}{\sigma ^{2}}=1000[/latex], the channel capacity (in kbps) with infinite bandwidth [latex](W\rightarrow \infty )[/latex] is approximately.
2014-set-2.subject: Communication Systems - Information Theory and Coding
2014-set-2.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} C&=W \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right) \\ C&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \times \frac{\sigma^{2}}{P} W \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right)\\ \text{when }\quad W &\rightarrow \infty \\ C_{\infty}&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \lim _{w \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P} \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right)\\ \text{as }\quad W &\rightarrow \infty, \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P}\text{ also }\rightarrow \infty \\ \therefore C_{\infty}&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \frac{\lim _{\alpha} \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P} \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P}}\right)}{P} \\ &\quad \left[\because \lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} x \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)=\log\right]\\ C_{\infty} &=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \log _{2} e\\ C_{\infty} &=1.44\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-2.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} C&=W \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right) \\ C&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \times \frac{\sigma^{2}}{P} W \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right)\\ \text{when }\quad W &\rightarrow \infty \\ C_{\infty}&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \lim _{w \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P} \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{P}{\sigma^{2} W}\right)\\ \text{as }\quad W &\rightarrow \infty, \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P}\text{ also }\rightarrow \infty \\ \therefore C_{\infty}&=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \frac{\lim _{\alpha} \frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P} \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\frac{\sigma^{2} W}{P}}\right)}{P} \\ &\quad \left[\because \lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} x \log _{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)=\log\right]\\ C_{\infty} &=\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \log _{2} e\\ C_{\infty} &=1.44\frac{P}{\sigma^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} &=\text{div}\left[r\left(\hat{a}_{x}+\hat{a}_{y}+\hat{a}_{z}\right)\right] \\ &=\text{div}\left(r \hat{a}_{x}+r \hat{a}_{y}+r \hat{a}_{z}\right) \\ &=\frac{\partial}{\partial x} r+\frac{\partial}{\partial y} r+\frac{\partial}{\partial z} r \\ &=1+1+1=3 \end{aligned}[/latex]

If a = [latex]\sqrt{5}[/latex] cm, the value of b (in cm) is______.
2014-set-2.subject: Electromagnetics - Waveguides
2014-set-2.explanation_text: Cut-off frequency of a rectangular waveguide is [latex] \begin{aligned} f_{c}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m \pi}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{n\pi}{b}\right)^{2}} \\ f_{c} \text{ for }\quad T E_{10}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1 \pi}{a}\right)^{2}}=\frac{c}{2 a} \\ f_{c} \text{ for }\quad T E_{20}&=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{2 \pi}{a}\right)^{2}}=\frac{c}{2 a} \\ f_{c} \text { for } \quad T E_{11} &=\frac{c}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\left(\frac{\pi}{a}\right)^{2}}+\left(\frac{\pi}{b}\right)^{2} \\ &=\frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}} \\ \text { Given, } f_{C T_{11}} &=\frac{f_{C_{I E 10}}+f_{C I E_{20}}}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}}&=\frac{\frac{c}{2 a}+\frac{c}{a}}{2} \\ \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}}&=\frac{1}{2 a}+\frac{1}{a}=\frac{3}{2 a} \\ \left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2}&=\frac{9}{4 a^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)^{2} &=\frac{5}{4 a^{2}} \\ b &=\frac{2 a}{\sqrt{5}}=\frac{2 \times \sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} \\ &=2 \mathrm{cm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-1.explanation_text: Given data: [latex] \begin{array}{l} i_{1}=2 \mathrm{A}, i_{4}=-1 \mathrm{A}, i_{5}=-4 \mathrm{A} \\ R=1 \Omega \end{array}[/latex] To calculate: [latex] i_{6}=?[/latex] Using KVL at all the three nodes we get, At node A [latex] i_{5}-i_{3}+i_{2}=0\qquad \ldots(i)[/latex] At node B [latex] i_{4}+i_{1}-i_{2}=0\qquad \ldots(ii)[/latex] At node C [latex] i_{6}+i_{3}-i_{1}=0 \qquad \ldots(iii)[/latex] By putting the value of [latex]i_{3}[/latex] and [latex]i_{2}[/latex] from equation (i) and (ii) in equation (iii) we get, [latex] \begin{aligned} i_{6}+\left(i_{2}+i_{5}\right)-i_{1}&=0 \\ i_{6}+\left(i_{1}+i_{4}+i_{5}\right)-i_{1}&=0 \\ \therefore \quad i_{6}+(2-1-4)-2&=0 \\ i_{6}&=5 \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] i_{6}=?[/latex]

At node A
[latex] i_{5}-i_{3}+i_{2}=0\qquad \ldots(i)[/latex]
At node B
[latex] i_{4}+i_{1}-i_{2}=0\qquad \ldots(ii)[/latex]
At node C
[latex] i_{6}+i_{3}-i_{1}=0 \qquad \ldots(iii)[/latex]
By putting the value of [latex]i_{3}[/latex] and [latex]i_{2}[/latex] from equation (i)
and (ii) in equation (iii) we get,
[latex] \begin{aligned} i_{6}+\left(i_{2}+i_{5}\right)-i_{1}&=0 \\ i_{6}+\left(i_{1}+i_{4}+i_{5}\right)-i_{1}&=0 \\ \therefore \quad i_{6}+(2-1-4)-2&=0 \\ i_{6}&=5 \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-1.text:
A continuous, linear time-invariant filter has an impulse response h(t) described
by [latex]h(t)=\left\{\begin{matrix} 3 &for \; 0\leq t\leq 3 \\ 0&otherwise \end{matrix}\right.[/latex] When a constant input of values 5 is applied to this filter, the steady state output is_____.
2014-set-1.html:
A continuous, linear time-invariant filter has an impulse response h(t) described by
[latex]h(t)=\left\{\begin{matrix} 3 &for \; 0\leq t\leq 3 \\ 0&otherwise \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]
When a constant input of values 5 is applied to this filter, the steady state output is_____.
2014-set-1.subject: Signals and Systems - Fourier Transforms, Frequency Response and Correlation
2014-set-1.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} h(t) &=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}3, & \text { for } 0 \leq t \leq 3 \\0, & \text { otherwise } \end{array}\right.\\ h(t) &=3[u(t)-u(t-3)] \\ H(s) &=3\left[\frac{1}{s}-\frac{e^{-3 s}}{s}\right] \\ \therefore \quad x(t) &=5 \\ \text { Then } x(s) &=\frac{5}{s} \end{aligned}[/latex] We know that [latex] Y(s)=H(s) X(s)=3\left[\frac{1}{s}-\frac{e^{-3 s}}{s}\right] \cdot \frac{5}{s} [/latex] Steady state output [latex] \begin{array}{l} =\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \cdot Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \cdot \frac{15}{s} \frac{\left(1-e^{-3 s}\right)}{s} \\ =15 \cdot \lim _{s \rightarrow 0} 3 e^{-3 s} \quad[\because \quad \text { L-Hospital's rule }] \\ \quad=45 \end{array}[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} h(t) &=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}3, & \text { for } 0 \leq t \leq 3 \\0, & \text { otherwise } \end{array}\right.\\ h(t) &=3[u(t)-u(t-3)] \\ H(s) &=3\left[\frac{1}{s}-\frac{e^{-3 s}}{s}\right] \\ \therefore \quad x(t) &=5 \\ \text { Then } x(s) &=\frac{5}{s} \end{aligned}[/latex]
We know that
[latex] Y(s)=H(s) X(s)=3\left[\frac{1}{s}-\frac{e^{-3 s}}{s}\right] \cdot \frac{5}{s} [/latex]
Steady state output
[latex] \begin{array}{l} =\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \cdot Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \cdot \frac{15}{s} \frac{\left(1-e^{-3 s}\right)}{s} \\ =15 \cdot \lim _{s \rightarrow 0} 3 e^{-3 s} \quad[\because \quad \text { L-Hospital's rule }] \\ \quad=45 \end{array}[/latex]

2014-set-1.text:
The forward path transfer function of a unity negative feedback system is given
 by [latex]G(s)=\frac{K}{(s+2)(s-1)}[/latex] The value of K which will place both the poles of the closed-loop system at the same location, is ______.
2014-set-1.html:
The forward path transfer function of a unity negative feedback system is given by
[latex]G(s)=\frac{K}{(s+2)(s-1)}[/latex]
The value of K which will place both the poles of the closed-loop system at the same location, is ______.
2014-set-1.subject: Control Systems - Stability Analysis
2014-set-1.explanation_text: Given that, [latex]\quad G(s)=\frac{K}{(s+2)(s-1)} [/latex] Using root locus method, the break point can be obtain as [latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad 1+G(s)&=0 \\ 1+\frac{K}{(s+2)(s-1)} &=0 \\ \text{or }\quad K&=-(s+2)(s-1)\\ \frac{d K}{d s} &=-2 s-1=0 \\ \text{or }\quad s &=-0.5 \end{aligned}[/latex] To have, both the poles at the same directions [latex] \begin{aligned} |G(s)|_{s=0.5} &=1 \\ K &=2.25 \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
Given that, [latex]\quad G(s)=\frac{K}{(s+2)(s-1)} [/latex]
Using root locus method, the break point can be obtain as


[latex] \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad 1+G(s)&=0 \\ 1+\frac{K}{(s+2)(s-1)} &=0 \\ \text{or }\quad K&=-(s+2)(s-1)\\ \frac{d K}{d s} &=-2 s-1=0 \\ \text{or }\quad s &=-0.5 \end{aligned}[/latex]
To have, both the poles at the same directions
[latex] \begin{aligned} |G(s)|_{s=0.5} &=1 \\ K &=2.25 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-1.explanation_text:
Channel capacity of BSC is [latex]
\begin{array}{l}
C=P \log _{2} P+(1-P) \log _{2}(1-P)+1 \\
C=0.5 \log _{2} 0.5+0.5 \log _{2} 0.5+1\\
C=0 
\end{array}[/latex] It is the case of channel with independent input 
and output. Hence C=0

A two-port network has scattering parameters given by [latex][S]=\begin{bmatrix} S_{11} &S_{12} \\ S_{21} & S_{22} \end{bmatrix}[/latex].  If the
port-2 of the two port is short circuited, the [latex]S_{11}[/latex]
 parameter for the resultant one port network is
2014-set-1.html: A two-port network has scattering parameters given by [latex][S]=\begin{bmatrix} S_{11} &S_{12} \\ S_{21} & S_{22} \end{bmatrix}[/latex]. If the port-2 of the two port is short circuited, the [latex]S_{11}[/latex] parameter for the resultant one port network is
2014-set-1.subject: Electromagnetics - Miscellaneous Topics
2014-set-1.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{array}{l} b_{1}=s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{12} \cdot a_{2} \qquad\ldots(i)\\ b_{2}=s_{21} \cdot a_{1}+s_{22} a_{2}\qquad\ldots(ii) \end{array}[/latex] When output is short, [latex]a_{2}=-b_{2} [/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} -a_{2} &=s_{21} \cdot a_{1}+s_{22} a_{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad a_{2} &=\frac{-s_{21} \cdot a_{1}}{1+s_{22}} \end{aligned}[/latex] Substituting in first equation, [latex] \begin{aligned} b_{1} &=s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{12}\left(\frac{-s_{21} \cdot a_{1}}{1+s_{22}}\right) \\ &=\frac{s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{11} \cdot s_{22} a_{1}-s_{12} \cdot s_{21} a_{1}}{1+s_{22}} \\ \frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}} &=s_{11}=\frac{s_{11}+s_{11} \cdot s_{22}-s_{12} \cdot s_{21}}{1+s_{22}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{array}{l} b_{1}=s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{12} \cdot a_{2} \qquad\ldots(i)\\ b_{2}=s_{21} \cdot a_{1}+s_{22} a_{2}\qquad\ldots(ii) \end{array}[/latex]
When output is short, [latex]a_{2}=-b_{2} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} -a_{2} &=s_{21} \cdot a_{1}+s_{22} a_{2} \\ \Rightarrow \quad a_{2} &=\frac{-s_{21} \cdot a_{1}}{1+s_{22}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Substituting in first equation,
[latex] \begin{aligned} b_{1} &=s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{12}\left(\frac{-s_{21} \cdot a_{1}}{1+s_{22}}\right) \\ &=\frac{s_{11} \cdot a_{1}+s_{11} \cdot s_{22} a_{1}-s_{12} \cdot s_{21} a_{1}}{1+s_{22}} \\ \frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}} &=s_{11}=\frac{s_{11}+s_{11} \cdot s_{22}-s_{12} \cdot s_{21}}{1+s_{22}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-1.html: The volume under the surface z(x,y) = x + y and above the triangle in the x-y plane defined by [latex]\{0\leq y\leq x \; and \; 0\leq x\leq 12\}[/latex] is _____.
2014-set-1.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2014-set-1.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { Volume } &=\iint_{12 x} z d x d y=\iint(x+y) d x d y \\ &=\int_{0}^{12}\int_{0}^{x} \int(x+y) d x d y \\ &=\left.\int_{0}^{12}\left(x y+\frac{y^{2}}{2}\right) \right|_{0} ^{x} d x \\ &=\int_{0}^{12}\left(x^{2}+\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right) d x \\ &=\frac{3}{2} \int_{0}^{12} x^{2} d x=\frac{3}{2} \times\left.\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right|_{0} ^{12} \\ &=864 \text { unit }^{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-1.text:
Consider a discrete time periodic signal [latex]x[n]=sin(\frac{\pi n}{5})[/latex]. Let [latex]a_{k}[/latex] be the complex Fourier series coefficients of x[n]. The coefficients [latex]\{a_{k}\}[/latex] are non-zero when
k = Bm[latex]{\pm }[/latex]1, where m is any integer. The value of B is ____.
2014-set-1.html: Consider a discrete time periodic signal [latex]x[n]=sin(\frac{\pi n}{5})[/latex]. Let [latex]a_{k}[/latex] be the complex Fourier series coefficients of x[n]. The coefficients [latex]\{a_{k}\}[/latex] are non-zero when k = Bm[latex]{\pm }[/latex]1, where m is any integer. The value of B is ____.
2014-set-1.subject: Signals and Systems - DTFS, DTFT and DFT
2014-set-1.explanation_text: From discrete Fourier series definition [latex] \begin{array}{l} x[n]=\sum_{K=0}^{N-1} a_{K} e^{j K\left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}\right) n}\\ =a_{-1} e^{-j \frac{2 \pi}{N} n}+a_{0}+a_{1} e^{i \frac{2 \pi}{N} n} \quad \ldots(i)\\ x[n]=\frac{-1}{2 j} e^{-i \frac{\pi}{5} n}+\frac{1}{2 j} e^{i \frac{\pi}{5} n} \end{array}[/latex] Also given [latex] x[n]=\sin \left(\frac{\pi n}{5}\right) [/latex] where [latex] N=10\left[\frac{2 \pi}{N}=\frac{\pi}{5} \Rightarrow N=10\right] [/latex] By comparison [latex]a_{1}=\frac{1}{2 j} and a_{9}=a_{-1}=\frac{-1}{2 j} [/latex] As the TFS coefficient [latex]a_{K}[/latex] is also periodic with period N=10. [latex] \begin{aligned} a_{1} &=a_{11}=a_{21} \cdots \\ a_{-1} &=a_{9}=a_{19} \cdots \end{aligned}[/latex] Given that [latex]a_{K}[/latex] is non-zero for [latex]K=B m \pm 1 [/latex] [latex] \begin{array}{cc} B m \pm 1=1& \quad 9 \cdots\\ -1 &\quad11\ldots\\ \text{For }m=0 \quad for& \quad m=1 \\ \end{array}[/latex] To satisfy this condition B must be '10' where 'm'  is any integer.
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
From discrete Fourier series definition
[latex] \begin{array}{l} x[n]=\sum_{K=0}^{N-1} a_{K} e^{j K\left(\frac{2 \pi}{N}\right) n}\\ =a_{-1} e^{-j \frac{2 \pi}{N} n}+a_{0}+a_{1} e^{i \frac{2 \pi}{N} n} \quad \ldots(i)\\ x[n]=\frac{-1}{2 j} e^{-i \frac{\pi}{5} n}+\frac{1}{2 j} e^{i \frac{\pi}{5} n} \end{array}[/latex]
Also given
[latex] x[n]=\sin \left(\frac{\pi n}{5}\right) [/latex]
where [latex] N=10\left[\frac{2 \pi}{N}=\frac{\pi}{5} \Rightarrow N=10\right] [/latex]
By comparison [latex]a_{1}=\frac{1}{2 j} and a_{9}=a_{-1}=\frac{-1}{2 j} [/latex]
As the TFS coefficient [latex]a_{K}[/latex] is also periodic with period N=10.
[latex] \begin{aligned} a_{1} &=a_{11}=a_{21} \cdots \\ a_{-1} &=a_{9}=a_{19} \cdots \end{aligned}[/latex]
Given that [latex]a_{K}[/latex] is non-zero for [latex]K=B m \pm 1 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{cc} B m \pm 1=1& \quad 9 \cdots\\ -1 &\quad11\ldots\\ \text{For }m=0 \quad for& \quad m=1 \\ \end{array}[/latex]
To satisfy this condition B must be '10' where 'm' is any integer.

2014-set-1.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{array}{l} \frac{10}{0.7 \times 10\left(\frac{s}{0.1}+1\right)\left(\frac{s}{1}+1\right)\left(\frac{s}{10}+1\right)} \\ =\frac{10}{\left(\frac{s}{0.1}+1\right)\left(\frac{s}{1}+1\right)\left(\frac{s}{10}+1\right)} \\ \text { Amount of shitt }=2010 \mathrm{g} \mathrm{K}=20 \mathrm{log} 10=20 \mathrm{dB} \end{array}[/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} -20dB&=\frac{20-0}{\log0.1-\log\omega_{gc}}\\ \text{or},\omega_{gc}&=1\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{sec}&\ldots(i)\\ \mathrm{PM}&=180^{\circ}+\angle GH(j\omega|_{at\omega=\omega_{wc}}&\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex] From the given transfer function, [latex] \begin{aligned} \angle G(j \omega)&=-\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{g c}}{0.1}\right)-\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{g c}}{1}\right) \\ &-\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{g c}}{10}\right) \\ \alpha \angle G(j(1)) &=-84.289^{\circ}-45^{\circ}-5.711^{\circ} \\ &=-135^{\circ} &\ldots(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex] \therefore [/latex] From equation(ii) and (iii) we get, [latex] \text { Phase margin } \mathrm{PM}=180^{\circ}-135^{\circ}=45^{\circ}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} -20dB&=\frac{20-0}{\log0.1-\log\omega_{gc}}\\ \text{or},\omega_{gc}&=1\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{sec}&\ldots(i)\\ \mathrm{PM}&=180^{\circ}+\angle GH(j\omega|_{at\omega=\omega_{wc}}&\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
From the given transfer function,

2014-set-1.text:
For the following feedback system [latex]G(s)=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}[/latex]. The 2% settling time of the step response is required to be less than 2 seconds.
Which one of the following compensators C(s) achieves this ?
2014-set-1.html: For the following feedback system [latex]G(s)=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)}[/latex]. The 2% settling time of the step response is required to be less than 2 seconds. Which one of the following compensators C(s) achieves this ?
2014-set-1.subject: Control Systems - Compensators and Controllers
2014-set-1.explanation_text: Given open loop transfer function is [latex] \begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)} \\ \therefore T(s)&=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)}=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)+1} \\ T(s)&=\frac{1}{s^{2}+3 s+3} &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex] Comparing equation (i) with standard transfer function [latex] \xi \omega_{n}=\frac{3}{2}=1.5 [/latex] [latex] \therefore [/latex] 2% settling time [latex] \tau_{s}=\frac{4}{\xi \omega_{n}}=\frac{4}{1.5}=2.67>2 \mathrm{sec} [/latex] Thus, in order to make settling time [latex]\left(\tau_{s}\right)[/latex] less than 2 sec, PD controller should be used. Hence, option (C) is the correct choice. Where, [latex]C(s)=2(s+4) [/latex] [latex] \therefore [/latex] New transfer function [latex]=T^{\prime}(G)[/latex] [latex] =\frac{C(s) G(s)}{1+C(s) G(s)}=\frac{2(s+4)}{s^{2}+3 s+2+2 s+8} [/latex] or [latex]T^{\prime}(s)=\frac{2(s+4)}{s^{2}+5 s+10}[/latex] [latex] \therefore \quad \tau_{s}=\frac{4}{\xi \omega_{n}}=\frac{4}{5 / 2}=\frac{4}{2.5}=1.6[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
Given open loop transfer function is
[latex] \begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)} \\ \therefore T(s)&=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)}=\frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)+1} \\ T(s)&=\frac{1}{s^{2}+3 s+3} &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Comparing equation (i) with standard transfer function
[latex] \xi \omega_{n}=\frac{3}{2}=1.5 [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] 2% settling time
[latex] \tau_{s}=\frac{4}{\xi \omega_{n}}=\frac{4}{1.5}=2.67>2 \mathrm{sec} [/latex]
Thus, in order to make settling time [latex]\left(\tau_{s}\right)[/latex] less than 2 sec, PD controller should be used. Hence, option (C) is the correct choice.
Where, [latex]C(s)=2(s+4) [/latex]
[latex] \therefore [/latex] New transfer function [latex]=T^{\prime}(G)[/latex]
[latex] =\frac{C(s) G(s)}{1+C(s) G(s)}=\frac{2(s+4)}{s^{2}+3 s+2+2 s+8} [/latex]
or [latex]T^{\prime}(s)=\frac{2(s+4)}{s^{2}+5 s+10}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \quad \tau_{s}=\frac{4}{\xi \omega_{n}}=\frac{4}{5 / 2}=\frac{4}{2.5}=1.6[/latex]

2014-set-1.text:
A fair coin is tossed repeatedly until a 'Head' appears for the first time. Let
L be the number of tosses to get this first ' Head' . The entropy H (L) in bits is
_____.
2014-set-1.html: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly until a 'Head' appears for the first time. Let L be the number of tosses to get this first ' Head' . The entropy H (L) in bits is _____.
2014-set-1.subject: Communication Systems - Information Theory and Coding
2014-set-1.explanation_text: If P=1, i.e. if 1 toss is required to gets first head. Then probability to get the first head [latex] \Rightarrow \quad P_{1}=\frac{1}{2} [/latex] If P=2; i.e. if 2 tosses are required to get first head. Then probability to get the first head [latex] \Rightarrow \quad P_{2}=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4} [/latex] If P=3; i.e. if 3 tosses are required to get first head. Then probability to get the first head [latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \quad P_{3}=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{8} \\ \text { Entropy } H=\sum_{i=1}^{N} P_{i} \log _{2} \frac{1}{P_{i}} \\ =\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 2}+\frac{1}{4} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 4}+\log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 8}+\frac{1}{16} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 16} \\ =\frac{1}{2} \times 1+\frac{1}{4} \times 2+\frac{1}{8} \times 3+\frac{1}{16} \times 4+\cdots \\ =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{(2)^{2}}+\frac{3}{(2)^{3}}+\frac{4}{(2)^{4}}+\cdots \\ H \simeq 2 \end{array}[/latex]

If P=3; i.e. if 3 tosses are required to get first head.
Then probability to get the first head
[latex] \begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \quad P_{3}=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{8} \\ \text { Entropy } H=\sum_{i=1}^{N} P_{i} \log _{2} \frac{1}{P_{i}} \\ =\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 2}+\frac{1}{4} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 4}+\log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 8}+\frac{1}{16} \log _{2} \frac{1}{1 / 16} \\ =\frac{1}{2} \times 1+\frac{1}{4} \times 2+\frac{1}{8} \times 3+\frac{1}{16} \times 4+\cdots \\ =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{(2)^{2}}+\frac{3}{(2)^{3}}+\frac{4}{(2)^{4}}+\cdots \\ H \simeq 2 \end{array}[/latex]

In spherical coordinates, let [latex]\hat{a}_{\theta },\hat{a}_{\phi }[/latex]
 denote unit vectors along the [latex]\theta, \phi[/latex]  directions. [latex]E=\frac{100}{r}sin\theta cos(\omega t-\beta r)\hat{a}_\theta V/m[/latex] and [latex]E=\frac{0.265}{r}sin\theta cos(\omega t-\beta r)\hat{a}_\phi A/m[/latex] represent the electric and magnetic field components of the EM wave at large
distances [latex]r[/latex]  from a dipole antenna, in free space. The average power (W) crossing
the hemispherical shell located at r = 1 km, [latex]0\leq \theta \leq \pi /2[/latex] is ____.
2014-set-1.html:
In spherical coordinates, let [latex]\hat{a}_{\theta },\hat{a}_{\phi }[/latex] denote unit vectors along the [latex]\theta, \phi[/latex] directions.
[latex]E=\frac{100}{r}sin\theta cos(\omega t-\beta r)\hat{a}_\theta V/m[/latex]
and
[latex]E=\frac{0.265}{r}sin\theta cos(\omega t-\beta r)\hat{a}_\phi A/m[/latex]
represent the electric and magnetic field components of the EM wave at large distances [latex]r[/latex] from a dipole antenna, in free space. The average power (W) crossing the hemispherical shell located at r = 1 km, [latex]0\leq \theta \leq \pi /2[/latex] is ____.
2014-set-1.subject: Electromagnetics - Antennas
2014-set-1.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{E} &=\operatorname{Re}\left[\frac{100}{r} \sin \theta e^{-\beta r} e^{j \omega t}\right] \hat{a}_{\theta} V / m \\ &=\operatorname{Re}\left[\frac{0.265}{r} \sin \theta e^{-\beta \beta r} e^{j \omega t}\right] \hat{a}_{\phi} V / m \end{aligned}[/latex] Poynting vector, [latex] \vec{P}=\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{Re}\left[\vec{E} \times \vec{H}^{*}\right]=\frac{26.5}{2 r^{2}} \sin ^{2} \theta \hat{a}_{r} W / m^{2}[/latex] The average power crossing the given hemispherical shell is, [latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Power } &=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \int_{\phi=0}^{2 \pi} \vec{P} \cdot r^{2} \sin \theta d \theta d \phi \hat{a}_{r} \\ &=\frac{26.5}{2} \times 2 \pi \int_{\theta=0}^{\pi / 2} \sin ^{3} \theta d \theta \\ &=\frac{26.5}{2} \times 2 \pi \frac{2}{3}=55.5 \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{E} &=\operatorname{Re}\left[\frac{100}{r} \sin \theta e^{-\beta r} e^{j \omega t}\right] \hat{a}_{\theta} V / m \\ &=\operatorname{Re}\left[\frac{0.265}{r} \sin \theta e^{-\beta \beta r} e^{j \omega t}\right] \hat{a}_{\phi} V / m \end{aligned}[/latex]
Poynting vector,
[latex] \vec{P}=\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{Re}\left[\vec{E} \times \vec{H}^{*}\right]=\frac{26.5}{2 r^{2}} \sin ^{2} \theta \hat{a}_{r} W / m^{2}[/latex]
The average power crossing the given
hemispherical shell is,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { Power } &=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \int_{\phi=0}^{2 \pi} \vec{P} \cdot r^{2} \sin \theta d \theta d \phi \hat{a}_{r} \\ &=\frac{26.5}{2} \times 2 \pi \int_{\theta=0}^{\pi / 2} \sin ^{3} \theta d \theta \\ &=\frac{26.5}{2} \times 2 \pi \frac{2}{3}=55.5 \mathrm{W} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-1.text: The input impedance of a [latex]\frac{\lambda }{8}[/latex] section of a lossless transmission line of characteristic impedance 50 [latex]\Omega[/latex] is found to be real when the other end is terminated by a load [latex]Z_{L}=(R+jX)\Omega[/latex]. If X is  30 [latex]\Omega[/latex], the value of R(in [latex]\Omega[/latex]) is_____.
2014-set-1.html: The input impedance of a [latex]\frac{\lambda }{8}[/latex] section of a lossless transmission line of characteristic impedance 50 [latex]\Omega[/latex] is found to be real when the other end is terminated by a load [latex]Z_{L}=(R+jX)\Omega[/latex]. If X is 30 [latex]\Omega[/latex], the value of R(in [latex]\Omega[/latex]) is_____.
2014-set-1.subject: Electromagnetics - Transmission Lines
2014-set-1.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} Z_{\text {in }}&=Z_{0}\left(\frac{Z_{L}+j Z_{o} \tan \beta l}{Z_{o}+j Z_{L} \tan \beta l}\right)\\ \text{at }\;l&=\frac{\lambda}{8} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \beta l&=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \times \frac{\lambda}{8}=\frac{\pi}{4} \\ \therefore \quad\tan \frac{\pi}{4}&=1 \\ Z_{\text {in }}&=Z_{o}\left[\frac{Z_{L}+j 50}{Z_{o}+j Z_{L}}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given},\quad Z_{L}&=R+j X=R+j 30 \text{ and }Z_{0}=50 \Omega \\ 30 R &=80(50+R) \\ Z_{\text {in }} &=50\left[\frac{R+j 30+j 50}{50+j(R+j 30)}\right] \\ &=50\left[\frac{R+j 80}{(50-30)+j R}\right]=50\left[\frac{R+j 80}{20+j R}\right] \\ &=50\left[\frac{(R+j 80)(20-j R)}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex] Since, only real part of [latex]Z_{\text {in }}[/latex] exists, so imaginary part of [latex]Z_{\text {in }}=0 [/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad Z_{\text {in }} &=50\left[\frac{20 R+1600 j-j R^{2}+50 R}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\right] \\ \text { Zimaginary } &=0=\frac{1600-R^{2}}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\\ \therefore \quad R^{2} &=1600 \\ R &=40 \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} Z_{\text {in }}&=Z_{0}\left(\frac{Z_{L}+j Z_{o} \tan \beta l}{Z_{o}+j Z_{L} \tan \beta l}\right)\\ \text{at }\;l&=\frac{\lambda}{8} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \beta l&=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \times \frac{\lambda}{8}=\frac{\pi}{4} \\ \therefore \quad\tan \frac{\pi}{4}&=1 \\ Z_{\text {in }}&=Z_{o}\left[\frac{Z_{L}+j 50}{Z_{o}+j Z_{L}}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given},\quad Z_{L}&=R+j X=R+j 30 \text{ and }Z_{0}=50 \Omega \\ 30 R &=80(50+R) \\ Z_{\text {in }} &=50\left[\frac{R+j 30+j 50}{50+j(R+j 30)}\right] \\ &=50\left[\frac{R+j 80}{(50-30)+j R}\right]=50\left[\frac{R+j 80}{20+j R}\right] \\ &=50\left[\frac{(R+j 80)(20-j R)}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, only real part of [latex]Z_{\text {in }}[/latex] exists, so imaginary
part of [latex]Z_{\text {in }}=0 [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad Z_{\text {in }} &=50\left[\frac{20 R+1600 j-j R^{2}+50 R}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\right] \\ \text { Zimaginary } &=0=\frac{1600-R^{2}}{20^{2}+R^{2}}\\ \therefore \quad R^{2} &=1600 \\ R &=40 \Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex] \therefore P(W \geq 0)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex]

[latex] s Y(s)-y(0)+k Y(s)=X(s) [/latex]
[latex] Y(s)[s+k]=X(s)+y(0) [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow Y(s)=\frac{X(s)}{s+k}+\frac{y(0)}{s+k} [/latex]
Taking inverse Laplace transform, we have
[latex] y(t)=e^{-k t} x(t)+y(0) e^{-k t} [/latex]
So if we want -2y(t) as a solution both x(t) and y(0) has to be multiplied by -2; hence change x(t) by -2x(t) and y(0) by -2y(0).

2013.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} Q &=C V \\ Q_{1} &=C_{1} V_{1}=10 \times 10^{-6} \times 10=100 \mu \mathrm{C} \\ Q_{2} &=C_{2} V_{2}=5 \times 10^{-6} \times 5=25 \mu \mathrm{C} \\ Q_{3} &=C_{3} V_{3}=2 \times 10^{-6} \times 2=4 \mu \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex] Capacitors [latex]C_{2}[/latex] and [latex]C_{3}[/latex] are in series. In series charge is same. So, the maximum charge on [latex]C_{2}[/latex] and [latex]C_{3}[/latex] will be minimum of [latex]\left(Q_{2}, Q_{3}\right)=\min (25 \mu C, 4 \mu C)=4 \mu C=Q_{23} [/latex] In series the equivalent capacitance of [latex]C_{2}[/latex] and [latex]C_{3}[/latex] is [latex] C_{23}=\frac{C_{2} C_{3}}{C_{2}+C_{3}}=\frac{5 \times 2}{5+2}=\frac{10}{7} \mu \mathrm{F}[/latex] So, the equivalent voltage [latex] V_{23}=\frac{Q_{23}}{C_{23}}=\frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{\frac{10}{7} \times 10^{-6}}=\frac{28}{10}=2.8 \mathrm{V}[/latex] In parallel, the voltage is same. [latex]\begin{aligned} Q &=C V \\ Q_{1} &=C_{1} V_{1}=10 \times 10^{-6} \times 10=100 \mu \mathrm{C} \\ Q_{2} &=C_{2} V_{2}=5 \times 10^{-6} \times 5=25 \mu \mathrm{C} \\ Q_{3} &=C_{3} V_{3}=2 \times 10^{-6} \times 2=4 \mu \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Capacitors [latex]C_{2}[/latex] and [latex]C_{3}[/latex] are in series.
In series charge is same. So, the maximum charge on [latex]C_{2}[/latex] and [latex]C_{3}[/latex] will be
minimum of [latex]\left(Q_{2}, Q_{3}\right)=\min (25 \mu C, 4 \mu C)=4 \mu C=Q_{23} [/latex]
In series the equivalent capacitance of [latex]C_{2}[/latex] and [latex]C_{3}[/latex] is
[latex] C_{23}=\frac{C_{2} C_{3}}{C_{2}+C_{3}}=\frac{5 \times 2}{5+2}=\frac{10}{7} \mu \mathrm{F}[/latex]
So, the equivalent voltage
[latex] V_{23}=\frac{Q_{23}}{C_{23}}=\frac{4 \times 10^{-6}}{\frac{10}{7} \times 10^{-6}}=\frac{28}{10}=2.8 \mathrm{V}[/latex]
In parallel, the voltage is same.
[latex] V_{1}=V_{23}=2.8 \mathrm{V}[/latex]
Charge in capacitor [latex]C_{1} [/latex]
[latex] Q_{1}=C_{1} V_{1}=10 \times 10^{-6} \times 2.8=28 \mu \mathrm{C}[/latex]
In parallel, the total charge
[latex] \begin{array}{l} Q=Q_{1}+Q_{23} \\ Q=4+28 \\ Q=32 \mu \mathrm{C} \end{array}[/latex]

[latex]t\frac{dx}{dt}+x=t[/latex] is
2012.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
2012.explanation_text: The given differential equation is [latex] t \frac{d x}{d t}+x=t[/latex] with initial condition [latex]x(1)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] which is same as [latex] \frac{d x}{d t}+\frac{x}{t}=1[/latex] Which is a linear differential equation [latex] \frac{d x}{d t}+P x=Q[/latex] Where, [latex]P=\frac{1}{t}[/latex] and Q=1 Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P t t=e^{1 \frac{1}{t} d t}} [/latex] [latex] =e^{\log _{e} t}=t[/latex] Solution is [latex] \begin{aligned} x \cdot(I F)&=\int Q \cdot(I F) d t+C \\ x \cdot t&=\int 1 \cdot t \cdot d t+C \\ x t&=\frac{t^{2}}{2}+C \\ x&=\frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t} \\ \text{Put},x(1)=\frac{1}{2}&\\ \Rightarrow\quad \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow\quad C&=0 \\ \text{So, }\left[x=\frac{t}{2}\right]& \text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}[/latex]
2012.explanation_html:
The given differential equation is [latex] t \frac{d x}{d t}+x=t[/latex] with initial condition [latex]x(1)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] which is same as [latex] \frac{d x}{d t}+\frac{x}{t}=1[/latex]
Which is a linear differential equation
[latex] \frac{d x}{d t}+P x=Q[/latex]
Where, [latex]P=\frac{1}{t}[/latex] and Q=1
Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P t t=e^{1 \frac{1}{t} d t}} [/latex]
[latex] =e^{\log _{e} t}=t[/latex]
Solution is
[latex] \begin{aligned} x \cdot(I F)&=\int Q \cdot(I F) d t+C \\ x \cdot t&=\int 1 \cdot t \cdot d t+C \\ x t&=\frac{t^{2}}{2}+C \\ x&=\frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t} \\ \text{Put},x(1)=\frac{1}{2}&\\ \Rightarrow\quad \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow\quad C&=0 \\ \text{So, }\left[x=\frac{t}{2}\right]& \text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2012.text: The radiation pattern of an antenna in spherical co-ordinates is given by [latex]F(\theta )=cos^{4}\theta ;0\leq \theta\leq \pi /2[/latex] The directivity of the antenna is
2012.html:
The radiation pattern of an antenna in spherical co-ordinates is given by
[latex]F(\theta )=cos^{4}\theta ;0\leq \theta\leq \pi /2[/latex]
The directivity of the antenna is
2012.subject: Electromagnetics - Antennas
2012.explanation_text:
[latex]F(\theta)=\cos ^{4} \theta, 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi / 2[/latex] we know that directivity D is [latex] D=\frac{4 \pi u_{\max }}{\pi_{\mathrm{rad}}} \qquad\ldots(1)[/latex] [latex] \mathrm{F}(\theta) [/latex] is nothing but radiation intensity [latex] u(\theta, \phi)[/latex] and [latex] W_{\mathrm{rad}} [/latex] is radiated power. [latex] W_{\mathrm{rad}}=\int_{0}^{2 \pi \pi / 2} \int_{0}^{2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin \theta d \phi\qquad\ldots(2)[/latex] above equation is written from the formula [latex] W_{\mathrm{rad}}=\iint_{\theta \phi} u(\theta, \phi) d \Omega[/latex] where [latex]\alpha \Omega[/latex] is solid angle and [latex]d \Omega=\sin \theta d \theta d \phi [/latex] So from (2) [latex] \begin{aligned} W_{\mathrm{rad}} &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi \pi / 2} \int_{0}^{2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin d \theta d \phi \\ W_{\mathrm{rad}} &=2 \pi \int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin \theta d \theta \\W_{\mathrm{rad}}&=-2 \pi\left[\frac{\cos ^{5} \theta}{5}\right]_{0}^{\pi / 2}\\
W_{\mathrm{rad}}&=\frac{2 \pi}{5}&\ldots(3)\\
\text { So, } \quad D&=\frac{4 \pi u_{\max }}{\left(\frac{2 \pi}{5}\right)}=10 u_{\max }=10\\
&\text { In } \mathrm{dB} \text { directivity }=10 \mathrm{log}_{10} \mathrm{D}=10 \mathrm{dB}\end{aligned}[/latex]
2012.explanation_html:
[latex]F(\theta)=\cos ^{4} \theta, 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi / 2[/latex]
we know that directivity D is
[latex] D=\frac{4 \pi u_{\max }}{\pi_{\mathrm{rad}}} \qquad\ldots(1)[/latex]
[latex] \mathrm{F}(\theta) [/latex] is nothing but radiation intensity [latex] u(\theta, \phi)[/latex] and
[latex] W_{\mathrm{rad}} [/latex] is radiated power.
[latex] W_{\mathrm{rad}}=\int_{0}^{2 \pi \pi / 2} \int_{0}^{2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin \theta d \phi\qquad\ldots(2)[/latex]
above equation is written from the formula
[latex] W_{\mathrm{rad}}=\iint_{\theta \phi} u(\theta, \phi) d \Omega[/latex]
where [latex]\alpha \Omega[/latex] is solid angle and [latex]d \Omega=\sin \theta d \theta d \phi [/latex]
So from (2)
[latex] \begin{aligned} W_{\mathrm{rad}} &=\int_{0}^{2 \pi \pi / 2} \int_{0}^{2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin d \theta d \phi \\ W_{\mathrm{rad}} &=2 \pi \int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \cos ^{4} \theta \sin \theta d \theta \\W_{\mathrm{rad}}&=-2 \pi\left[\frac{\cos ^{5} \theta}{5}\right]_{0}^{\pi / 2}\\ W_{\mathrm{rad}}&=\frac{2 \pi}{5}&\ldots(3)\\ \text { So, } \quad D&=\frac{4 \pi u_{\max }}{\left(\frac{2 \pi}{5}\right)}=10 u_{\max }=10\\ &\text { In } \mathrm{dB} \text { directivity }=10 \mathrm{log}_{10} \mathrm{D}=10 \mathrm{dB}\end{aligned}[/latex]

2012.text: A system with transfer function [latex]G(s)=\frac{(s^{2}+9)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)}[/latex] is excited by sin([latex]\omega[/latex] t). The steady-state output of the system is zero at
2012.html:
A system with transfer function
[latex]G(s)=\frac{(s^{2}+9)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)}[/latex]
is excited by sin([latex]\omega[/latex] t). The steady-state output of the system is zero at
2012.subject: Control Systems - Frequency Response Analysis
2012.explanation_text: Transfer function is [latex] \begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \\ \text{Input }\quad X(s)&=L \cdot T[\sin \omega t]\\ X(s)&=\frac{\omega}{s^{2}+\omega^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex] So output [latex] Y(s)=\frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \cdot \frac{\omega}{\left(s^{2}+\omega^{2}\right)}[/latex] Now [latex] \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} y(t)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} S Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \cdot \frac{\omega}{\left(s^{2}+\omega^{2}\right)}[/latex] this will be zero if [latex] s^{2}+\omega^{2}[/latex] will cancel [latex]\left(s^{2}+9\right)[/latex] term as only then final value theorem will be applicable. So at [latex]\omega^{2}=9 \Rightarrow \omega=3 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec},[/latex] steady state output will be zero.
2012.explanation_html:
Transfer function is
[latex] \begin{aligned} G(s)&=\frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \\ \text{Input }\quad X(s)&=L \cdot T[\sin \omega t]\\ X(s)&=\frac{\omega}{s^{2}+\omega^{2}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
So output
[latex] Y(s)=\frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \cdot \frac{\omega}{\left(s^{2}+\omega^{2}\right)}[/latex]
Now
[latex] \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} y(t)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} S Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s \frac{\left(s^{2}+9\right)(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+4)} \cdot \frac{\omega}{\left(s^{2}+\omega^{2}\right)}[/latex]
this will be zero if [latex] s^{2}+\omega^{2}[/latex] will cancel [latex]\left(s^{2}+9\right)[/latex] term as only then final value theorem will be applicable.
So at [latex]\omega^{2}=9 \Rightarrow \omega=3 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec},[/latex] steady state output will be zero.

2012.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} y&=\int_{-\infty}^{t} x(\tau) \cos (3 \tau) d \tau \\ y\left(t-t_{0}\right)&=\int_{-\infty}^{t-t_{0}} x(\tau) \cos (3 \tau) d \tau \\ y^{\prime}(t) \text { for input } &x\left(t-t_{0}\right) \text { , is }\\ y^{\prime}(t)&=\int_{-\infty}^{t} x\left(\tau-t_{0}\right) \cos 3 \tau d \tau \\ y^{\prime}(t)&=\int_{-\infty}^{\left(t-t_{0}\right)} x(\tau) \cos 3\left(\tau+t_{0}\right) d \tau \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex] y^{\prime}(t) \neq y\left(t-t_{0}\right)[/latex] so system is not time invariant for input [latex]x(\tau)=\cos (3 \tau)[/latex] (bounded input) [latex] y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t} \cos ^{2}(3 \tau) d \tau \rightarrow \infty \text { as } t \rightarrow \infty[/latex] So, for bounded i/p, o/p is not bounded therefore system is not stable.

so system is not time invariant for input [latex]x(\tau)=\cos (3 \tau)[/latex] (bounded input)

2012.explanation_text: Characteristic equation is [latex] 1+G(s)H(s)=0[/latex] [latex] 1+\frac{K(s+1)}{s^{3}+a s^{2}+2 s+1}=0 [/latex] [latex] s^{3}+a s^{2}+(2+K) s+(1+K)=0 [/latex] array for this is Routh [latex] \begin{array}{l|lr} s^{3} & 1 & (2+K) \\ s^{2} & a & (1+K) \\ s^{1} & \frac{a(2+K)-(1+K)}{a} \\ s^{0} & (1+K) & \end{array}[/latex] For oscillation [latex]\frac{a(2+K)-(1+K)}{a}=0 [/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow \quad a=\left(\frac{1+K}{2+K}\right) [/latex] Now [latex] \begin{aligned} a s^{2}+(1+K)&=0 \\ -a \omega^{2}+(1+K)&=0 \\ \text{given }\quad \omega&=2 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \\ -4 a+(1+K)&=0 \\ -4 \frac{(1+K)}{(2+K)}+(1+K)&=0 \\ -4(1+K)+(2+K)(1+K)&=0 \\ (1+K)[(2+K)-4]&=0 \\ K=-1,2 \end{aligned}[/latex] but K=-1 is not possible as system will not  oscillate for this as a=0 So, K=2 [latex] a=\frac{1+K}{2+K}=\frac{3}{4}=0.75[/latex]
2012.explanation_html:
Characteristic equation is
[latex] 1+G(s)H(s)=0[/latex]
[latex] 1+\frac{K(s+1)}{s^{3}+a s^{2}+2 s+1}=0 [/latex]
[latex] s^{3}+a s^{2}+(2+K) s+(1+K)=0 [/latex]
array for this is Routh
[latex] \begin{array}{l|lr} s^{3} & 1 & (2+K) \\ s^{2} & a & (1+K) \\ s^{1} & \frac{a(2+K)-(1+K)}{a} \\ s^{0} & (1+K) & \end{array}[/latex]
For oscillation [latex]\frac{a(2+K)-(1+K)}{a}=0 [/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \quad a=\left(\frac{1+K}{2+K}\right) [/latex]
Now
[latex] \begin{aligned} a s^{2}+(1+K)&=0 \\ -a \omega^{2}+(1+K)&=0 \\ \text{given }\quad \omega&=2 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \\ -4 a+(1+K)&=0 \\ -4 \frac{(1+K)}{(2+K)}+(1+K)&=0 \\ -4(1+K)+(2+K)(1+K)&=0 \\ (1+K)[(2+K)-4]&=0 \\ K=-1,2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
but K=-1 is not possible as system will not oscillate for this as a=0
So, K=2
[latex] a=\frac{1+K}{2+K}=\frac{3}{4}=0.75[/latex]

2012.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{2 \cos \omega \sin 2 \omega}{\omega}&=H(\omega) \\ H(\omega)=2 \cos \omega&\left(\frac{2 \sin 2 \omega}{2 \omega}-H_{1}(j \omega) \cdot H_{2}(j \omega)\right)\\ \text { where, } \quad H_{1}(j \omega)&=2 \cos \omega\\ H_{2}(j \omega)=\frac{2 \sin 2 \omega}{2 \omega}&=2 \operatorname{Sa}(2 \omega) \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex] H_{1}(j \omega)=2 \cos \omega=\left(e^{j \omega}+e^{-j \omega}\right)=e^{j \omega t}+e^{j \omega(-1)} [/latex] So [latex] H(j \omega)=2 \cos \omega H_{2}(j \omega)=\left(e^{j \omega}+e^{-j \omega}\right) H_{2}(j \omega) [/latex] [latex] H(j \omega)=e^{j \omega} H_{2}(j \omega)+e^{-j \omega} H_{2}(j \omega) [/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow \quad h(t)=h_{2}(t+1)+h_{2}(t-1) [/latex] So, [latex]h(O) = 1[/latex]

[latex] H_{1}(j \omega)=2 \cos \omega=\left(e^{j \omega}+e^{-j \omega}\right)=e^{j \omega t}+e^{j \omega(-1)} [/latex]
So

P( no. of toss is 1)=P (Head in first toss) [latex]=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] P(no. of toss is 3) = P(tail in first toss, tail in second toss and head in third toss) [latex] =\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{8}[/latex] P(no. of toss is 5)=P(T, T, T, T, H)[latex]=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{5}=\frac{1}{32} [/latex] ... etc. So P( no. of tosses is odd )[latex]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{32}+\cdots [/latex] Sum of infinite geometric series with [latex] \begin{aligned} a&=\frac{1}{2} \text{ and }r=\frac{1}{4} \\ &=\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{1-\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{3}{4}}=\frac{2}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2012.text: The maximum value of [latex]f(x)=x^{3}-9x^{2}+24x+5[/latex] in the interval [1, 6] is
2012.html: The maximum value of [latex]f(x)=x^{3}-9x^{2}+24x+5[/latex] in the interval [1, 6] is
2012.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2012.explanation_text:
We need absolute maximum of [latex]
f(x)=x^{3}-9 x^{2}+24 x+5 [/latex] in the interval [1,6] First find local maximum if any by putting  [latex]f^{\prime}(x)=0 [/latex] [latex]
\begin{aligned}
\text{i.e.}\quad f^{\prime}(x)&=3 x^{2}-18 x+24=0\\
\text{i.e.}\quad  x^{2}-6 x+8&=0 \\
x &=2,4 \\
\text { Now } \quad f^{\prime \prime}(x) &=6 x-18 \\
f^{\prime \prime}(2) &=12-18=-6 \lt 0\\
&\text{(So  x=2  is a point of local maximum)}\\
\text{ and  }f^{\prime \prime}(4)&=24-18=+6 \gt 0 \\
&\text{(So  x=4  is a point of local minimum)}
\end{aligned}[/latex] Now tabulate the values of  f  at end point of interval 
and at local maximum point, to find absolute 
maximum in given range, as shown below: [latex]
\begin{array}{l|l}
x & f(x) \\
1 & 21 \\
2 & 25 \\
6 & 41
\end{array}[/latex] Clearly the absolute maxima is at  x=6  
and absolute maximum value is 41.

2012.html: Given that [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 & -3\\ 2&0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] and [latex]I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], the value of [latex]A^{3}[/latex] is
2012.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
2012.explanation_text: [latex]A=\left[\begin{array}{rr}-5 & -3 \\ 2 & 0\end{array}\right] \text{ and } I=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right] [/latex] Characteristic equation of A is [latex] \begin{aligned} \left|\begin{array}{rr}-5-\lambda & -3 \\ 2 & 0-\lambda\end{array}\right|&=0\\ (-5-\lambda)(-\lambda)+6&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \lambda^{2}+5 \lambda+6&=0 \\ \text{ So,}\quad A^{2}+5 A+6 I&=0 \\ &\text{(by Cayley Hamilton theorem) }\\ \Rightarrow \quad A^{2}=-5 A-6 I& \end{aligned}[/latex] Multiplying by A on both sides, we have, [latex] \begin{aligned} A^{3} &=-5 A^{2}-6 A \\ \Rightarrow \quad A^{3} &=-5(-5 A-6 I)-6 A \\ &=19 A+30I \end{aligned}[/latex]
2012.explanation_html:
[latex]A=\left[\begin{array}{rr}-5 & -3 \\ 2 & 0\end{array}\right] \text{ and } I=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right] [/latex]
Characteristic equation of A is
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left|\begin{array}{rr}-5-\lambda & -3 \\ 2 & 0-\lambda\end{array}\right|&=0\\ (-5-\lambda)(-\lambda)+6&=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \lambda^{2}+5 \lambda+6&=0 \\ \text{ So,}\quad A^{2}+5 A+6 I&=0 \\ &\text{(by Cayley Hamilton theorem) }\\ \Rightarrow \quad A^{2}=-5 A-6 I& \end{aligned}[/latex]
Multiplying by A on both sides, we have,
[latex] \begin{aligned} A^{3} &=-5 A^{2}-6 A \\ \Rightarrow \quad A^{3} &=-5(-5 A-6 I)-6 A \\ &=19 A+30I \end{aligned}[/latex]

2012.explanation_text: Case (i): [latex] \begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{DC}}&=10 \mathrm{V}, R_{L}=1 \Omega, I=3 \mathrm{A} \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=I\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+R_{L}\right)=3\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+1\right)\\ \Rightarrow \quad V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=3 R_{\mathrm{Th}}+3 &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex] Case (ii): [latex] \begin{aligned} R_{L}&=2.5 \Omega, I=2 \mathrm{A}, V_{\mathrm{DC}}=10 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=2\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+2.5\right) \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=2 R_{\mathrm{Th}}+5 &\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex] From equations (i) and (ii) [latex] V_{\mathrm{Th}}=9 \mathrm{V} and R_{\mathrm{TH}}=2 \Omega \quad\ldots(iii)[/latex] Now, [latex]V_{Th}[/latex] depends on independent voltage source and varies with applied voltage. [latex]R_{Th}[/latex] does not depend on voltage source and is same for any applied voltage source, since voltage_ source is short circuited while calculating [latex]R_{Th}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{For }V_{\mathrm{DC}}&=6 \mathrm{V}, R_{\mathrm{L}}=1 \Omega, I=7 / 3 \\ V_{T h}&=I\left(R_{T h}+R_{L}\right) \\ V_{T h}&=\frac{7}{3}(2+1)=7 V &\ldots(iv) \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex] \because [/latex]The network is linear and non reciprocal, it may contain dependent voltage source [latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad V_{T h}&=a V+b \\ \Rightarrow \quad 9&=a 10+b \quad \text{from equation (iii)} \\ \text{and }\quad 7&=a 6+b \quad\text{from equation (iv)} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex] Solving, we get a=1/2 and b=4 [latex] \therefore \quad V_{\mathrm{Th}}=\frac{V}{2}+4=\frac{8}{2}+4=8 \mathrm{V}[/latex]
2012.explanation_html:
Case (i):
[latex] \begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{DC}}&=10 \mathrm{V}, R_{L}=1 \Omega, I=3 \mathrm{A} \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=I\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+R_{L}\right)=3\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+1\right)\\ \Rightarrow \quad V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=3 R_{\mathrm{Th}}+3 &\ldots(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Case (ii):
[latex] \begin{aligned} R_{L}&=2.5 \Omega, I=2 \mathrm{A}, V_{\mathrm{DC}}=10 \mathrm{V} \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=2\left(R_{\mathrm{Th}}+2.5\right) \\ V_{\mathrm{Th}}&=2 R_{\mathrm{Th}}+5 &\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
From equations (i) and (ii)
[latex] V_{\mathrm{Th}}=9 \mathrm{V} and R_{\mathrm{TH}}=2 \Omega \quad\ldots(iii)[/latex]
Now, [latex]V_{Th}[/latex] depends on independent voltage source and varies with applied voltage. [latex]R_{Th}[/latex] does not depend on voltage source and is same for any applied voltage source, since voltage_ source is short circuited while calculating [latex]R_{Th}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{For }V_{\mathrm{DC}}&=6 \mathrm{V}, R_{\mathrm{L}}=1 \Omega, I=7 / 3 \\ V_{T h}&=I\left(R_{T h}+R_{L}\right) \\ V_{T h}&=\frac{7}{3}(2+1)=7 V &\ldots(iv) \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex] \because [/latex]The network is linear and non reciprocal, it may
contain dependent voltage source
[latex] \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad V_{T h}&=a V+b \\ \Rightarrow \quad 9&=a 10+b \quad \text{from equation (iii)} \\ \text{and }\quad 7&=a 6+b \quad\text{from equation (iv)} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solving, we get a=1/2 and b=4
[latex] \therefore \quad V_{\mathrm{Th}}=\frac{V}{2}+4=\frac{8}{2}+4=8 \mathrm{V}[/latex]

2011.explanation_text: In the first toss, results can be 1,2,3,4,5 For 1, the second toss results can be 2,3,4,5,6 For 2 , the second toss results can be 3,4,5,6 For 3, the second toss results can be 4,5,6 For 4, the second toss results can be 5,6 For 5, the second toss results can be 6 The required probability [latex] =\frac{1}{6} \cdot \frac{5}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \cdot \frac{4}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \cdot \frac{3}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \cdot \frac{2}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \cdot \frac{1}{6}=\frac{5}{12}[/latex]

s^{2}+\frac{1}{R C} s+\frac{1}{L C}=0[/latex] where, Bandwidth= [latex]\frac{1}{RC}[/latex] (i) It is clear that the bandwidth of a parallel RLC

input impedance attains its maximum value 
at resonance.

(iii) In parallel RLC circuit, the admittance is minimum at resonance. Hence magnitude of input impedance attains its maximum value at resonance.

2010.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2010.explanation_text: [latex]e^{y}=x^{1 / x}[/latex] Taking natural log on both sides. [latex] y=\frac{1}{x} \ln x[/latex] Differentiating on both sides, [latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x} &=\frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{1}{x}-\frac{\ln x}{x^{2}}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}(1-\ln x) \\ \Rightarrow & d x \\ \Rightarrow 1-\ln x &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \ln x &=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad x &=\mathrm{e} \\ \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} &=\frac{-2}{x^{3}}[1-\ln x]+\frac{1}{x^{2}}\left(\frac{-1}{x}\right) \\ &=-\frac{1}{x^{3}}[2-\ln x+1] \\ \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} &=-\frac{1}{x^{3}}[3-\ln x]\\ \text{Putting, }x&=e_{1} \\ \left.\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}\right|_{x=e}&=\frac{-1}{e^{3}}[3-1]=\frac{-2}{e^{3}} \lt 0 \end{aligned}[/latex] Since, second derivative is negative, therefore, y has maxima at x= e.
2010.explanation_html:
[latex]e^{y}=x^{1 / x}[/latex]
Taking natural log on both sides.
[latex] y=\frac{1}{x} \ln x[/latex]
Differentiating on both sides,
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{d y}{d x} &=\frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{1}{x}-\frac{\ln x}{x^{2}}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}(1-\ln x) \\ \Rightarrow & d x \\ \Rightarrow 1-\ln x &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \ln x &=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad x &=\mathrm{e} \\ \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} &=\frac{-2}{x^{3}}[1-\ln x]+\frac{1}{x^{2}}\left(\frac{-1}{x}\right) \\ &=-\frac{1}{x^{3}}[2-\ln x+1] \\ \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} &=-\frac{1}{x^{3}}[3-\ln x]\\ \text{Putting, }x&=e_{1} \\ \left.\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}\right|_{x=e}&=\frac{-1}{e^{3}}[3-1]=\frac{-2}{e^{3}} \lt 0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since, second derivative is negative, therefore,
y has maxima at x= e.

2010.text:
A fair coin is tossed independently four times. The probability of the event "the
number of time heads shown up is more than the number of times tail shown up"
2010.html: A fair coin is tossed independently four times. The probability of the event "the number of time heads shown up is more than the number of times tail shown up"
2010.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
2010.explanation_text: The only 5 events when the number of times of heads show up is more than the number of times tails show up are given below: [latex] \begin{array}{cccc} H&H&H&H\\ H&H&H&T\\ H&H&T&H\\ H&T&H&H\\ T&H&H&H \end{array}[/latex] since fair coin is tossed independently four times, the probability of each above events is [latex] \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{16} [/latex] All above events are mutually exclusive, so, total probability [latex] =\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16}=\frac{5}{16}[/latex]

2010.html: If [latex]\vec{A}=xy\hat{a}_{x}+x^{2}\hat{a}_{y}[/latex], then [latex]\oint_{0}^{C}\vec{A}\cdot \vec{dl}[/latex] over the path shown in the figure is
2010.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2010.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{A} &=x y \hat{a}_{x}+x^{2} \hat{a}_{y} \\ \vec{l} &=x \hat{a}_{x}+y \hat{a}_{y} \\ \vec{d} t &=d x \hat{a}_{x}+d y \hat{a}_{y} \\ \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d} t &=x y d x+x^{2} d y \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} P-Q&\\ y&=1,dy=0\\ \int_{P}^{0} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d} i &=\int_{1 / \sqrt{3}}^{2 / \sqrt{3}} x d x=\left.\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right|_{1 / \sqrt{3}} ^{2 / \sqrt{3}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ Q-R: &=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, d x=0 \\ \int_{0}^{R} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d} t &=\int_{1}^{3}\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^{2} d y=\frac{4}{3}(3-1)=\frac{8}{3}\\ R-S: & \\ y&=3, d y=0 \\ \int_{A}^{S} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d} t &=\int_{2 / \sqrt{3}}^{1 / \sqrt{3}} 3 x d x=\left.\frac{3}{2} x^{2}\right|_{2 / \sqrt{3}} ^{\sqrt{3}} \\ &=\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{4}{3}\right)=\frac{-3}{2} \\ S-P & \\ x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, & d x=0 \\ \int_{S}^{P} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d} i &=\int_{3}^{1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^{2} d y=\frac{1}{3}(1-3)=\frac{-2}{3} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \text { So, } \oint_{C} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d} \vec{l}=& \int_{P}^{Q} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d} \vec{t}+\int_{Q}^{R} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d}+\int_{R}^{S} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d}+\int_{S}^{P} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d} \\ &=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{8}{3}-\frac{3}{2}-\frac{2}{3}=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
2010.explanation_html:

[latex]\begin{aligned} \text { So, } \oint_{C} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d} \vec{l}=& \int_{P}^{Q} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d} \vec{t}+\int_{Q}^{R} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d}+\int_{R}^{S} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d}+\int_{S}^{P} \vec{A} \cdot \vec{d} \\ &=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{8}{3}-\frac{3}{2}-\frac{2}{3}=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2010.text: The residues of a complex function [latex]X(z)=\frac{1-2z}{z(z-1)(z-2)}[/latex] at its poles are
2010.html: The residues of a complex function [latex]X(z)=\frac{1-2z}{z(z-1)(z-2)}[/latex] at its poles are
2010.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Analysis
2010.explanation_text: Given that, [latex] \begin{aligned} X(z)&=\frac{1-2 z}{z(z-1)(z-2)} \\ \text{Res}(0)&=\lim _{z \rightarrow 0} 1 \cdot\left[\frac{1-2 z}{(z-1)(z-2)}\right]=\frac{1}{2} \\ \text{Res}(1)&=\lim _{z \rightarrow 1} 1 \cdot\left[\frac{1-2 z}{z(z-2)}\right]=\frac{-1}{1(-1)}=1 \\ \text{Res}(2)&=\lim _{z \rightarrow 2} 1 \cdot\left[\frac{1-2 z}{z(z-1)}\right] \\ &=\frac{1-4}{2(2-1)}=\frac{-3}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2010.explanation_text: [latex]\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} f(t)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s F(s) [/latex] Given that, [latex] \begin{array}{l} \quad F(s)=\left[\frac{3 s+1}{s^{3}+4 s^{2}+(K-3) s}\right] \\ \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} f(t)=1 \\ \Rightarrow \lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s\left[\frac{3 s+1}{s^{3}+4 s^{2}+(K-3) s}\right]=1 \\ \Rightarrow \lim _{s \rightarrow 0}\left[\frac{3 s+1}{s^{2}+4 s+(K-3)}\right]=1 \\ \Rightarrow \frac{1}{K-3}=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad k-3=1 \\ \Rightarrow \quad K=4 \\ \end{array}[/latex]

At [latex]t\geq 0^{+}[/latex], the circuit ins-domain is shown below: [latex] [L = 15 mH, i(O+) = i(O^{-}) = 0.75 A][/latex] The above circuit can be rearranged as given below: Applying nodal analysis, [latex]\begin{aligned} &\frac{V(s)-\frac{1.5}{s}}{10}+\frac{V(s)}{10}+\frac{V(s)+15 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.75}{10+15 \times 10^{-3} s}=0 \\ &\frac{\frac{V(s)}{10}+\frac{V(s)}{10}+\frac{V(s)}{10+15 \times 10^{-3} s}}{10 s}-\frac{15 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.75}{10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}} \\ &=\frac{15}{10}\left[\frac{10+15 \times 10^{-3} s+5}{5\left(10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}\right]\\ & \text { V(s) }\left[\frac{10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}+5}{5\left(10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}\right] \\ =& 15\left[\frac{10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}-10 \mathrm{s} \times 10^{-3} \times 0.75}{10\left(10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}\right] \\ & \text { (1 }\left.+10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right) V(s)=\frac{\left(10+7.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}{2 s}\left[\frac{s+1000}{1000}\right] \\ &V(s) =\frac{10000+7.5 \mathrm{s}}{2000 \mathrm{s}} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{array}{l} V(s)=\frac{10000+7.5 s}{2 s(s+1000)} \\ =\frac{10000}{2 \times 1000 s}+\frac{\{10000+7.5(-1000)\}}{2(-1000)(s+1000)} \\ =\frac{5}{s}-\frac{1.25}{s+1000} \end{array}[/latex] Taking inverse Laplace transform, [latex] \begin{aligned} v(t)&=5-1.25 e^{-1000 t} \mathrm{V}\\ i(t) &=\frac{v(t)}{10} \\ &=0.5-0.125 e^{-1000 t} \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex] Method 2: [latex] \begin{aligned} i\left(0^{+}\right)&=\frac{0.75}{2}=0.375 \mathrm{A}\\ i(\infty) &=0.5 \mathrm{A} \\ i(t) &=i(\infty)-\left\{i(\infty)-i\left(0^{+}\right)\right\} e^{-R t L} \end{aligned}[/latex] where, R = equivalent resistance seen across L with current source opened [latex] \begin{aligned} R &=10+(10 \| 10)=15 \Omega \\ i(t) &=0.5-\{0.5-0.375\} e^{-15 t 15 \times 10^{-3}} \\ &=0.5-0.125 e^{-1000 t} \mathrm{A} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Method 1:

Applying nodal analysis,
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\frac{V(s)-\frac{1.5}{s}}{10}+\frac{V(s)}{10}+\frac{V(s)+15 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.75}{10+15 \times 10^{-3} s}=0 \\ &\frac{\frac{V(s)}{10}+\frac{V(s)}{10}+\frac{V(s)}{10+15 \times 10^{-3} s}}{10 s}-\frac{15 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.75}{10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}} \\ &=\frac{15}{10}\left[\frac{10+15 \times 10^{-3} s+5}{5\left(10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}\right]\\ & \text { V(s) }\left[\frac{10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}+5}{5\left(10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}\right] \\ =& 15\left[\frac{10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}-10 \mathrm{s} \times 10^{-3} \times 0.75}{10\left(10+15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}\right] \\ & \text { (1 }\left.+10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right) V(s)=\frac{\left(10+7.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{s}\right)}{2 s}\left[\frac{s+1000}{1000}\right] \\ &V(s) =\frac{10000+7.5 \mathrm{s}}{2000 \mathrm{s}} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2010.subject: Digital Circuits - Sequential Circuits

2010.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{array}{ll} \text { Initially, } & Q_{A}=Q_{B}=Q_{C}=0 \\ & D_{A}=Q_{B} \odot Q_{C}=1, D_{B}=Q_{A}=0 \\ & D_{C}=Q_{B}=0 \end{array}[/latex]
After one clock pulse,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} Q_{A}=1, Q_{B}=0, Q_{C}=0\\ D_{A}=Q_{B} \odot Q_{C}=1 \\ D_{B}=Q_{A}=1, D_{C}=Q_{B}=0 \end{array}[/latex]
After two clock pulse,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} Q_{A}=1, Q_{B}=1, Q_{C}=0\\ D_{A}=Q_{B} \odot Q_{C}=0 \\ D_{B}=Q_{A}=1, D_{C}=Q_{B}=1 \end{array}[/latex]
After three clock pulses,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} Q_{A}=0, Q_{B}=1, Q_{C}=1 \\ D_{A}=Q_{B} \odot Q_{C}=1 \\ D_{B}=Q_{A}=0, D_{C}=Q_{B}=1 \end{array}[/latex]
After four clock pulse,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} Q_{A}=1, Q_{B}=0, Q_{C}=1\\ D_{A}=Q_{B} \odot Q_{C}=0 \\ D_{B}=Q_{A}=1, D_{C}=Q_{B}=0 \end{array}[/latex]
After five clock pulse,
[latex] \begin{array}{l} Q_{A}=0, Q_{B}=1, Q_{C}=0\\ D_{A}=Q_{B} \odot Q_{C}=0 \\ D_{B}=Q_{A}=0, D_{C}=Q_{B}=1 \end{array}[/latex]
After six clock pulse,
[latex] Q_{A}=0, Q_{B}=0, Q_{C}=1[/latex]
Therefore, the count sequence observed at [latex]Q_{A}[/latex] is
[latex] 0110100 \ldots \ldots[/latex]

2010.explanation_text: [latex]\frac{d^{2} y(t)}{d t^{2}}+\frac{4 d y(t)}{d t}+3 y(t)=\frac{2 d x(t)}{d t}+4 x(t) [/latex] Taking Laplace transform on both sides (assuming zero initial conditions). [latex] \begin{aligned} s^{2} Y(s)+4 s Y(s)+3 Y(s)&=2 s X(s)+4 X(s) \\ \text{or }\quad \frac{Y(s)}{X(s)}&=\frac{2 s+4}{s^{2}+4 s+3} \\ &=\frac{2(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)} \end{aligned}[/latex] Given that [latex] \begin{aligned} x(t) &=e^{2 t} u(t) \\ x(s) &=\frac{1}{s+2} \\ Y(s) &=\frac{2(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+2)} \\ &=\frac{2}{(s+1)(s+3)} \\ &=\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{1}{s+3} \end{aligned}[/latex] Taking inverse Laplace transform on both sides. [latex] y(t)=(e^{-t}-e^{-3t})u(t)[/latex]

[latex]\frac{d^{2} y(t)}{d t^{2}}+\frac{4 d y(t)}{d t}+3 y(t)=\frac{2 d x(t)}{d t}+4 x(t) [/latex]
Taking Laplace transform on both sides (assuming
zero initial conditions).
[latex] \begin{aligned} s^{2} Y(s)+4 s Y(s)+3 Y(s)&=2 s X(s)+4 X(s) \\ \text{or }\quad \frac{Y(s)}{X(s)}&=\frac{2 s+4}{s^{2}+4 s+3} \\ &=\frac{2(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Given that
[latex] \begin{aligned} x(t) &=e^{2 t} u(t) \\ x(s) &=\frac{1}{s+2} \\ Y(s) &=\frac{2(s+2)}{(s+1)(s+3)(s+2)} \\ &=\frac{2}{(s+1)(s+3)} \\ &=\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{1}{s+3} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Taking inverse Laplace transform on both sides.
[latex] y(t)=(e^{-t}-e^{-3t})u(t)[/latex]

Load impedance,
[latex] Z_{L}=Z_{1}+Z_{2}=j 30+6[/latex]
Magnitude of reflection coefficient,
[latex]\begin{aligned} |\Gamma|&=\left|\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}\right|=\left|\frac{60+j 30-60}{60+j 30+60}\right|\\ &=\left|\frac{j 30}{120+j 30}\right|=\mid \frac{j 1}{4+j \mid} \\ &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{16+1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
VSWR on 60 \Omega line,

2010.html:
Consider a baseband binary PAM receiver shown below. The additive channel noise n(t) is with power spectral density [latex]S_{N}(f)=N_{0}/2=10^{-20}W/Hz[/latex]. The lowpass filter is ideal with unity gain and cut-off frequency 1 MHz. Let [latex]Y_{k}[/latex] represent the random variable y([latex]t_{k}[/latex]).
[latex]Y_{k}[/latex]= [latex]N_{k}[/latex] if transmitted bit [latex]b_{k}=0[/latex]
[latex]Y_{k}=a+ N_{k}[/latex] if transmitted bit [latex]b_{k}=1[/latex]
Where [latex]N_{k}[/latex] represents the noise sample value. The noise sample has a probability density function, [latex]P_{Nk}(n)=0.5\alpha e^{-\alpha |n|}[/latex] (This has mean zero and variance 2/[latex]\alpha ^{2}[/latex] ). Assume transmitted bits to be equiprobable and threshold z is set to a/2 = [latex]10^{-6}[/latex] V.

The probability of bit error is
2010.subject: Communication Systems - Random Processes
2010.explanation_text:
When a '1' is transmitted: [latex] \begin{array}{l} Y_{K}=a+N_{K} \\ \text { Threshold } Z=\frac{a}{2}=10^{-6} \\ a=2 \times 10^{-6} \end{array}[/latex] For error to occur, [latex]Y_{K} \lt 10^{-6} [/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} 2 \times 10^{-6}&+N_{K}\lt 10^{-6} \\ N_{K} & \lt -10^{-6} \\ P(0 / 1) &=\int_{-\infty}^{-10^{-6}} P_{N K}(n) d n \\ &=\int_{-\infty}^{-10^{-6}} 0.5 \alpha e^{\alpha n} d n \text { with } \alpha=10^{7} \\ P(0 / 1) &=0.5 e^{-10} \end{aligned}[/latex] When a '0' is transmitted: [latex] Y_{K}=N_{K} [/latex] For error to occur, [latex]Y_{K} \gt 10^{-6} [/latex] [latex] \therefore \; P(1 / 0)=\int_{10^{-6}}^{\infty} P_{N K}(n) d n=0.5 \times e^{-10} [/latex] since, both bits are equiprobable; [latex] P(0)=P(1)=\frac{1}{2} [/latex] the probability of bit error [latex] =P(1) \cdot P(0 / 1)+P(0) \cdot P(1 / 0) [/latex] [latex] =\frac{P(0 / 1)+P(1 / 0)}{2}=0.5 \times 
 e^{-10}[/latex]
2010.explanation_html:
When a '1' is transmitted:
[latex] \begin{array}{l} Y_{K}=a+N_{K} \\ \text { Threshold } Z=\frac{a}{2}=10^{-6} \\ a=2 \times 10^{-6} \end{array}[/latex]
For error to occur, [latex]Y_{K} \lt 10^{-6} [/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} 2 \times 10^{-6}&+N_{K}\lt 10^{-6} \\ N_{K} & \lt -10^{-6} \\ P(0 / 1) &=\int_{-\infty}^{-10^{-6}} P_{N K}(n) d n \\ &=\int_{-\infty}^{-10^{-6}} 0.5 \alpha e^{\alpha n} d n \text { with } \alpha=10^{7} \\ P(0 / 1) &=0.5 e^{-10} \end{aligned}[/latex]
When a '0' is transmitted:
[latex] Y_{K}=N_{K} [/latex]
For error to occur, [latex]Y_{K} \gt 10^{-6} [/latex]
[latex] \therefore \; P(1 / 0)=\int_{10^{-6}}^{\infty} P_{N K}(n) d n=0.5 \times e^{-10} [/latex]
since, both bits are equiprobable;
[latex] P(0)=P(1)=\frac{1}{2} [/latex]
the probability of bit error
[latex] =P(1) \cdot P(0 / 1)+P(0) \cdot P(1 / 0) [/latex]
[latex] =\frac{P(0 / 1)+P(1 / 0)}{2}=0.5 \times e^{-10}[/latex]

2009.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} A&=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\0 & 1\end{array}\right] \\ B&=\left[\begin{array}{l}p \\q\end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex] For controllabil itycondition is [latex] \begin{aligned} Q_{C}&=\left[B, A B, \ldots A^{n-1} B\right] \neq 0\\ A \cdot B&=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\0 & 1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}p \\q\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}p+0 \\0+q\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}p \\q\end{array}\right]\\ \text{So}\quad Q_{c}&=\left[\begin{array}{ll}p & p \\ q & q\end{array}\right]=0 \end{aligned}[/latex] So, the system is uncontrollable for all values of p and q
2009.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} A&=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\0 & 1\end{array}\right] \\ B&=\left[\begin{array}{l}p \\q\end{array}\right] \end{aligned}[/latex]
For controllabil itycondition is
[latex] \begin{aligned} Q_{C}&=\left[B, A B, \ldots A^{n-1} B\right] \neq 0\\ A \cdot B&=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\0 & 1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}p \\q\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}p+0 \\0+q\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}p \\q\end{array}\right]\\ \text{So}\quad Q_{c}&=\left[\begin{array}{ll}p & p \\ q & q\end{array}\right]=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, the system is uncontrollable for all values of p and q

2009.text: Consider two independent random variables X and Y with identical distributions. The variables X and Y take values 0, 1 and 2 with probabilities [latex]\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}\;  and \; \frac{1}{4}[/latex] respectively. What is the conditional probability P(X+Y=2|X-Y=0)?
2009.html: Consider two independent random variables X and Y with identical distributions. The variables X and Y take values 0, 1 and 2 with probabilities [latex]\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}\; and \; \frac{1}{4}[/latex] respectively. What is the conditional probability P(X+Y=2|X-Y=0)?
2009.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
2009.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{array}{c} P(A \mid B)=\frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \\ P(X+Y=2 \mid X-Y=0) \\ =\frac{P(X+Y=2, X-Y=0)}{P(X-Y=0)} \\ P(X-Y=0)=P(X=0, Y=0)\\ +P(X=1, Y=1)+P(X=2, Y=2) \\ =P(X=0) \cdot P(Y=0)+P(X=1) \cdot P(Y=1) \\ +P(X=2) \cdot P(Y=2) \\ =\frac{3}{8} \\ P(X+Y=2, X-Y=0)=P(X=1, Y=1) \\ =P(X=1) \cdot P(Y=1) \\ =\frac{1}{16} \\ \therefore \quad P(X+Y=2 \mid X-Y=0)=-\frac{1}{16} \times \frac{8}{3}=\frac{1}{6} \end{array}[/latex]
2009.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{array}{c} P(A \mid B)=\frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \\ P(X+Y=2 \mid X-Y=0) \\ =\frac{P(X+Y=2, X-Y=0)}{P(X-Y=0)} \\ P(X-Y=0)=P(X=0, Y=0)\\ +P(X=1, Y=1)+P(X=2, Y=2) \\ =P(X=0) \cdot P(Y=0)+P(X=1) \cdot P(Y=1) \\ +P(X=2) \cdot P(Y=2) \\ =\frac{3}{8} \\ P(X+Y=2, X-Y=0)=P(X=1, Y=1) \\ =P(X=1) \cdot P(Y=1) \\ =\frac{1}{16} \\ \therefore \quad P(X+Y=2 \mid X-Y=0)=-\frac{1}{16} \times \frac{8}{3}=\frac{1}{6} \end{array}[/latex]

2009.text:
The Taylor series expansion of  [latex]\frac{sin x}{x-\pi }[/latex] at x = [latex]\pi[/latex]
 is given by
2009.html: The Taylor series expansion of [latex]\frac{sin x}{x-\pi }[/latex] at x = [latex]\pi[/latex] is given by
2009.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2009.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)=f(\pi) &+\frac{x-\pi}{1 !} \cdot f^{\prime}(\pi)+\frac{(x-\pi)^{2}}{2 !} f^{\prime \prime}(\pi) \ldots \\ \text { Now } f(\pi) &=\lim _{x \rightarrow \pi} \frac{\sin x}{x-\pi} \\ &=\lim _{x \rightarrow \pi} \frac{\cos x}{1}=-1 \\ f^{\prime}(\pi) &=0 \\ f^{\prime \prime}(\pi) &=-1 / 6 \end{aligned}[/latex] So the expansion is [latex] \begin{aligned} f(x)&=-1+(-1 / 6)(x-\pi)^{2}+\ldots \\ f(x)&=-1-\frac{(x-\pi)^{2}}{3 !} \cdot+\ldots \end{aligned}[/latex]
2009.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)=f(\pi) &+\frac{x-\pi}{1 !} \cdot f^{\prime}(\pi)+\frac{(x-\pi)^{2}}{2 !} f^{\prime \prime}(\pi) \ldots \\ \text { Now } f(\pi) &=\lim _{x \rightarrow \pi} \frac{\sin x}{x-\pi} \\ &=\lim _{x \rightarrow \pi} \frac{\cos x}{1}=-1 \\ f^{\prime}(\pi) &=0 \\ f^{\prime \prime}(\pi) &=-1 / 6 \end{aligned}[/latex]
So the expansion is
[latex] \begin{aligned} f(x)&=-1+(-1 / 6)(x-\pi)^{2}+\ldots \\ f(x)&=-1-\frac{(x-\pi)^{2}}{3 !} \cdot+\ldots \end{aligned}[/latex]

2009.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} 1+G(s) H(s) &=0 \\ 1+\frac{K\left(s^{2}-2 s+2\right)}{s^{2}+2 s+2} &=0 \\ k &=-\frac{s^{2}+2 s+2}{s^{2}-2 s+2} \\ \text{put }\quad \frac{\partial K}{\partial s}&=0\text{ we have}\\ \left(s^{2}-2 s+2\right)(s+1) &-\left(s^{2}+2 s+2\right) \\ (s-1) =0 \\ 2 s^{2}-4 s^{2}+4 &=0 \\ 2 s^{2} &=+4 \\ s &=\pm \sqrt{2} \\ \text{Angle of departure is}\\ \phi_{D}=\phi\\ \text { where } &=\Sigma \phi_{2}-\Sigma \phi_{p} \\ &=225^{\circ} \\ \phi_{D} &=\pm 225^{\circ} \end{aligned} \\ \text{No option is matching.}[/latex]

2009.text:
An LTI system having transfer function [latex]\frac{s^{2}+1}{s^{2}+2s+1}[/latex]
 and input [latex]x(t) = sin(t+1)[/latex] is in steady state. The output is sampled at a rate [latex]\omega_{s}[/latex]  rad/s to obtain the final output {y(k)}. Which of the following is true ?
2009.html: An LTI system having transfer function [latex]\frac{s^{2}+1}{s^{2}+2s+1}[/latex] and input [latex]x(t) = sin(t+1)[/latex] is in steady state. The output is sampled at a rate [latex]\omega_{s}[/latex] rad/s to obtain the final output {y(k)}. Which of the following is true ?
2009.subject: Signals and Systems - Sampling
2009.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} x(t) &=\sin (t+1) \\ \omega  &=1 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \\ X(s) &=\frac{\omega }{(\omega )^{2}+s^{2}} \cdot e^{s}=\frac{1}{1^{2}+s^{2}} \theta^{s}=\frac{e^{s}}{s^{2}+1} \\ H(s) &=\frac{Y(s)}{X(s)} \\ Y(s) &=H(s) X(s)\\ Y(s)&=\frac{s^{2}+1}{s^{2}+2 s+1} \times \frac{e^{s}}{s^{2}+1}=\frac{e^{s}}{s^{2}+2 s+1}\\ Y(s)&=\frac{e^{s}}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ y(t) &=(t+1) e^{(t+1)} \\ y(\infty) &=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \frac{s e^{s}}{(s+1)^{2}}=0 \end{aligned}[/latex] So, at steady state y remains zero for all sampling frequencies [latex] \omega_{S}[/latex]
2009.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x(t) &=\sin (t+1) \\ \omega &=1 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} \\ X(s) &=\frac{\omega }{(\omega )^{2}+s^{2}} \cdot e^{s}=\frac{1}{1^{2}+s^{2}} \theta^{s}=\frac{e^{s}}{s^{2}+1} \\ H(s) &=\frac{Y(s)}{X(s)} \\ Y(s) &=H(s) X(s)\\ Y(s)&=\frac{s^{2}+1}{s^{2}+2 s+1} \times \frac{e^{s}}{s^{2}+1}=\frac{e^{s}}{s^{2}+2 s+1}\\ Y(s)&=\frac{e^{s}}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ y(t) &=(t+1) e^{(t+1)} \\ y(\infty) &=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} s Y(s)=\lim _{s \rightarrow 0} \frac{s e^{s}}{(s+1)^{2}}=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, at steady state y remains zero for all sampling frequencies [latex] \omega_{S}[/latex]

2009.explanation_text: Signal power, [latex] \begin{aligned} S &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} f_{X}(x) d x=\int_{-5}^{5} \frac{1}{10} x^{2} d x=\frac{25}{3} \\ S Q N R &=43.5 \mathrm{dB} \text { (or) } 10^{(4.35)} \\ N_{O} &=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{12}=\frac{S}{\mathrm{SQNR}} \\ \text{So},\quad \Delta &=\sqrt{\frac{12(S)}{\mathrm{SQNR}}}=\sqrt{\frac{12 \times 25}{3\left(10^{4.35}\right)}}=0.0668 \mathrm{V} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Hence, [latex] P\left(\Delta_{1}\right)=P\left(\Delta_{2}\right)=0.50[/latex] So, the quantization noise power will be [latex] \begin{aligned} N_{0} &=\frac{\Delta_{1}^{2}}{12} P\left(\Delta_{1}\right)+\frac{\Delta_{2}^{2}}{12} P\left(\Delta_{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{24}\left(\Delta_{1}^{2}+\Delta_{2}^{2}\right)=\frac{125}{24 \times 10000}=\frac{1}{1920} \end{aligned}[/latex] Signal power, [latex] \begin{aligned} S &=\frac{25}{3} \\ S Q N R &=\frac{S}{N_{0}}=\frac{1920 \times 25}{3}=16000 \end{aligned}[/latex] In decilogs, [latex] [\mathrm{SQNR}]=10 \log _{10}(\mathrm{SONR})=42 \mathrm{dB}[/latex]

Signal power,
